events.title: Elon Musk spends $366m to bolster Republican Party in US midterm elections
events.summary: The barrage of spending comes as Republicans fight to overcome Trump’s declining popularity and cost of living concerns. Elon Musk, the trillionaire tech mogul and backer of far-right causes , has reportedly spent $366m since last year to buoy the Republican Party in the United States midterm elections. The New York Times first reported on Monday that Musk has spent $276m since July alone, including $158m for a super PAC focused on Republican Senate candidates, making him the largest single donor this year. list 1 of 3 Trump gives top US science awards to Elon Musk and other tech executives list 2 of 3 US judge rules Trump administration’s use of voter data unlawful list 3 of 3 Is Trump signalling a return to war with Iran after the midterms? Musk is considered a close ally of President Donald Trump , the leader of the Republican Party, and was a special government adviser to the White House last year. Musk’s political action committee, America PAC, has confirmed the spending totals. In a statement to The New York Times, a spokesperson framed the record amount as necessary to defend Congress from a Democratic takeover during the midterm races. “These robust investments have allowed the GOP apparatus to get its message out so Republicans can have a fighting chance to defy history,” America PAC spokesman Andrew Romeo told the Times. The barrage of spending by Musk comes as Republican candidates are fighting to overcome Trump’s low popularity and rising concerns about the cost of living among US voters. Democrats are hoping to capitalise on voter dissatisfaction with Trump’s tenure to seize control of Congress, where Republicans currently hold majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate. The influence of wealthy donors and PACs has long been the subject of criticism. Opponents argue that such spending distorts US politics in favour of powerful interests . Musk became the world’s first trillionaire in June, when his aerospace company SpaceX made its initial public offering (IPO) on the Nasdaq stock exchange. The tech entrepreneur had previously said that he planned to step back from his involvement in US politics, stating in May that he had “done enough” and did not have plans for large spending efforts. Still, Musk has leveraged his tech holdings and wealth to support right-wing groups around the world. Last year, for instance, politicians in Germany accused Musk of trying to meddle in the national election. Musk has been a vocal backer of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, which has been accused of adopting a discriminatory stance on immigration and other issues. Voters in the US will head to the polls on November 3 to cast their ballots in the midterms, which will decide key state and local races, as well as congressional majorities. The Republican Party is considered to have a sizeable financial advantage over the Democrats ahead of the race, with heavy spending from groups such as MAGA Inc, a pro-Trump super PAC named for the president’s “Make America Great Again” movement. As of August, MAGA Inc reportedly had $416m in its coffers. The tracking site AdImpact found that it had spent $22m over the past month alone on the tight race unfolding for the open Senate seat in Texas. Trump has also increased his campaign activities, hosting a string of rallies in the final weeks before the election to help Republicans push their message . But Democrats appear confident that the Republicans’ spending advantage will not be enough to counter the effects of growing dissatisfaction with Trump. “Republicans are hoping to buy these elections, injecting tens of millions into races to try and outrun their unpopular candidates, unpopular president and unpopular economy,” said Lauren French, a spokesperson for Democrats’ Senate Majority PAC.

events.title: How to make economy feel like an upgrade, according to a travel expert who's spent 3,500 hours in premium cabins
events.summary: Flight expert Zach Griff shares how to bring the luxuries of first and business class to the economy cabin. Courtesy of Zach Griff Flying economy can feel crowded, cramped, and generally unpleasant. But it doesn't have to be. Here's how to give yourself an upgrade when you're stuck in economy. Economy seats may be smaller than those in upgraded classes, but that doesn't mean you have to be cramped between passengers. Economy tickets may not include a meal, but that doesn't mean you can't have a fine-dining experience. The economy cabin will never be as comfortable as first class , but that doesn't mean you can't make the most of it. Enter Zach Griff, travel expert and author of the travel newsletter From the Tray Table . Griff estimates he's spent 3,500 hours flying more than 1.8 million miles in business and first-class cabins . He flies 150,000 miles a year on average, including roughly 50,000 in economy. With so much experience in premium cabins , Griff has a few tips that make his economy flights feel like an upgrade. Start by booking a flight during an unpopular travel time. Joey Hadden/Business Insider One of the big perks of premium cabins is having more personal space. If you can avoid flying in a crowded economy cabin, you may be more likely to end up with an empty seat next to you, which can feel like an upgrade, Griff told Business Insider. According to Griff, the earliest and latest departures of the day tend to have the most empty seats. Aim for a Saturday or midweek booking, he added. Try to find a flight with two-seater rows. Chris Cooper/Bloomberg via Getty Images Griff said sitting in a row without a middle seat can make economy feel like an upgrade, too. There are rows like this on some wide-body planes, which have two aisles and are typically used for long-distance travel. So while you're searching for flights for your next international trip, take a look at the seat map before you book. Keep checking for open seats until boarding and move to the row with the most space. Joey Hadden/Business Insider When Griff flies economy, he starts checking the seat map for his trip two days before departure to see how full it is. "If it's looking like maybe another row has more space, I'd always move to that row to see if that may end up open," he said. "Monitor the seat map until the minute before boarding starts and move around to optimize your chances of finding an empty seat." You may even end up with your own row. Treat yourself to a nice meal. Courtesy of Zach Griff In many cases, business and first-class tickets come with the added perk of an in-flight meal. If you're in economy, Griff recommends bringing your own dish or getting some takeout on your way to the gate. "Treat yourself to something a little bit nicer because you're sitting in economy," he added. Make sure you're not missing out on any perks from airline status or credit cards. Lino Mirgeler/picture alliance via Getty Images Even if you're flying economy, having a credit card or elite status with the airline may make you eligible for free checked bags, earlier boarding, or possibly better seats, Griff said. Finally, pack your own amenities to stay comfortable. Courtesy of Zach Griff To make flying economy more comfortable, dress in athleisure and pack a sleep mask and noise-canceling headphones, Griff said. If you have a small massage gun, toss that in your carry-on, too, he added. With your mask on, earbuds in, a full belly, and an empty seat next to you, you may feel like you're on the other side of the cabin curtain. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Renewed mineral sands mine bid 'a turd in glitter', resident says
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Victorian government 'manipulating' planning laws to win critical minerals race, expert says Kane Busch and his family have been farming vegetables in the Lindenow Valley for 100 years. ( ABC Rural: Fiona Broom ) The Victorian government is assessing a mineral sands mine project it has already rejected. The global critical minerals race is behind the renewed attempt to green light the project, experts argue. The company behind the proposal says claims the project has not been altered since its previous rejection are "misleading and false". The Victorian government is "manipulating" its own planning system to fast track approval for a mining project it already rejected, a leading planning expert claims. The Fingerboards Mineral Sands Project proposed for eastern Victoria was knocked back by the government in 2021, because it would "pose a significant risk to the environment and valuable horticulture industry". But the government is now considering what it calls a "new and modified" bid to get the project off the ground, a description that RMIT emeritus professor of planning and environment Michael Buxton said was a "blatant deception". "The project is not a different project and it's not substantially altered," he said. Michael Buxton worked at the Victorian planning department for more than a decade. ( ABC News: Sean Warren ) Nearby residents who have spent years fighting the mine have a different description of the latest proposal. The company behind the project, Gippsland Critical Minerals (GCM), rejected these claims and said its new bid for approval included significant changes. GCM said the site was a rich source of a range of minerals, which had been deemed critical by the Australian government. Miners have been exploring the Lindenow Valley, 270 kilometres east of Melbourne, for mineral sands since the 1970s. Irrigated areas of the Lindenow flats. ( ABC Rural: Emma Field ) Between 2015 and 2023, global demand doubled for mineral sands, which contain concentrated amounts of heavy minerals such as rare-earth elements. Organisations from mining giants such as Rio Tinto to junior mining companies have had a stake in the region, but no project has ever been considered commercially or environmentally viable. After almost a decade of review, in November 2021 the Victorian government rejected a mining project proposed by Kalbar Resources, later Kalbar Operations. In 2023, Kalbar was renamed to Gippsland Critical Minerals (GCM) and submitted a "rescoped" proposal. Gippsland Critical Minerals has dug a test pit on its Fingerboards mineral sands site. ( ABC Rural: Fiona Broom ) Dr Buxton, who has been involved in planning for 50 years, including at the Environment Protection Authority and state planning department, said the government failed to follow proper process by accepting the Fingerboards project for a second review. "The minister could have just refused to consider this application — and in my view, should have," he said. Australia's strategic focus on critical minerals for economic and national security reasons was behind the renewed push for the East Gippsland mineral sands mine, he said. "This has provided companies with the opportunity to argue that it's a critical resource." Under the state government's critical minerals road map launched in December 2024, which outlines efforts to build a globally competitive critical minerals sector, eight mines are at various stages of approval. University of Sydney professor of global governance Susan Park said she was "not surprised at all" that rejected minerals projects were getting a second look. Dr Park said trade and security agreements between Australia and allies such as the United States were driving state and federal support for mining projects. The proposed Fingerboards mine site, 25 kilometres west of Bairnsdale. ( Supplied: Gippsland Critical Minerals ) In February, the Australian government gave the Fingerboards proposal Major Project Status, which gives "strategically significant projects" extra support to navigate regulatory approvals. GCM bills the project as a major source of "ex-China production" of the rare-earth oxides dysprosium and terbium, elements on Australia's critical minerals list. China controls almost all of the world's production and rare-earth refining. Terbium and dysprosium oxides, used in renewable energy and military technologies, are almost completely supplied by China. The Lindenow Valley is a highly fertile region known for its leafy salad vegetables, brassicas and sweet corn. Up to 2,000 workers harvest about 200,000 tonnes of food every year.

events.title: Losing your job after age 50 could derail your career
events.summary: Thomas Heep (left), Steven Fielding (center), and Jon McCarty (right) struggled to find work after losing their jobs later in life. Thomas Heep (left), Steven Fielding (center), and Jon McCarty (right) Some Americans who lose their jobs after age 50 spend years struggling to find comparable work. In September, the average unemployment duration for workers ages 55 to 64 was over eight months. Some older job seekers suspect age discrimination is hurting their chances of finding work. Cathy Valentine lost her job as a transformation lead in 2023. After three years struggling to find a comparable full-time job, the 61-year-old is now a prep cook at a cafe. She said she earns about an eighth of her previous salary. "It just feels like I tried to do everything right and I still am stuck," said Valentine, who lives in Florida. Some older workers who lose their jobs can afford to retire, while others find a comparable role fairly quickly. But those who don't risk getting stuck in a job search that drags on for months or even years — and is getting longer. On some metrics, older Americans are doing just fine in the job market . As of September, older workers had lower unemployment rates than younger workers, and when they were jobless, the median length of that unemployment was shorter. But those figures obscure a worse trend for older job seekers . While half of 55 to 64-year-olds were jobless for a relatively low three months, the group's average unemployment duration was more than eight months in September. That means some older workers have been unemployed for so long that they're pulling the average way up. The gap between the average and median has widened in recent months, suggesting the longest job searches may be growing even longer. In September, about 173,000 unemployed Americans ages 55 to 64 had been out of work for at least six months, and some are facing far longer stretches of unemployment. A Bureau of Labor Statistics analysis found that only 57% of workers ages 55 to 64 who lost their long-held jobs any time between 2023 and 2025 had found new jobs as of January 2026. By contrast, 73% of workers ages 25 to 54 who lost long-held jobs in that period had found new work. Some older workers may have taken their job loss as a sign they should retire. But for others, it marked the beginning of an uphill battle to find another job. The struggle to get hired after 50 As their searches drag on for months or years, older job seekers like Valentine often blame age discrimination for at least part of their struggles. Thomas Heep, a Denver resident in his 60s, has been searching for full-time work since losing his operations manager role in April 2025. He's struggled to pay his bills and filed for bankruptcy earlier this year. Heep suspects some employers may favor younger job seekers over someone his age because they worry he won't remain in the workforce much longer. "Even if a company loves my résumé, skill set, and work history, they're going to look at my age and go: How long is he going to stay? He's close to retirement age. It's too risky." he said. Thomas Heep has struggled to find full-time work since losing his job last year. Thomas Heep Other older workers suspect their salary expectations may be working against them. A former Big Tech employee in her early 60s who lost her job last year said she worries her years of experience may put her at a disadvantage compared with younger candidates willing to accept lower pay. events.title: IonQ to acquire cybersecurity firm Elisity in an all-stock deal for up to $1.3 billion
events.summary: Quantum computing platform IonQ said it will acquire cybersecurity company Elisity in an all-stock deal for up to $1.3 billion, including up to $150 million in performance-based earnouts. The combined entity will give IonQ expanded tools to detect and defend against AI-driven cyberattacks. IonQ's shares were down about 9% Monday. Quantum computing platform IonQ said on Monday it will acquire cybersecurity company Elisity in an all-stock deal worth up to $1.3 billion, including up to $150 million in performance-based earnouts. The move is designed to defend against and uncover attackers targeting generative artificial intelligence large-language models and AI agents, and to protect against emerging quantum threats, the companies said in a press release . CEO Niccolo de Masi told CNBC's Morgan Brennan on Monday that the addition of Elisity's platform will help bolster his company's quantum security strategy. "This means that we can protect not only critical infrastructure — we believe better than anyone in the world — but of course the Fortune 500," de Masi said. The all-stock deal is expected to close in the fourth quarter, subject to regulatory approval, and would expand the quantum-computing company's cybersecurity portfolio. IonQ shares fell more than 9% in afternoon trading. Other quantum computing stocks, including Rigetti Computing and D-Wave Quantum , also traded lower. Elisity will retain its current leadership, including CEO James Winebrenner. AI's quiet safety gatekeepers are stepping into the spotlight Microsoft's Nadella says AI needs an 'emergency brake' that humans control Nvidia GPUs are everywhere. Here are the ways companies are accessing them Hollywood takes on Zuckerberg, Musk and Altman amid widespread anxiety over AI IonQ's stock has surged in recent months amid a buying spree. Most recently, the company bought semiconductor maker SkyWater Technology for $1.8 billion in July. In the past year and a half, IonQ has acquired several quantum companies, most notably U.K.-based quantum computing startup Oxford Ionics . The deal follows two June executive orders from President Donald Trump aimed at building a quantum computer for scientific research by 2028 and protecting government systems from cyber threats. IonQ said in the release that the orders underscored the urgency of preparing for quantum computing threats. De Masi told CNBC on Monday that the need for quantum-level security integration into government and business as outlined in the executive order will become all-important as "Q-Day" — the era where quantum computers can break today's standard encryption software — draws closer. "Lab leaks" from frontier AI companies such as OpenAI 's high-profile Hugging Face hack are just the beginning compared to cyber capabilities a year from now, de Masi said. "Our technologies help you today. They also set you up, of course, as well as you can today, for an era where the bad guys will eventually get quantum computers. They will eventually be able to marry them, I fear, with LLMs, and so the world that we're in today is already dangerous," De Masi told CNBC, adding that LLM's "could do even more dastardly things." "Frankly, people are not ready," he said.

events.title: NATO says will do ‘anything and everything’ if alliance is attacked
events.summary: NATO commander issues warning as European officials suggest potential Russian attacks. NATO’s top commander has warned that his forces would destroy “anything and everything” if someone was “foolish enough” to attack the alliance, as European concerns have mounted over a potential Russian attack on its territory amid the war in Ukraine. “We will block the initial attack. If the attack persists, we will blunt it and prevent any enemy advance. And if required, we will break the enemy’s forces and the operational war-fighting system arrayed against us,” US Air Force General Alexus Grynkewich told the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday, without mentioning Russia by name. list 1 of 3 ‘Energy ceasefire’: What’s behind Trump’s love-hate ties to Russian oil? list 2 of 3 Ukraine’s Zelenskyy accuses Russia of violating Trump’s ‘energy ceasefire’ list 3 of 3 From a ‘dangerous competitor’ to an unknown: Who could replace Zelenskyy? Grynkewich stressed that NATO is a defensive alliance and that he does not believe that a conflict is imminent or inevitable. The most effective way to preserve peace is to prepare for war and to maintain open lines of communication to “resolve misunderstandings”, he added. European governments have accused Moscow of stepping up a campaign of sabotage, drone incursions and cyberattacks against them, while Russia warned last month it could use nuclear weapons if NATO attempted to cut off its Baltic Kaliningrad exclave where it has a major military outpost. NATO’s 10-year strategy, created in 2022, described Russia as the alliance’s most significant security threat. “We will, in short, ensure any attack, against any ally, proves utterly futile,” Grynkewich said. Attacking anything that ‘supports, sustains and controls that force’ Grynkewich added that NATO’s response would not be limited to forces involved in an initial attack. “Should the adversary choose to press the attack or commit his reserves, we will break the warfighting system engaged against us,” he said. “This includes not just the attacking force itself, but anything and everything that supports, sustains and controls that force.” Russian President Vladimir Putin said this month that Russia had no plans to attack any European country and wanted to coexist peacefully. Such declarations have not reassured European leaders, who cite similar statements by Russia before its 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Moscow has also repeatedly denied involvement in sabotage and other hybrid operations. Grynkewich said he had decided to talk publicly about NATO’s plans because recent acts of sabotage and arson had made people around the alliance nervous. “What I want to do is assure the one billion citizens of our alliance that we’ve got this. We know what we need to do. We know how we would do it,” he said. Grynkewich sought to downplay concerns about Washington’s commitment to the alliance , citing President Donald Trump’s reception at a NATO summit in Ankara in July. “I was in the room and I felt the love,” he said.

events.title: One chart shows white-collar biz is thriving even as jobs dry up
events.summary: Employment in white-collar sectors has dipped, while output is surging. Maskot/Getty Images Employment has dropped in white-collar sectors, while output has continued to surge. AI and economic uncertainty are two likely reasons for the sluggish white-collar job market. Still, how productive AI makes companies remains a question. The white-collar sector is doing more with less. While the number of total jobs has slid in industries like finance, tech, and professional services, output has been on a tear. Gad Levanon, the chief economist at the Burning Glass Institute, examined how employment in white-collar-heavy sectors compares with real gross domestic product . He wrote in a Substack article that employment in finance, insurance, information, and professional and business services is collectively down roughly 2% since the end of 2022, while real output for these sectors has soared by 16%. The ongoing slow decline in employment for this group goes against historical patterns and highlights how workers and job seekers are facing a largely frozen, low-hire, low-fire job market . "A growing share of the work businesses used to get done by consultants, contractors, call centers and their own back-office staff is now delivered by software, cloud and IT firms, which produce far more per worker and add almost no staff," Levanon told Business Insider. "That is why the sector's output keeps rising while its hiring has stopped." The divergence also risks breaking the traditional link between economic growth and rising fortunes for everyday Americans. "Even a strong, continual growth in GDP may not translate into jobs for people, may not translate into a higher quality of life for people as well," said Cory Stahle, an economist at the Indeed Hiring Lab. People looking in these kinds of sectors may be having a challenging time. "It's important to remember for these job seekers that a career is not necessarily built over the course of two or three years," Stahle said. "It's usually built over the course of two or three decades. So what the pattern is now could easily shift a couple of years from now. So it's important to be reactive but not overreact to what we're seeing in the data, either." Have you been job searching in these white-collar sectors? Have you had to make a career pivot? Reach out to this reporter to share what that's been like at mhoff@businessinsider.com . Levanon said on Substack that there's demand in these white-collar fields, but firms can meet it with fewer workers. Part of that could be due to employers shifting their priorities toward leveraging AI . Levanon said "the back-office and junior tasks" that AI performs best at are concentrated in the white-collar sectors he looked at. Dante DeAntonio, senior director at Moody's Analytics, previously told Business Insider that the lack of hiring in white-collar fields is largely due to uncertainty around economic policy and AI. Other job market experts have noted that in Big Tech, employers pulled back after the pandemic-era hiring surge. The job market's woes can be especially difficult for people who lack years of experience. "Firms, I think, are certainly diving in with both feet, trying to find ways to gain efficiency from AI," DeAntonio said. "And certainly the first domino to fall is likely to be a pullback in hiring amongst younger workers, new college grads, positions where firms think they might be able to get some uptick from AI, and some sort of replacement value from AI." Whether companies are actually more productive because they're incorporating AI tools remains a question. Eric Kutcher, a senior partner and chair of McKinsey North America, recently said that there are individual productivity increases , rather than institutional-level gains. "You have people that are getting more productive as individuals, but they're just changing some of the work that they're doing," he said. Bureau of Labor Statistics data showed general labor productivity has increased, but not at a wildly accelerated clip. "We have seen that things have slowed down in the last few years, but output per worker and productivity was climbing even before we saw ChatGPT and AI starting to come onto the scene," Stahle said. "To me, that says that AI is part of the story here, but not the complete story. This is part of a longer-term trend." Have you been job searching in these white-collar sectors? events.title: Jeremy Strong argued with Aaron Sorkin in-character as Mark Zuckerberg over this one line in 'The Social Reckoning'
events.summary: Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in "The Social Reckoning." Sony Jeremy Strong loves going Method, talking and acting like his character even when cameras aren't rolling. So "Social Reckoning" director Aaron Sorkin wasn't surprised Strong acted like Mark Zuckerberg on set. He was surprised, though, that Strong became such a big Zuck defender. Jeremy Strong is known for his intense Method acting on set. But even "The Social Reckoning" director Aaron Sorkin was surprised by how all-in Strong went in embodying Mark Zuckerberg . Sorkin, who had worked with the acclaimed actor on two of his previous directing efforts, "Molly's Game" and "The Trial of the Chicago 7," wasn't shocked when Strong showed up on " The Social Reckoning " set speaking and acting like the Facebook founder. But Sorkin never imagined Strong would end up becoming a staunch Zuckerberg defender in the process. "I knew he's a very immersive actor," Sorkin told Business Insider . "I never heard him use his own voice. He only spoke as Mark, he only behaved as Mark. But I didn't expect that he was going to be a constant defender of Mark. Not just on the set, but the emails I would get at night at the hotel." Sorkin said this continued even in post-production, when Strong, still in-character as Zuckerberg, argued with his director over a line in the movie. "The Social Reckoning" tells the story of former Facebook employee turned whistleblower Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison), who leaked hundreds of thousands of documents to Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz (Jeremy Allen-White) that revealed Facebook's algorithm was designed to spread inflammatory content and encouraged extremism, at the expense of users' safety and mental health. Jeremy Strong and Aaron Sorkin. Sean Zanni/Getty Images Strong-as-Zuckerberg wrote Sorkin about a scene in which his character has been debating Bill Burr's character Charlie, a fictionalized former Facebook investor, about free speech and fact-checking advertisements. "He ends the debate by saying, 'It's a business, Charlie. You know why we don't fact-check ads? Because we don't have to. Are you new?'" Sorkin recalled. "Jeremy felt that it was just about money. That Mark was saying this is a business, it's about money, and that's why we do it," Sorkin continued. "But that was not the argument that Mark had been making for the entire movie, which is that it's a free speech thing. That Facebook is the town square. So my feeling was Mark isn't saying it's about the money, Mark actually, in that moment, is making the same argument Frances is making at the end, which is, talk to the people who make the laws. I'm not your guy, talk to Congress . Well, that line is in the movie, so I won the argument."  Despite the challenges, Sorkin said he wouldn't change anything about how Strong goes about his job. And it doesn't sound like Strong has plans to. "If some people feel that I'm taking it too seriously, or it changes the molecules in the room in a way that makes something uncomfortable, I guess that's something that I don't feel that I need to apologize for," Strong said in a recent interview with The New Yorker about his acting style. "The Social Reckoning" is in theaters now. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Billions in the bin as economy struggles with true cost of food waste
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Food waste is costing Australian businesses and the economy billions Topic: Food and Beverage Processing Industry Karl Riseborough was shocked when he realised how much food was wasted at his brewery each week. ( ABC News: Fletcher Yeung ) Australia wastes about 7.6 million tonnes of food each year, costing the economy more than $36 billion. Less than a quarter of businesses regularly inspect their food waste, and operational methods mean it can go unnoticed. The federal government has committed to halving food waste by 2030, but some experts are concerned about progress. When Karl Riseborough realised how much food went to waste each week at his Sydney pub and brewery, he was shocked. Grain left over from the beer-making process was thrown out, as well as food waste from the kitchen. What surprised him most was "the volume" of waste on top of the spent grain. "The food scraps coming back, the plate waste, the kitchen prep waste … you don't really notice when it was all going straight into the bin," Mr Riseborough said. Food waste expert Belinda Chellingworth says many traders have no idea how much waste they are generating, or how much it is affecting their bottom line. A pile of landfill at the Reedy Creek rubbish tip on the Gold Coast. ( ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale ) Every year about 7.6 million tonnes of food is wasted in Australia at a cost of more than $36 billion to the economy . Of that wasted food, 70 per cent is edible and there are critical knock-on effects for landfill management, food security and the climate. With the support of Ms Chellingworth, who happily calls herself a "garbologist", Mr Riseborough has stopped throwing away 50 kilograms of spent grain from each batch of beer he brews. Karl Riseborough is saving thousands a year after some simple changes. ( ABC News: Fletcher Yeung ) "So now I have regular users who come and collect it once I've brewed and use it for the benefit of their gardens or their animals," Riseborough said. "We had two 240-litre bins that were getting collected each week. We're now down to one bin collected each fortnight." He says that saves him about $5,000 a year. Australia's hospitality sector wastes 1.2 million tonnes of food each year, according to the Sustainable Restaurant Association. The economic impact of food waste in the food service sector is about $6.4 billion , averaging about $66,000 annually per business. Belinda Chellingworth says many businesses don't realise how much food they waste. ( ABC News: Fletcher Yeung ) Ms Chellingworth said less than a quarter of businesses regularly inspected their food waste. "Typically, many businesses, if they've got food left over at the end of their operations or the end of the day, then it will be landfilled," she said. "For many businesses, and particularly large businesses, the cost of food waste across their operations isn't fully realised because they incur it multiple times, but it's not obvious." Food waste will be a point of discussion at the COP31 conference. ( ABC South West WA: Jacqueline Lynch ) For example, over-ordering food is a cost to the kitchen. If it's not sold, that's a revenue cost, and then whatever goes into the bin also involves a cost for collection. "So they're paying for it multiple times, but they're different departments, different cost centres, and it's often not added together, so they don't understand the full cost across the whole business," Ms Chellingworth said. Landfills are nearing capacity in parts of Australia. ( ABC News: Che Chorley ) She says landfill capacity is reaching critical levels in many areas. Some tips in Perth are set to run out of space in two years and sites in New South Wales are set to reach capacity in four years . Victoria's capacity is expected to be reached in the next 10 years. To combat the economic and environmental impacts of food waste, the federal government has committed to halving food waste reduction by 2030 . But UNSW food and health professor Johannes le Coutre does not believe we are on track. Johannes le Coutre says tackling food waste will help to ease food insecurity. ( ABC News: Fletcher Yeung ) "I'm not sure if that's attainable or achievable with the current landscape," he said. "In Australia we have a unique situation in that we are dealing with a big distance and that even in the food industry a lot of value-added manufacturing occurs overseas.

events.title: Pope Leo to undergo surgery to remove lung nodule in Rome
events.summary: Vatican officials expect a one-week hospital recovery for the 71-year-old religious leader ahead of his scheduled Latin America tour. Pope Leo XIV is to undergo surgery to remove a lung nodule, the Vatican has announced. The 71-year-old leader of the Catholic Church will enter Rome’s Gemelli Hospital late on Tuesday morning for the procedure, which is expected to require about a week of inpatient recovery and has forced the cancellation of upcoming papal audiences. list 1 of 3 Pope Leo to undergo surgery to remove lung nodule list 2 of 3 Pope Leo says AI risk concerns not ‘fake news’ list 3 of 3 Pope says death penalty ‘inadmissible’ as US plans to livestream execution During his weekly blessing in St Peter’s Square on Sunday , Leo told pilgrims that a small nodule was found on his left lung during a routine checkup and said it was “well-contained” and had been spotted early. “The doctors believe it’s best to take action, so, following their advice, I’ve decided to have surgery to remove it,” he said during remarks delivered in Italian. Later, the Vatican said a week of recovery time is expected after Leo’s surgery, and his audiences have been cancelled until October 20. Spokespeople did not clarify whether the nodule is believed to be malignant. The pope has no reported history of serious illness and is considered physically active, routinely swimming and playing tennis. The upcoming surgery comes ahead of an official Latin America tour scheduled for November 6–17, with stops planned across Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru. Whether the operation and subsequent recovery will force changes to the itinerary remains unclear, though the pontiff told reporters on Sunday that he intends to make the journey. The late Pope Francis, Leo’s predecessor, died at age 88. Francis was hospitalised several times and grew frail in his later years. He did not usually announce his hospital visits in advance, sometimes sparking intense media speculation about his health .

events.title: Meta says it's launching the biggest and best AI models it has ever built
events.summary: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg. Chris Unger/Zuffa LLC Meta says its latest AI models have finally caught up with its rivals. Meta tailored its models, Muse Wonder and Wonder Full, for work and completing multi-step tasks. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg teased the release by posting a photo of a watermelon. Meta has launched a new series of AI models, Muse Wonder, that it says has caught up to labs like Anthropic and OpenAI. "Muse Wonder is a much larger and more advanced class of models that brings us to the frontier," CEO Mark Zuckerberg posted on X on Monday. It’s the latest sign that Meta’s big bet on AI — which has raised questions from investors — is paying off after the launch of its personal AI assistant, Muse . Meta is spending hundreds of billions of dollars on AI, prompting some investor doubts earlier this year. The Wonder series comes in two versions: Muse Wonder, a smaller, fast model Meta expects people to use for daily work, and Wonder Full, a larger and more capable version, the company said in a statement. Meta built its new AI models to complete complex multi-step tasks, such as disputing an insurance claim. To handle that, the AIs have features such as memory and the ability to try alternative approaches. The Muse Wonder series was internally codenamed Watermelon, according to a person familiar with the matter. In July, Business Insider reported that Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang had told staff that Watermelon had caught up to OpenAI. "Watermelon uses an order of magnitude more compute than Avocado," he said at the time, referring to Meta's codename for Muse Spark, a prior family of models. events.title: Cuba forges ahead with renewable energy plans amid US oil blockade
events.summary: Trump, Netanyahu and the Iran question How Iran war fallout may shape US elections Cuban energy minister denies link to fuel shipments intercepted by US, says oil imports by private firms insufficient. The Cuban government is pushing ahead with its plans to transition to renewable energy, amid a de facto oil blockade from the United States that has strangled the island’s economy. In an interview with the Reuters news agency on Monday, Cuban Minister of Energy and Mines Vicente de la O Levy explained that the blockade has forced Cuba to explore domestic alternatives to foreign fuel imports. list 1 of 4 Cuba works to restore power after another major nationwide blackout list 2 of 4 US open to Cuba talks on government change, Marco Rubio says list 3 of 4 Cuba condemns US ‘collective punishment’ as Trump predicts deal list 4 of 4 Cuba accuses US at UN of deliberately inflicting humanitarian suffering “We are seeking our own alternative solutions, using our own resources, our sun, wind, tides, fuel, Cuban crude oil and the gas produced in our wells,” de la O Levy said. He said 144 solar farms with a combined capacity of about 1,418 megawatts have been installed on the island in recent years. China has been the largest supplier of solar panels to the island, and shipments have increased since the blockade began in early January. At the time, US President Donald Trump halted all oil shipments from Venezuela, a close ally of the Cuban government. Later that month, Trump also announced he would impose heavy tariffs on any country that exported oil to Cuba, justifying the threat by calling the island’s government a “national security” threat. Since then, only a single oil tanker from Russia has reached Havana. The US has increased its shipments of oil to Cuba’s private sector, but it has largely barred fuel exports for nationalised industries on the communist-led island. The government-run electrical grid, widely considered to be antiquated, relies heavily on fossil fuels. Only 40 percent of Cuba’s electricity comes from ‌‌‌‌domestic ‌‌‌‌oil production, according to the International Energy Agency. As of 2023, only nine percent of the country’s energy consumption was covered by renewable sources. De la O Levy admitted in his interview with Reuters that the country was facing difficulties. The blockade has caused shortages of medicine, water and fuel, pushing Cuba to the brink of a humanitarian crisis. “We are surviving and moving forward, little by little, even if not at the pace we would like,” he said. “We face long hours of blackouts and lack fuel for cooking and transportation. We lack fuel, but we are gradually making headway through our own solutions and our people.” Cuba’s production of domestic crude oil remains stable, he added, but is almost entirely allocated to power plants. The United Nations and human rights watchdogs have criticised the oil blockade as a violation of international law. Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez Parrilla also condemned the oil blockade in his speech at the UN General Assembly last month. “It is an unusual and unprecedented action,” Rodriguez said of the blockade. “A superpower unilaterally deprives all states of their right to export the commodities that they wish to the country that they wish.” The US has maintained an economic embargo on Cuba for more than 60 years, since the Cold War era. But since taking office for a second term as president, Trump has sought to squeeze Cuba’s economy further, as part of a “maximum pressure” campaign. His administration has indicated that it wants to topple Cuba’s government . On October 7, US authorities announced they had seized 90 biodiesel fuel shipments valued at over $2.8m destined for Cuba. “These shipments were part of an attempt to unlawfully export fuel to Cuba in violation of federal export laws,” US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) said in a statement. But in his interview with Reuters, de la O Levy denied the Cuban government had any link to the shipments. “No Cuban state-owned company has managed to secure a fuel contract, whether for small or large quantities,” he said. He added that any US oil shipments to private firms fall far short of the country’s requirements. “I would venture to say that the amount entering the country doesn’t even cover 3 percent of its fuel needs,” de la O Levy said.

events.title: UK blames Iran for airbase plot, sanctions two Iranian nationals
events.summary: Iran’s ambassador tells British officials Tehran willing to assist in UK investigation. Britain’s Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said that a suspected plot targeting Royal Air Force (RAF) base Fairford was “almost certainly” directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), raising the diplomatic stakes over the largely unexplained incident for which Tehran has denied any responsibility. “We will not tolerate these threats on our soil,” Burnham told parliament on Monday, adding that the government, “will crack down on Iran’s use of criminal networks, using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams”. “We will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity of Iran and the IRGC to do us harm”, he said. The incident near the airbase in southern England occurred in the early hours of September 27 when five British men in their 20s were arrested on suspected “terrorism” and explosives offences. Police said they found a supply of petrol in three vans linked to the suspects, but no explosives. They were later released without charge on ‌‌‌‌police ⁠⁠⁠⁠bail “under stringent conditions”. Last week, Counter Terrorism Policing arrested a 22-year-old British national on suspicion of a “terror” offence linked to the security incident. Earlier this month, a 25-year-old British-Iranian man was arrested in London. In a statement on X, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said Britain was sanctioning two Iranians for their “role in facilitating or engaging in hostile activity on behalf of the Iranian regime”, without specifying their identity. “We have repeatedly made clear to Iran, Britain will not tolerate threats on our soil”, he said. The move came as 29 countries, including Britain, the US, most European states, Canada, Australia and New Zealand issued a joint statement on Monday blaming Iran for the attempted infiltration. “Any attempt by Iran to threaten, silence, intimidate, harass, harm, or coerce people on our territories through proxies or any other means is unacceptable”, it said. On Monday, Ali Mousavi, Iran’s ambassador to the UK, met Stephen Doughty, the UK’s minister for the Middle East, and “categorically rejected” allegations of any Iranian role while urging “the British side to refrain from any unsubstantiated statements”. Mousavi told British authorities that Tehran is willing to cooperate with the investigation into the incident , Iran’s ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠state news agency IRNA reported. Iran’s embassy in London issued a statement last month saying Iran “categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations” attempting to link the country to the arrests, adding that it will “fuel Iranophobia propaganda”. The US moved its B-52 and B-1 bombers from the base earlier this month. RAF Fairford has served as a stopping point for US bombers participating in the war against Iran, which began more than seven months ago, on February 28. Located roughly 160km (100 miles) west of London, RAF Fairford is the preferred European base for US bombers. Their withdrawal was made over concerns about a suspected Iranian plot to carry out a complex drone attack on the facility, according to US officials.

events.title: This entrepreneur says Amazon nearly destroyed his business. He still shops on it every week. 'It's crazy.'
events.summary: Business Insider Jack Nekhala's Bed Scrunchie sales faced a major hit after Amazon deactivated his seller account. Nekhala says the loss left the founders in debt, yet he still shops on Amazon several times a week. The habit bothers him more than he can explain. Jack Nekhala has every reason to stop shopping on Amazon . His company, Bed Scrunchie, generated about $4.5 million in 2024 and was on track for more, Nekhala said. However, Amazon deactivated its seller account just before the holidays that year, cutting off its biggest sales channel. "Once the collapse happened through Amazon, it basically collapsed the entire business," Nekhala told Business Insider for our So Expensive video series. That makes his next admission harder to say. "I still shop on Amazon ," Nekhala said. "I have a daughter. She needs bikes. She needs a scooter, she needs all sorts, she needs different things. And that's the place we go to." He said he shops on Amazon two to three times a week and sometimes has several orders in a single day. The habit bothers him more than he can explain, he said. "Continuing to shop there feels like being forced to sit down to dinner with the institution that upended your life." Founders of the Bed Scrunchie: Jack Nekhala (left) and Michael Nusinkis (right). Courtesy of Jack The account shutdown, he said, left him and his business partner carrying debt and trying to rebuild the financial security they had spent nearly 20 years creating for their young families. "My life has not been the same," he said. For Nekhala, his Amazon shopping habit reflects how deeply the online marketplace has become embedded in everyday life. In a recent survey of shoppers across the US and Europe, 75% of consumers said they buy from Amazon at least once a month. "I do not shop there because I have forgiven what happened. I shop there because Amazon has made itself so convenient and embedded in everyday life that even people who feel harmed by it continue to depend on it," Nekhala said. "It's crazy," he added of his own shopping habits . "It's really incredible what they've accomplished." Amazon became the default Jack Nekhala launched his Bed Scrunchie product in 2019. Business Insider The appeal of Amazon isn't just price. It's the convenience, Nekhala said. Amazon already has his payment information, shipping addresses, and purchase history. Adding one more item to an order is often easier than creating an account somewhere else, he said. "They remove all the friction," Michael Nusinkis, Nekhala's business partner, said. "I think you just have this muscle memory. I need to buy something — Amazon," Nusinkis added. The founders saw that same behavior from their own customers. Before Amazon deactivated their seller account, the pair aired a national television infomercial directing viewers to a website where they could buy the Bed Scrunchie directly for $39.99. On Amazon, the product sold for $44.95. And they said Amazon sales of the item consistently spiked whenever the infomercial aired. "All advertising roads lead back to Amazon," Nekhala said. Nekhala said customers would likely discover the product on television or the company's website, then go to Amazon to compare options, read reviews, and buy it—even at a higher price. Surveys suggest up to three-quarters of Amazon shoppers start their product searches there. Even after losing their account, the business couldn't leave Amazon The bed scrunchie is designed to prevent sheets and mattress toppers from sliding off a mattress. Business Insider After months of disputes with Amazon , including allegations that the company had infringed its own patent and violated Amazon's review policies, Nekhala and Nusinkis lost their seller account. The founders dispute both allegations. They now sell Bed Scrunchie to a third-party distributor, which keeps it available on Amazon for $49.99. Nekhala estimates that Amazon still accounts for 70% to 80% of the company's sales. That means shoppers may see the Bed Scrunchie name on Amazon without realizing they are buying from a reseller—not the small business that created it, he said. "Amazon shut out the people who invented and built the product, yet the product remains on its platform at a higher price," Nekhala added. "That contradiction is what makes continuing to shop there so painful." Nekhala said the company would rather sell the product for less on its own website. But he believes Amazon's pricing policies make that difficult: Listing it more cheaply elsewhere, he said, could mean the product loses visibility or prominent placement on Amazon. As a result, he said, sellers keep prices in line across retailers, even when it means customers pay more. That's one of the practices at the center of a lawsuit California's attorney general filed against Amazon, alleging it pressures brands and third-party sellers to raise prices at competing retailers so Amazon isn't undercut. In a statement to Business Insider, Amazon says its goal is to protect customers from overpaying and maintain trust in its marketplace by comparing prices with other reputable retailers. If a product is listed for less elsewhere, Amazon says it may choose not to prominently feature that offer, though it remains available for purchase. Amazon also argues California's case relies on a handful of emails taken out of context and says the challenged practices are common retail negotiations designed to deliver "low prices, vast selection, and unmatched convenience" for customers. events.title: Loophole allowing new coal and gas to avoid stricter climate laws
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Coal and gas avoiding stricter laws by expanding existing mines, Climate Council warns Hunter Valley Operations was recently approved for an extension that will include mining new seams and additional emissions. ( ABC News ) Coal and gas mines have to follow less strict emissions laws when they are expanded compared to outright new mines. The Climate Council says that amounts to a "loophole" being used by the industry to add new emissions without having to follow "best-practice" limits. The Safeguard Mechanism, which sets emissions laws for heavy industry, is under review. Coal and gas mines are using what the Climate Council warns is a "loophole" to expand operations and add new emissions while avoiding stricter laws imposed on new coal and gas projects. The Climate Council says unless emissions from mine expansions are treated the same as emissions from new mines, it will cause an additional 4.5 million tonnes of CO2 a year by 2035. Coal and gas mines are among the roughly 200 facilities covered by the Safeguard Mechanism — climate laws that require Australia's biggest polluters to cut or offset emissions by about 5 per cent a year or else face heavy penalties. Under the laws, which are currently being reviewed, new coal and gas facilities are required to follow more strict, "best-practice" limits that take into account the most efficient technologies available for mines. But existing facilities are not required to meet that higher standard when expanding or extending the life of an existing mine. Modelling by Reputex has estimated that across 22 planned coal and gas expansions and extensions over the next decade, which will be treated as existing facilities, they will be able to emit 11 times more than if they were treated as new facilities. The Climate Council says expansions are being used widely across the industry, taking advantage of that favourable treatment and leading to more emissions. "Companies have an incentive to characterise everything as an expansion rather than a new facility," chief executive Amanda McKenzie said. "We're arguing that is one of the loopholes that needs to be shut." Amanda McKenzie says less stringent climate laws for mining expansions compared to new facilities amount to a "loophole" that should be closed. ( Supplied ) The Safeguard Mechanism is under review and due to be revisited next year, when the government will decide whether to set a steeper trajectory towards net zero emissions by 2050. The Climate Council says when that time comes, "best-practice" CO2 limits should be applied to all new coal and gas emissions, regardless of whether they come from a new mine or an expanded one. It says fossil fuel facilities are not doing enough to transition to net zero, and those covered by the Safeguard Mechanism actually increased emissions in the most recent year. Most new coal and gas emissions from expansions The council says since the Safeguard Mechanism laws were amended in 2022, more than three quarters of all new coal development have been expansions or extensions to projects. It pointed to last month's approval for an open-cut coalmine in the Hunter Valley , which owners Yancoal and Glencore applied to extend by more than a decade. Its life extension into the 2040s, which includes the mining of deeper coal seams, represents an additional $2.7 billion capital investment and will add an extra 809 megatonnes of CO2 emissions — or a bit less than two years' worth of Australia's annual emissions. The NSW Independent Planning Commission approves plans that will allow Hunter Valley Operations to continue coal mining at a site near Singleton until 2045. Because the Yancoal-Glencore owned coalmine was already covered by the Safeguard Mechanism, the extension will be treated under rules for existing projects, which the Climate Council estimates will result in emissions 60 per cent higher than if it was treated as a new project. The NSW Independent Planning Commission, which approved the life extension, said while it would contribute to climate change and add to Australia's emissions, that was outweighed by its benefits, including supporting up to 1,400 local jobs and ongoing tax revenue from the mine. "Despite these new investments being significant enough to require a new environmental approval, the vast majority of their pollution will not be considered 'new' by the Safeguard Mechanism," the council said.

events.title: A massive trade just happened in surging shares of Snap
events.summary: Don't call it a comeback yet, but shares of beleaguered social media stock Snap Inc. are up almost 20% this month and options traders are betting it's about to go on a big run. Snap shares have traded under $10 since July 2025 following a near-complete collapse from over $80 at the stock's high in 2021 to a low of $3.81 in April. But now, as excitement swirls over social media giant Meta Platforms' AI agent, traders are pouring into Snap call options on Monday, propelling trading volume to more than four times the month-long average, Cboe LiveVol data show. Almost 140,000 options on Snap traded Monday, including about 64,000 call trades that were likely initiated by buyers, compared to under 7,000 puts. Traders sold more than 12,000 puts, and just over 34,000 calls. The net trade sentiment, as well as net directional bias according to options deltas, was positive, according to Barchart. Nine out of the top 10 trades by volume were calls, and of the $5.5 million in premium exchanged, $5 million was tied to calls, SpotGamma data show. The most popular contract to buy was the 8-strike call expiring Dec. 18, which traded 26,000 times. That contract costs about 37 cents and needs Snap to rally 30% before expiry to pay off. If that happens, it would be the highest the stock's traded since February. The owner of photo-sharing and messaging app Snapchat also offers augmented-reality `Specs' glasses. Shareholder Blue Duck Capital issued an open letter to Snap's board of directors last week urging the company to raise dedicated capital to support the product, saying it could lead to a $12-$14 share price.

events.title: Fridges in French supermarkets hit by cyber attack
events.summary: Published 12 October 2026, 15:30 BST Hundreds of French supermarkets have been hit by a cyber attack that caused their fridges and freezers to heat up, spoiling fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros. Hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units, forcing some to warm to 50C (120F) overnight, according to one supermarket chain affected. The chief executive of Coopérative U said several of its supermarkets had been hit by the "extremely serious and unprecedented" attack. More than 100 of the chain's supermarkets were targeted, while 180 stores from Intermarché and its Netto brand were affected, with a spokesman saying that another 100 shops were urgently disconnected from the internet to prevent the same thing happening to them. Other major food retailers including Carrefour, Monoprix and E.Leclerc were also hit by the attack, which targeted software provided by Danish engineering firm Danfoss. The software allows retailers to manage their cold units remotely. Normally, supermarket freezers go through a short period of defrosting overnight, in which temperatures rise slightly. But the hackers ordered the units to heat up and stay hot, although Danfoss did not confirm any reports about just how warm the fridges and freezers could become in that process. Danfoss said the affected cold units were older models whose security software could not be updated to ward off a risk they had identified. The firm added in s statement that it had "long advised" businesses to keep supported systems up to date. "Reliable refrigeration is critical to our customers' operations, and we remain committed to supporting our customers and helping them maintain secure and reliable systems they are used to." The full scale of the attack is unclear, but figures supplied by individual chains suggest about 400 stores were affected out of 15,000 or so overall in France. Carrefour said fridges in 80 of its 6,000 stores were hacked, while Monoprix said 5% of its 400-plus stores had been hit, with food removed from sale if its condition could not be guaranteed. In a statement to the BBC, Mousquetaires Group - which owns Intermarché and Netto - said some fresh and frozen food display units remained out of service on Monday afternoon. The stores had "taken all necessary precautions to remove the products from these units", it said, adding that staff were working to restock the shelves "as soon as possible". Intermarché said its fridges had heated up to 50C for six hours overnight into Monday, and the retailer had thrown away all the affected food to avoid health risks, the Reuters news agency reported. As a result of the attack, managers arriving at branches of several supermarket chains on Monday morning were hit by a wave of hot air from the freezers. In some places there were even small fires. French broadcaster BFMTV published an image showing a freezer in an ice cream aisle displaying a temperature of 26.5C. Two supermarkets in the Alsace region reported losses of €270,000 (£228,000) between them, the broadcaster added, meaning the nationwide total could run into the millions. French prosecutors have opened a specific cyber-crime investigation into the incident, which the Paris prosecutor's office called a "large-scale cyber-attack affecting the refrigerators of several major food retail chains across France". European Food Commissioner Christophe Hansen condemned the hack in a post on X and added: "Food security requires more attention at all levels. Because the weaponisation of food has become a reality." In a post on X, Coopérative chief executive Dominique Schelcher said staff were "fully mobilised, in co-ordination with refrigeration specialists, to restore the situation as quickly as possible". He called for an investigation into the hack and said targeting equipment essential to the French food supply was "unacceptable". Have you been affected by this cyber attack? Share your experience . events.title: Election odds are coming to your TV this fall. 60% of Americans oppose betting on elections
events.summary: Americans can turn their predictions about who will control Congress into a bet, but most don’t think they should. With the midterms approaching, 60% of U.S. adults oppose using prediction markets to wager on election results, while 13% support it and 24% are unsure, according to a Reuters /Ipsos poll provided to Fortune . They’ll see the odds anyway. CBS News said Sept. 30 it would add real-time prices from Kalshi to its midterm coverage, alongside its own polling. Kalshi has similar deals with CNN and CNBC, and it licenses vote counts and race calls from the Associated Press. CBS News and CNN now share an owner: Skydance, which completed its purchase of CNN’s parent, Warner Bros. Discovery , on Oct. 6. Those prices can rest on a small number of traders. On Polymarket’s global platform, the top 1% of wallets account for 68% of trading volume on 2026 congressional markets, and 80% of those markets have fewer than 100 wallets trading, according to an August analysis by the Anti-Corruption Data Collective , a nonprofit research and advocacy group. The opposition crosses party lines, with 69% of Democrats and 61% of Republicans opposing election betting. Three-quarters of Americans consider prediction-market wagering a form of gambling. Only 7% of respondents said they had used a prediction market to bet money. “Most view prediction markets as a form of gambling, and it’s clear that they do not see elections or government decision-making as appropriate subjects for it,” Alec Tyson, a senior vice president and lead pollster at Ipsos U.S. Public Affairs, told Fortune . Ipsos surveyed 4,506 U.S. adults from Sept. 30 through Oct. 5. The margin of sampling error is plus or minus 1.5 percentage points. But monthly global trading volume and public approval measure different things. Sports offer what elections struggle to match: frequent events and fast-changing odds that give people more reasons to trade, said Dustin Gouker, a gambling industry analyst and author of the prediction market newsletter The Event Horizon .   A poll or campaign development can move an election market. A sports game can move odds and produce those shifts within minutes as teams score and leads change.  “I don’t think it’s necessarily that election trading isn’t popular,” Gouker told Fortune . “It’s more that it doesn’t feature some of the things that we see in these markets that are seeing more volume.” Combined monthly trading volume on Kalshi and Polymarket more than doubled, from about $26 billion in May to $53 billion in July, according to a September Pew Research Center analysis. Sports drove most of that increase. Users buy and sell contracts on whether an event will happen; winning contracts pay $1 and losing ones pay nothing. Those totals cover all trading and count contracts at their potential $1 payout rather than their purchase price. They don’t represent company revenue or the cash traders spent. Kalshi challenges the findings Kalshi called the poll biased, challenging how it described prediction markets and asked about wagering on government events.  “It’s not hard to bias a poll and this poll is biased,” a Kalshi spokesperson said in a statement to Fortune. “Ask leading questions about whether people support ‘betting on war,’ and you’ll get the answers this poll arrived at. Kalshi doesn’t even offer war markets.”  The questionnaire didn’t use the word “war.” It described prediction markets as allowing people to “wager money on the outcome of real-world events.” It then asked separately about elections, military actions, government policy decisions, and sports and did not measure familiarity. A March Ipsos poll for the American Institute for Boys and Men found just 21% of Americans were very or somewhat familiar with prediction markets. “We welcome research on our industry, but a clearer picture would come from research that measures familiarity, uses neutral wording, and reports all responses,” Kalshi said. Ipsos did not respond to Kalshi’s criticism by publication time. Traders sued Kalshi earlier this year in March over its handling of a market on whether Iran’s supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, would leave office. The dispute followed his killing in U.S.-Israeli strikes. Kalshi told Reuters at the time that the rules excluded death-related outcomes and that it had reimbursed trading fees and net losses. Election odds aren’t election results Polymarket argues that its audience extends beyond bettors. More than 90% of visits are to view markets rather than trade, a spokesperson told Fortune. “Prediction markets are a way to get unbiased, accurate information about the events that impact our lives,” the spokesperson said. Gouker said election markets attract viewers by distilling polls and news into a probability, but turning those visitors into traders is a separate business challenge. He expects election trading to pick up as the midterms approach, though doubts it will get to the level of sports betting. He also expects the 2028 presidential election to draw more trading than this year’s midterms.  He cautioned against treating high odds as a call of the race. Gouker pointed to Abdul El-Sayed’s Michigan primary, saying markets showed him as an overwhelming favorite around the close of voting before incoming results suggested a closer contest. El-Sayed led by just under one percentage point when the Associated Press called the race. A candidate with a 70% chance of winning still has a 30% chance of losing. To judge a market’s accuracy, Gouker said, look at whether outcomes occur as often as the odds suggest: “When a market says something should happen, it happens roughly the amount of times we would expect it to.” “You have to look at them as probabilities and not as these crystal balls,” he said. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Rep. Ilhan Omar blasts federal criminal raid on home: 'I will not be silenced'
events.summary: The Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, a Minnesota Democrat, was raided as part of a federal criminal investigation. Omar, who was born in Somalia and brought to the U.S. as a child, has been repeatedly criticized by President Donald Trump. The raid took place less than a month before November's midterms, where Omar is seeking reelection. "For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns," Omar said. "This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced." Federal authorities raided the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar on Monday morning as part of a criminal investigation of the Minnesota Democrat. Omar, who has not been charged with a crime, said she was being targeted for political purposes because of her opposition to President Donald Trump . A person familiar with the situation, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the nonpublic investigation, told CNBC that the probe of the 44-year-old congresswoman is complex and has been going on for years. MS NOW reported that a law enforcement source with direct knowledge of the raid — which comes weeks before November's midterm election — said the investigation into Omar is based on allegations of fraud. Fox News , which first reported the raid, cited a source familiar with the probe as saying it is focused on her immigration paperwork, which was filled out by her father when she emigrated to the U.S. with him from Somalia as a child. Homeland Security Investigations, a division of the Department of Homeland Security , conducted the raid. HSI investigators were seen outside Omar's home in the Northeast quadrant of Washington throughout the morning. Omar, who is seeking reelection, has been a target of criticism by Trump for years. She heckled the president during his State of the Union address to Congress on Feb. 24, which came on the heels of aggressive immigration enforcement actions in Minneapolis by federal authorities. Omar, who is deputy chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, blasted the raid and the investigation in a post on X on Monday. "Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement. For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation," she wrote. Omar became a U.S. citizen in 2000 at 17. She was elected to Congress in November 2018 to represent Minnesota's 5th District, which includes all of Minneapolis. She and Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., became the first two Muslim women elected to Congress. Russian lab worker dies amid plague reports — here's what we know Trump's nemesis in Europe: Why Spain's Sanchez is calling a snap election Trump tells South Korea to sign on to Alaska LNG deal or 'I'll just charge them more' The Department of Justice, in a statement to CNBC when asked about the raid, said, "Today in the Washington, D.C., area, Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice." "This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal investigation," the DOJ said. Omar's spokeswoman, Jacklyn Rogers, in a statement said, "This raid by Trump's DHS is an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies." "For a decade, Donald Trump has relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Ilhan Omar with inflammatory rhetoric, repeatedly putting a target on her back," Rogers said. "Now, those attacks have escalated to a pointless federal raid. The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong. No president should be able to use the power of the federal government to intimidate his political enemies." In September, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin told right-wing commentator Benny Johnson at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas that DHS was investigating issues around Omar and her family's immigration to the United States. "There may be more to this, the whole family migration and possibly some illegal activity for them to come to the United States to begin with," said Mullin. He said the investigation could end with deportations. The DOJ, for years, has had a policy regarding the announcement and initiation of federal investigations and prosecutions close to elections. The policy discourages beginning an investigation, taking investigative steps, bringing criminal charges, or making public statements for the purpose of affecting an election or to give a candidate an advantage or disadvantage. The person familiar with the raid on Omar's home told CNBC on Monday that the DOJ does not consider that action to violate the policy because the raid was not meant to be public. Republican John Nagel is running against Omar in a race the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter rates "solid Democrat." The general election is just over three weeks away on Nov. 3.
