events.title: I'm a former flight attendant who still travels all the time. Here are 6 dos and don'ts for surviving long-haul economy.
events.summary: As a former flight attendant, I've learned ways to make long-haul economy flights more bearable. Alona Vasylieva I was a flight attendant for nearly 10 years and still fly frequently as a passenger. I bring different outfits for the plane and the airport, and a plastic bag for clutter. I skip the neck pillow and never drink airplane coffee. Before I stepped away from my flight attendant job after nearly 10 years in the sky, I picked up a lot of tricks for making long-haul travel more bearable. Now, as a passenger who regularly flies economy, I stick to the same system every time. From packing multiple outfits to deplaning last, here are my 6 dos and don'ts for long flights . I get to the airport extra early — and I switch outfits twice. I get lounge access via credit card benefits. Alona Vasylieva Some people want to spend as little time as possible at airports , but I prefer to arrive super early to take advantage of my credit card's lounge benefits for a mental preflight. Having that quiet, unhurried time allows me to get into the right headspace before stepping into a metal tube for hours on end. And right before boarding begins, I head to the restroom and change out of my street clothes for a soft, breathable tracksuit so my body can relax right away. Then, right before landing, I pop into the lavatory to change back into my original outfit. That quick final wardrobe change acts as a complete mental reset — it switches my brain into "arrival mode," so I step off the aircraft feeling fresh , organized, and sharp. I bring a small plastic bag to keep from feeling cluttered. I always bring a way to keep my already small space clear of litter. Alona Vasylieva I don't want to linger in the aisle during boarding, so I split my packing into two categories: my main carry-on suitcase stays overhead until after landing, while a compact pouch under the seat holds my earplugs, snacks, cables, a change of clothes, and moisturizer. But my favorite habit for long-haul comfort is tucking a small plastic trash bag into my seat pocket. Flying with my family always turns into a quiet contest of how fast snack wrappers, empty bottles, and used wipes can take over our row. Bringing a small trash bag keeps everything in one place, so we aren't stuck spending a long flight sitting in a pile of clutter . I book seats near the emergency exit and use the call button sparingly. I always try to book an aisle seat near the exit row. Al Drago/Getty Images Old habits run deep, so I always book an aisle seat — mostly because my flight attendant brain still feels a deep need to be within quick reach of an emergency exit. It's an instinct I can't shake from years of safety drills. My flight attendant days also guide how I interact with the crew. I remember answering endless call lights for simple requests during busy meal services or safety checks, so I make it a point, as a passenger, to save the overhead button for urgent needs or when I can't safely wait. Instead, I wait until the crew isn't mid-service and it's safe to move around the cabin to stretch my legs or walk to the galley for more water. And when nature calls, I time my trip using operational cues: I find the lavatories are often cleanest and have the shortest queues right before the galley carts head out for meal service or halfway through trash collection. I skip the neck pillow and sleep aids in favor of a simple eye mask. I prefer the airline's provided linens when flying. Aviation-images.com/Universal Images Group via Getty Images As soon as I sit down on the plane, I adjust my watch and phone to my destination's local time. If it's 2 a.m. there, I try to rest right away, even if it's bright outside or meal service carts are rolling down the aisle. I used to take sleep aids like melatonin, but stopped because it often left me groggy after landing. Now I rely on a light-blocking eye mask, magnesium, which I find helps me unwind, and mental timing. I also skip the neck pillow. A hoodie hood and a standard airline pillow work for me. What I've found works best for sleeping upright in economy is using the headrest, reclining slightly, supporting my lower back with a rolled sweater, and keeping my seatbelt fastened so flight attendants don't have to wake me during turbulence. And I don't recommend trying TikTok sleep hacks without first checking the airline's rules: those viral Amazon foot hammocks, for example, are banned by some carriers because they attach to the tray tables and could hinder evacuations. I stick to bottled water and lighter meals on overnight flights. One of the meals served on defunct Ukraine International Airlines, the carrier I worked for before leaving during COVID to be a journalist. Courtesy of Alona Vasylieva I avoid tap water, coffee, and tea on flights. Aircraft water is regulated and often safe, but a January 2026 study by the Center for Food as Medicine & Longevity, a nonprofit, found that water quality and tank maintenance can vary by airline. So, personally, I prefer to bring my own sealed water bottle. I also add electrolytes to my bottled water because I find they help me feel better in the dry cabin air, which can otherwise leave me with post-flight headaches and exhaustion. And I completely skip the late-night hot meal service on overnight flights. For me, digesting a heavy dinner at 30,000 feet while sitting leaves me bloated and makes it harder to sleep. Instead, I always pack a small tote bag full of healthy, high-protein snacks from home — like nuts, seeds, and berries — to keep me nourished without feeling heavy. I'm always among the last people to deplane. Unless I'm rushing to make a connection or an activity at my destination, I am the last person to deplane. Patrick Smith/Getty Images The exact moment the plane touches down and the seatbelt sign turns off, people often leap out of their seats and stand, squeezed shoulder to shoulder in the aisle. I do the exact opposite: I sit back, let the initial crowd filter out, and take my time. I use those extra quiet minutes to check every seat pocket, the floor, and the overhead bin above me. In my crew days, I handled plenty of forgotten items, and the process of getting them back is nowhere near as quick as people think. Once you step off the plane, you usually can't simply walk back on to grab a lost phone or passport. In many cases, the crew has to log every item on an official form, hand it over to ground staff, and wait for it to be processed through airport lost and found. Spending a few extra seconds taking inventory can save hours of bureaucratic panic later. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Tasmania's financial windfall from mine leads to creation of future fund
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Windfall from King Island tungsten mine shares to support new Tasmanian future fund The Dolphin Tungsten Mine recommenced operations at Grassy on King Island and in 2023 started commercial production of tungsten concentrate. ( ABC News: Morgan Timms ) In 2023, the Tasmanian government acquired 12 per cent of the shares of a struggling tungsten mine after its owner could not repay a $10 million loan. The price of tungsten has since significantly increased. A recovery fund will be set up to insulate Tasmanians in major industries from workforce impacts. The Tasmanian government will create a $20 million future fund to help regional communities "navigate economic disruption" and "attract new investment". It follows the government stepping in financially to save King Island Dairy, and industrials Bell Bay Aluminium and Nyrstar from collapse, as well as dealing with the loss of more than 200 jobs after Australia's last manganese smelter Liberty Bell Bay shut down. The money for the new Recovery Fund for Regional Resilience will come from the government's $10 million investment in King Island's tungsten mine. The mine is on King Island's south-east coast. ( Facebook: Group 6 Metals ) The Dolphin mine, which boasts the largest tungsten deposit in the country, is owned by Australian company Group 6 Metals. The mine shut for more than two decades due to low tungsten prices, but reopened in 2023 with the help of the $10 million loan. Under new ownership, the initial $10 million loan was converted into shares, of which Tasmania's government holds 12 per cent. The mine has since experienced a significant financial turnaround, rewarding investors like the government. Tungsten is classified as a critical mineral used in heavy machinery and defence manufacturing. The state government also lent the mine a further $7.5 million last year. The Dolphin mine is Australia's largest mined tungsten deposit. ( Supplied: Group 6 Metals ) Mine proceeds to help reduce state debt Premier Jeremy Rockliff said the government's investment in the mine would allow it to reinvest in regional communities. Government issues loan to mine after becoming a shareholder A struggling tungsten mine couldn't pay back a $10 million loan as it sat on the brink of administration. So a state government became a shareholder — and issued a new loan. "Our regional communities are at the heart of Tasmania's economic success and they deserve the confidence that comes from knowing support will be there when it is needed most," Mr Rockliff said. ​"The strong investment made by the Tasmanian government to support the future of the King Island tungsten mine has allowed us to reinvest a significant portion of the windfall back into the very regions that helped generate that success. ​"This fund is about transforming a one-off financial return into an enduring asset for regional Tasmania." The government said the fund will be able to support communities experiencing significant economic disruption, including responding to major industry change, employer closures, workforce impacts and other economic shocks. "Too often, governments are forced to react after a major employer closes or an industry undergoes significant change," he said. ​"Instead, we are getting ahead of those challenges by establishing a fund that will help communities navigate economic disruption, attract new investment and create new opportunities for the future. ​"The Recovery Fund for Regional Resilience will help support economic diversification, workforce transition, investment attraction and community-led recovery initiatives when communities face significant economic disruption." The government said proceeds from the mine investment would also go towards reducing the state's debt, which is estimated to peak at just under $10 billion by the end of the decade. events.title: What colleges and universities need from donors to thrive
events.summary: Graduates pass the John Harvard Statue during Harvard University's commencement on May 29, 2025. Harvard was the school's first big donor. Craig F. Walker/The Boston Globe via Getty Images In 1638, John Harvard , an English-born Puritan minister and teacher in the Massachusetts Bay Colony, bequeathed 400 books and half his £779 estate, today equivalent to roughly US$2 million, to the college that would be renamed in his honor after his death. In addition to launching America’s oldest university, Harvard’s donation began a tradition of philanthropy for U.S. colleges and universities that has continued ever since. Today, philanthropy is an important source of higher education funding that covers an average of 10% of college and university budgets . Based on our decades of experience as scholars , academic administrators and school fundraisers , we believe that donors – and not just big ones – are especially important to colleges and universities in tough times. In the crosshairs Since January 2025, the Trump administration has targeted colleges and universities with research funding cuts , student financial aid caps and new restrictions on how long international students can stay in the United States . University endowments have been in the crosshairs since the first Trump administration’s 2017 tax reform package . The big 2025 tax-and-spending package Trump signed raised the taxes on some schools’ endowments . A rule the Trump administration proposed in September 2026 would threaten private schools’ tax-exempt status if any of their programs use race-based criteria. There are demographic problems too. Fewer students are choosing to go to college, and the number of high school graduates who could attend is falling due to a declining birthrate . Although colleges and universities are providing more financial aid than ever , students and their families are still struggling to pay for college . Some schools are being forced to close their doors. Sixteen colleges shut down in 2025 alone , including Indiana’s only predominantly Black college, Martin University, and ecologically focused Sterling College in Vermont. And at least 40 colleges have been acquired by other schools since 2020, including Marymount Manhattan College and Mills College , which are now part of Northeastern University’s global network. A sticky note spotted at Hampshire College’s Harold F. Johnson Library on May 16, 2026, months before the school was slated to be closed for good, assured students that alumni would support them. Finn Gomez/The Boston Globe via Getty Images Higher education giving Donors contributed $79 billion to colleges and universities in 2025, up 4% in constant dollars from the year before. The richest Americans dominate giving to higher education: 89% of the funds raised came from only 2% of donors in 2025. Also in 2025, Phil and Penny Knight, the Nike co-founder and his wife, made what was then the largest single gift to a university in history when they gave the Oregon Health & Science University $2 billion for cancer research . On Sept. 30, 2026, investor Ken Griffin broke that record by giving Carnegie Mellon University more than $3 billion to build a new campus in Miami and meet some other priorities. It’s hardly the only megagift a university has received in 2026: Michael and Susan Dell, whose fortune comes from his computer hardware company, gave the University of Texas at Austin $750 million for its medical center. The Knights gave $1 billion to the University of Oregon for a new engineering college. Software billionaire David Duffield pledged $371 million to Cornell University . And many other schools have drawn gifts in excess of $100 million . The vast majority of these huge gifts are reserved for specific purposes . The share of totally unrestricted gifts to colleges and universities , those given with no strings attached, has been dwindling for decades . In 2024 it slipped below 7% . Unrestricted giving did pick up somewhat in 2025 . Perhaps that was a sign that some donors were responding to federal funding cuts with their gifts. Michael Dell, CEO of Dell Computer, and his wife Susan have given more than $1 billion to the University of Texas at Austin, with much of that funding reserved for specific purposes. Robert Daemmrich Photography Inc/Corbis via Getty Images How donors can help In an article in Change: The Magazine of Higher Learning in September 2026, we listed ideas for college and university fundraising efforts. These tie to three recommendations for donors – and not only those making multimillion-dollar gifts. 1. Pooling donations Donations to colleges and universities don’t have to end in lots of zeros to make a big difference. In 2015, the grassroots Saving Sweet Briar campaign kept the small women’s college operating even after its trustees had voted to close it. The largest gift the rural Virginia school received was $2 million, and the smallest was $1.50 from a graduate’s grandchild. This is the exception rather than the rule. Financial pressures were too much for Hampshire College, a New England private college that is slated to close after the fall semester of 2026, to withstand – even with a fundraising campaign and $5 million gift from alum and documentary filmmaker Ken Burns. Giving Days are high-profile fundraising campaigns through which many alumni and other supporters raise millions. For example, Oregon State University Dam Proud Day 2026 drew 12,400 gifts and raised over $4.1 million. Purdue University’s annual “day of giving” has generated nearly $500 million over the past decade. In 2024, it garnered $76 million from 32,000 donors. Sweet Briar College alumni take a selfie in 2015 at a pop-up fundraiser to save the womens’ college in Virginia. Evelyn Hockstein/For The Washington Post via Getty Images 2. Donating with few or no strings attached Donations with few restrictions or none at all help colleges and universities meet their greatest needs. Even if they’re mostly intended for a new building or to fund a particular program, large gifts can also include unrestricted portions to help cover costs as needs arise and priorities change. Brandeis University , Indiana University , Princeton University and other schools encourage unrestricted annual gifts. These flexible funds are helping to cover research funding shortfalls at Cornell University, undergraduate scholarships at Georgetown University and general operations at the College of the Atlantic. Novelist and philanthropist MacKenzie Scott, the former wife of Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, has given more than $26 billion in unrestricted donations to nonprofits, including to colleges and universities. Historically Black colleges and universities as well as other schools with diverse student bodies , such as Robeson Community College in rural North Carolina, Oklahoma’s Carl Albert State College and Wisconsin’s Fond du Lac Tribal and Community College, have received Scott’s big gifts. events.title: 7 red flags to look out for when getting a manicure, according to salon owners
events.summary: There are a few things clients should look out for before sitting down for a manicure. ViewStock/Shutterstock Business Insider asked salon owners about the red flags to watch out for when getting a manicure. Unidentifiable products and overly aggressive techniques can make for a poor experience. Look for dirty or loose tools and poor ventilation when entering a salon. Whether you want a Japanese gel manicure or French tips for your next big event, choosing the right nail salon is crucial to achieving the look you desire and preserving your long-term nail health. That's why Business Insider asked salon owners about the red flags clients should look out for when getting a manicure at a new salon. Here's what they said. Check to make sure your nail tech isn’t using dirty tools. Lipatova Maryna/Shutterstock Patricia Reign, a licensed manicurist and the owner of Traveling Aura Mobile Spa in Florida, told BI that one of the most important things to check for before getting a manicure is that the tools are properly sanitized. "Tools like nail clippers, cuticle nippers, and pushers should be taken from a clean, sealed packet — which often indicates the salon uses an autoclave, a professional-grade sterilization device," Reign said. "However, be cautious. Some salons may use these packets without sterilizing the tools." She added that if the nail technician pulls tools directly from a drawer, they may have been placed there after being used on another client. Misused sanitization boxes can also be an issue. webphotographeer/Getty Images Amy Ling Lin, CEO and founder of the nail-care brand and NYC salon chain Sundays , told BI that misusing sanitization equipment, notably LED-light sanitization boxes, is just as bad for clients as using dirty implements. "For salons that use an LED light sanitization box, ensure no paper towels are under the tool plates. Paper towels can block the light, preventing proper sterilization of the tools," Lin said. Beware of unusual odors and poor ventilation in the salon. Edvard Nalbantjan/Shutterstock Reign told BI that unusual odors in a salon are a major red flag health-wise. "Any strange or strong odors in the salon could signal poor ventilation or the use of low-quality products, which might contain harmful chemicals," Reign said. "A salon should be well-ventilated and free from overpowering chemical smells." A messy workstation is a no-go. Patricio Nahuelhual/Getty Images Jessie Pang, owner of New York-based business Jessie P Nails , told BI that a messy workstation containing spilled nail products or personal items is one of the biggest red flags to watch out for. She said to take note of any nail clippings, food crumbs, or stains left at the station. "Cleanliness should be the priority at the station," Pang said. Unidentifiable products are often a bad sign. Anton Starikov/Shutterstock High-quality salons will typically use well-known, professional products, according to Reign. "If the products being used are not clearly labeled or identifiable, this could be a sign that the salon isn't using professional-grade products," Reign told BI. Don't hesitate to ask questions about any of the products a nail technician uses. Not including nail preparation and cuticle care in the service can lead to poor results. Marc Calleja Lopez/Getty Images According to Kasia Pukeca, owner of Gloss Nail Co. in Florida, some salons don't offer full manicures as part of services like gel polish or dipping powder. However, she said things like nail preparation and cuticle care are a must. "There is no way to achieve an ideal product application if the nail plate and cuticles are improperly prepared," Pukeca said. Overly aggressive techniques during a service can cause issues for the client. Yuliia Pavaliuk/Getty Images Monica Victoria, owner of Nail Garden Austin , encourages all salon goers to pay attention to any pain or discomfort they experience during their manicures. "Aggressive filing, cutting, or scraping of cuticles or nails can lead to small cuts or tears in the skin, resulting in open wounds, infections, or long-term damage to your nails and the surrounding skin," Victoria said. The best way to avoid long-lasting, unnecessary issues from aggressive techniques is to tell your technician to stop as soon as possible. "Promptly addressing these issues allows the technician to adjust their technique or properly clean and disinfect the area to prevent further harm," Victoria told BI. This story was originally published on April 22, 2025, and most recently updated on October 12, 2026. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Egypt’s press union chief rejects pressure over detained journalists
events.summary: Six journalists from independent platform Matsadaash allege torture in detention, which Egypt denies. The head of Egypt’s Journalists Syndicate has insisted the organisation will continue to fight for press freedom after it came under fire for defending six journalists who were detained last month and charged with joining a “terrorist” group. “What happens to one colleague affects us all, and may happen to others tomorrow,” Khaled Elbalshy said in a statement on Sunday. “An infringement of one journalist’s freedom is an infringement of everyone’s freedom and a weakening of the safeguards protecting that freedom.” list 1 of 3 Deadly gold mine air strikes highlight Egypt-Sudan border insecurity list 2 of 3 Israeli academic and Al Jazeera contributor Ori Goldberg dies at 50 list 3 of 3 If Netanyahu goes, does anything really change for Palestinians? His comments came after the syndicate filed a complaint with Egypt’s public prosecutor over allegations that the detained journalists, who work for the investigative website Matsadaash, had been tortured. Egyptian authorities denied the accusations, while pro-government commentators criticised the organisation for defending the journalists. Mohamed Adel, Mohamed Ashraf Abu Emeira, Islam Barakat, Omar Helal, Mohamed Mahmoud and Abdallah Qadry were arrested on September 28 and 29 and have since appeared before the Supreme State Security Prosecution, which prosecutes national security cases. They have been ordered to be held in pretrial detention for 15 days pending investigations. Egyptian prosecutors have accused the six journalists of working for a media organisation tied to the Muslim Brotherhood, a group Egyptian authorities have cracked down on for years following a 2013 coup against democratically elected Egyptian President Mohamed Morsi, who was a member. Egypt has officially designated the Muslim Brotherhood as a “terrorist” group, an allegation the organisation has strongly denied, while human rights groups have accused Egyptian authorities of repressing freedoms. Matsadaash co-founder Abdelrahman Mansour has also rejected any links between the media platform and the Muslim Brotherhood. In his statement, Elbalshy said: “The fundamental principle governing all such matters, particularly when dealing with accused persons in general and vulnerable people in particular, remains that an accused person is innocent until proven guilty.” The Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), whose lawyers are representing the six journalists, said they were initially held for five days without any contact with their families or lawyers. After complaints, the journalists appeared before prosecutors and were questioned in the presence of their lawyers and a representative from the Journalists Syndicate. The EIPR said the journalists were being held under Egypt’s 2015 Counterterrorism Law that allows for suspects to be held in custody before appearing before prosecutors “when there is a risk of a terrorist crime and a necessity to confront that risk”. The rights group, however, noted that the prosecution only alleges that the journalists published rumours or “false” reports. “The public prosecution should have identified the imminent terrorist threat that required denying them their right to appear before a judicial authority within 24 hours of their arrest,” the EIPR said on October 7. The EIPR has also said that most of the six journalists said they were tortured following their arrests, including being beaten and subjected to electric shocks. It added that several of the detained had been forced to record fabricated confessions. Egypt’s Interior Ministry has rejected the allegations. Matsadaash was founded in 2018 as a fact-checking platform, but has since expanded into investigative journalism. Its website is blocked in Egypt, but it has more than 1.3 million followers on Facebook. The outlet has previously faced pressure from Egyptian authorities, including in 2023, when one of its journalists, Karim Asaad, was arrested after Matsadaash published an investigation into a suspected smuggling scandal involving a plane that had flown from Cairo to Zambia. He was later released.

events.title: Disney's new CTO tells staff he 'won't pretend it will be easy' to win in the changing media landscape
events.summary: Disney hired Karandeep Anand from Character.AI to oversee its technology strategy. Manaure Quintero / AFP via Getty Images; Illustration by Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via Getty Images New Disney tech chief Karandeep Anand told staffers he's optimistic, despite difficult competition. In a note, Anand said Disney is "uniquely positioned to win" but "won't pretend" it will be easy. Read Anand's full memo to Disney employees after his first full week. Disney's new tech chief said in a memo to employees that he "won't pretend it will be easy" to win in the changing media environment. Karandeep Anand, the Mouse House's first-ever companywide CTO, was hired by CEO Josh D'Amaro to lead Disney's tech transformation. He started in early October. Under D'Amaro, Disney is investing in tech to better compete with Netflix and YouTube in streaming. Anand previously ran Character.AI, an AI startup that Disney sent a cease-and-desist letter to last fall. (Disney told Character.AI not to make chatbots from its copyrighted characters without permission, and the startup complied.) Anand told staffers on Friday afternoon that the media business is "at an inflection point," adding that he's confident Disney has a strong hand thanks to its deep, iconic content library and a passionate fan base. "With our rich IP and global fan community, I strongly believe we are uniquely positioned to win," Anand said in his memo, which was obtained by Business Insider. The new tech chief said that winning in this highly competitive media landscape "will take focus, speed, and the willingness to say no to good ideas so we can say yes to great ones." Anand also said he's "admired Disney for as long as I can remember" and said he had constructive conversations in his first full week inside the Mouse House. "What stands out most is the talent and care this team puts into its work, the craft Disney has perfected, and the strong foundation you've built," Anand said. Disney has leaned into tech this year by embracing AI and further unifying Disney+ and Hulu — the first step in building a streaming super app that includes games and merchandise . Anand highlighted the same three top priorities that D'Amaro listed in the memo announcing his hire: great storytelling as our North Star, technology in service of creativity, and operating as One Disney. D'Amaro is contending with Disney's listless stock price. Shares have fallen more than 1% in the past year, compared to a 17.3% gain for the S&P 500, and are down over 38% in the past five years, while US stocks broadly have risen more than 74%. Read Anand's full memo below: Team, As I close out my first week at Disney, thank you for the warm welcome you gave me and the colleagues who joined me. I've admired Disney for as long as I can remember, so walking the lot, attending the Tech Showcase, and meeting so many of you has been an unforgettable start. What stands out most is the talent and care this team puts into its work, the craft Disney has perfected, and the strong foundation you've built. It's only been a few days, but I'm more excited than when I accepted this job. Josh has laid out three priorities: great storytelling as our North Star, technology in service of creativity, and operating as One Disney. Our job in technology is to make those real, and the possibilities are enormous. We're at an inflection point in the tech and media industry, and with our rich IP and global fan community, I strongly believe we are uniquely positioned to win. I won't pretend it will be easy. It will take focus, speed, and the willingness to say no to good ideas so we can say yes to great ones. I'll be direct with you about priorities and tradeoffs as I learn them. But I'm confident we can get there, and do it quickly. Over the coming weeks I'll be meeting with teams across the company, and I look forward to sharing how I'm thinking about our priorities soon. Until then, please keep doing the great work you're doing. Thank you again. I'm glad and privileged to be on this team. Karan Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: UK PM Andy Burnham met Man City chairman during time as Manchester mayor
events.summary: Statement comes after criticism of Burnham’s initial response ⁠to City being found guilty of serious financial breaches. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham met Manchester City Chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak at an investment summit several years ago when he was mayor of the city, the Greater Manchester Combined Authority has said. The announcement on Monday comes after Burnham said he would be “really concerned” if City’s owners sold the football club following the decision to find the 10-time English champions guilty of breaching the Premier League’s financial rules. Burnham, who was mayor of Greater Manchester from 2017 to June 2026, faced criticism for appearing to express support for City’s hierarchy. Downing Street subsequently had to backtrack, insisting no one was “above the rules”. But there were demands for clarification regarding Burnham’s relationship with City’s owners, who have driven significant investment in Manchester through partnerships with local authorities. City are owned by Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG), controlled by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, a member of the United Arab Emirates’ royal family. A Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) spokesman said: “In October 2021, Andy Burnham, in his role as mayor of Greater Manchester, had a formal meeting with Khaldoon Al Mubarak at the UK Government’s Global Investment Summit arranged by the Department for International Trade. “In his capacity as mayor, he was a guest of Manchester City FC at home matches on a small number of occasions, including attending Vincent Kompany’s testimonial match in September 2019, where he met the chairman informally in the stands. These have been declared in the usual way.” The statement added that during Burnham’s time as mayor “representatives of Greater Manchester sporting clubs would routinely join business delegations as part of mayoral international visits. “This included representatives from Manchester United travelling to Austin and Dublin, Lancashire Cricket Club joining a delegation to India, and Manchester City FC staff supporting visits to China and Japan.” But Louie French, the opposition Conservatives spokesman for sport, said the statement contained “precious little information about these meetings, what was discussed and what may have been agreed”. It was far “from the full transparency that football fans deserve. Burnham cannot hide behind the GMCA – he must take responsibility for this himself”, French added. City have been found guilty of breaking more than 100 Premier League financial regulations by arranging “sham” contracts to artificially inflate revenues and reduce costs in a nine-season run between 2009 and 2018. The Premier League leaders have appealed against the verdict, saying it contains “clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe”. City could be hit with a huge points deduction or even face expulsion from the Premier League if they lose the appeal.

events.title: Stolen Renoir paintings found behind wall in France following arrests
events.summary: Renoir art heist suspects were planning ‘imminent’ second robbery, prosecutors say. Two paintings by the impressionist master Renoir which were stolen from a French museum last month have been found damaged behind a false wall in a private home after police made several arrests ahead of what prosecutors say was an imminent second heist. Marseille prosecutor Nicolas Bessone said six suspects were arrested on Wednesday after authorities discovered they were planning to target the Fondation Maeght in Saint-Paul-de-Vence, home to one of Europe’s largest collections of modern art. Bessone said the arrests were prompted by the “very strong suspicion that another heist was imminent”. “We were very clearly looking at the repetition of a criminal scheme”, said Eric Antonetti, the head of the Alpes-Maritimes judicial police. On September 8, thieves used an electric saw to cut through a fence to enter the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer on the French Riviera, according to investigators. An alarm sounded and police officers arrived four minutes later, a swift response that “apparently caused the perpetrators to panic,” Bessone said. The stolen works, “Madame Colonna Romano” and “Young Woman at the Well” by impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir, were valued at about 4.2m euros ($4.7m), Bessone said. The thieves also attempted to steal two other Renoir paintings, “Madame Pichon” and “Coco Reading”, which depicts Renoir’s young ‌son ‌Claude. They abandoned them in the museum gardens while fleeing police. “As they fled, they were unable to take all four paintings and abandoned two of them, which were later found in a protective sleeve,” he said. The paintings were found hidden behind a false wall in a house on Friday. Both works were damaged and will need ⁠restoration. One of the paintings, “Madame Colonna Romano”, had been torn. “These two paintings are not simply works of art. They are part of our city’s history,” Bryan Masson, the mayor of Cagnes-sur-Mer, near Nice, said on Friday. “Knowing they have been recovered is an immense relief.” The recovery came almost exactly one month ⁠after the theft, following an investigation that used ⁠DNA evidence, mobile phone geolocation data and surveillance video. The two key suspects include a 29-year-old, who was charged after investigators recovered DNA from a bag left behind during the getaway. They ⁠were charged with organised theft and other offences. A third man, accused of hiding the paintings, was charged with organised handling of stolen goods. A fourth suspect, who investigators say was approached about buying the artworks, was charged ‌with handling stolen goods and taking part in a criminal conspiracy. Bessone said the suspects had denied planning a second museum raid, but he added that he did “not believe the principal suspect visited that ‌museum simply out of a love of art”.

events.title: Ethiopian forces enter strategic Tigray town of Adwa, witnesses say
events.summary: Ethiopian Airlines resumed flights to Tigray’s capital, Mekelle, on Sunday. Ethiopian government forces have entered the town of Adwa without a fight, days after capturing Adigrat from rebel fighters as flights resumed to Mekelle in the country’s northern Tigray region. Residents of the northwestern town of Adwa, roughly 40km (24 miles) from Eritrea’s border, said federal forces and an allied militia entered the town on Sunday, a day after the withdrawal of fighters from the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). list 1 of 3 Ethiopia, Eritrea ramp up rhetoric: Are they inching towards war? list 2 of 3 At least 139 dead, 84 missing as migrant boat capsizes off Djibouti list 3 of 3 Eritrea urges UN to intervene in standoff with Ethiopia TPLF Vice President Amanuel Assefa said he “did not wish to comment”. “All the shops in the town are closed. Last night, many government institutions, including Adwa Hospital, were looted,” Aferwerki, a local resident who gave only one name, told AFP. Conflict monitor ACLED said that Ethiopian drone strikes targeted a hotel in Adwa on October 4, wounding between “five and nine people, including security personnel”, who were taken to hospital. Some ACLED sources indicated that TPLF Chairman Debretsion Gebremichael and other senior officials were at the hotel, but stressed the information had not been verified. Another resident who requested anonymity confirmed the TPLF forces withdrew from Adwa but said that although government forces were deployed in the town, they had not reached the centre. “The roads are deserted. People are very afraid of theft,” he said. Last week, Ethiopian forces captured Tigray’s regional capital Mekelle, days after the TPLF confirmed that it had withdrawn from the city and moved its regional administration “temporarily” to another location. Ethiopian Airlines resumed flights from the capital, Addis Abba, to Mekelle on Sunday for the first time since September 23, when a seven-group armed alliance , including the TPLF, started fighting Ethiopian forces and captured the airport. “I would like to assure you on this occasion that we will bring visible change, a change beyond mere hope,” Getachew Reda, a former Tigray leader who now advises Ethiopia’s Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed told supporters greeting Reda and Ethiopia’s intelligence chief Redwan Hussein at Mekelle airport. Ethiopia has accused Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt of backing the rebel alliance. Khartoum and Cairo have denied involvement. Eritrea, which fought alongside Ethiopia’s federal army in the 2020-2022 war, severed diplomatic ties with Ethiopia over the accusations last week.

events.title: Meet the Anthropic Engineer Keeping Its AI Agent Trustworthy
events.summary: If you’ve ever wondered how Claude and similar AI agents can answer complex questions in seconds and where they get the information, you’re not alone. Gurmeet Saran works to find that answer every day as an engineer at Anthropic in San Francisco, the AI research company behind Claude. The IEEE senior member is developing an infrastructure to understand the mechanics behind the chatbot’s behavior and to ensure its underlying architecture produces reliable outputs. Gurmeet Saran Employer Anthropic in San Francisco Title Member of technical staff Member grade IEEE senior member Alma maters University of Kalyani, in India; Birla Institute of Technology and Science, in Pilani, India “My job is to make sure the data is accurate, structured, and trustworthy, and that private data stays private,” he says. “As I learned earlier in my career, privacy can’t be a layer you bolt on—it has to be part of the architecture from the start.” If you can’t trust the logic, he adds, you can’t make reliable claims about the behavior, and that has real safety implications. Safety is a priority for Anthropic, he says. According to Claude’s mission statement , the company wants the AI agent to be “genuinely helpful to the people it works with or on behalf of, as well as to society, while avoiding actions that are unsafe, unethical, or deceptive.” Crucial to the mission is ensuring that researchers can observe and understand how AI models behave, a challenge that is especially acute for large language models , Saran says. “We have decent tools to monitor databases and web services,” he says, “but for LLMs, we’re still figuring it out.” Solving data quality problems at Yahoo, Intuit, and Meta Saran’s interest in computing systems dates back to his childhood in Kolkata, where he logged as much time as he could in the school computer lab. “I remember the first time I used one of the computers,” he says. “What struck me was that you could write instructions, and the machine would follow them exactly. No ambiguity. “That felt magical to me.” After graduating from high school in 1999, he stayed in India to pursue advanced degrees. He earned a bachelor’s degree in electronics and telecommunication engineering in 2004 at the University of Kalyani . In 2010, he earned a master’s degree in software engineering from the Birla Institute of Technology and Science in Pilani. While a graduate student, he began his career in 2007 at Yahoo as a technical lead of the data team in Bengaluru, India. While there, he encountered the project that shaped his career trajectory: working on web analytics and business intelligence reporting solutions. “We kept running into a frustrating problem,” he recalls. “Different teams would calculate the same website metric—something like daily active site users—using slightly different logic, and end up with conflicting answers. It sounds like a small issue, but when leadership is making decisions about resource allocation and product development using that data, not knowing which number is correct becomes a problem.” The team built a central data repository with defined metrics, essentially serving as a single source of truth. Saran created a model that defined what “daily active site users” means, breaking down which events counted, how to handle edge cases (or when standard code fails), and more. With the new model, data teams across the company could rely on a standard method to determine the number of daily active users for the projects and sites they were responsible for and obtain comparable results using the same logic. From there, Saran and his team built Yahoo! Digits , an internal web analytics tool used for all the company’s products. Saran left Yahoo in 2010 to join Intuit as a staff engineer in Mountain View, Calif. He helped build the analytics infrastructure that unified data across the company’s products, including TurboTax and QuickBooks accounting software. During his tenure, Intuit developed a feature that detected fraudulent tax filings in real time. It required Saran and other engineers to build a system to protect taxpayer data while adhering to strict U.S. Internal Revenue Service policies. “IEEE operates in a lot of countries where engineers don’t have easy pathways into the global professional community. That kind of connection matters as AI development spreads beyond a handful of organizations.” “This taught me that privacy and governance can’t be layers you bolt onto software after the fact,” he says. “They have to be part of the architecture from the start.” Saran joined Meta (known as Facebook at the time) in 2016 as a lead software engineer in Menlo Park, Calif. The company was facing controversy over its video metrics: Meta publicly acknowledged an error that caused it to overstate the number of views for posted videos . “This wasn’t a coding bug; it was an architectural problem,” Saran says. He built a system that worked similarly to what he had developed at Intuit, whereby one single truth was defined to govern all video view metrics across the site. That system, Metric360 , eventually became part of the site’s architecture. By the time he left Meta in 2021, he says, Metric360 was being used across the company to calculate video metrics. He left the company to become a principal software engineer at Wealthfront , a financial services company in Palo Alto, Calif. He helped build the company’s data infrastructure. Building trustworthy AI systems at Anthropic Saran joined Anthropic in 2025 as a member of the technical staff. To describe the implications of his work, he uses a medical analogy: “Imagine a doctor is monitoring a patient’s vital signs and making treatment decisions based on those numbers. What if one or a few of the medical devices used were slightly miscalibrated? Even if most readings are fine, it’s a serious problem because the difficult decisions happen in the margins. “It’s the same with AI systems. My job is essentially to make sure the instruments are giving accurate readings—that the data means what it says it means.” His job comes with high stakes and complex problems to solve. “ AI agents are especially tricky to observe,” he says. “When a system is taking sequences of actions [generating conversational responses with different users], you need a way to capture what it did, what information it was working from, and whether outcomes matched what the end user expected. And you have to do all of that without exposing anyone’s private information—the systems are designed to recognize sensitive data and keep it protected as it flows through. It’s a much more demanding observability problem than anything I’ve worked on before.” Solving for system reliability while AI is still in its early days of adoption is both Saran’s passion and the problem that keeps him up at night, he says. “I think making AI systems genuinely auditable and transparent is one of the more important engineering problems of the next decade,” he says, “and it does

events.title: Korean cosmetic surgery events raise Australian regulatory concerns
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts South Korean company cancels cosmetic surgery event after ABC raises questions A South Korean cosmetic surgery company has cancelled a Sydney event where prospective patients were due to meet Korean doctors. The company had been questioned about promotions featuring doctors who were not registered to practise in Australia. Women who travel to South Korea for procedures are documenting the process online. A South Korean cosmetic surgery company has cancelled a Sydney event where prospective patients were due to meet Korean doctors, after questions were raised by the ABC. The two-day, appointment-only event was advertised by South Korean company Restory Plastic Surgery, featuring two doctors who were not registered to practise in Australia. Examples of some of the advertisements promoting the now cancelled Korean surgeons' visit. ( Supplied: Restory Plastic Surgery ) National laws prohibit doctors who are not registered in Australia from providing medical consultations or services in the country. Previous advertising stated both doctors would attend the event. ( Supplied ) In response to questions about the event and the legalities of foreign doctors providing medical consultations in Australia, the South Korean company pulled down its advertising. "Dr. I Yung Moon and Dr. Myung Joon Lee will not be travelling to Australia and will not be attending the Sydney event," the company told the ABC. "We acknowledge that the presentation of the promotional material may have created the impression that the doctors themselves would be travelling to Sydney, and we would like to clarify that this is not the case." Pia Marshall documented her procedure on social media. ( Supplied/ABC News: Pete Mullins ) The ABC understands similar medical expo events are held regularly, prompting warnings from Australia's peak plastic surgery body about the risks of overseas procedures and the rules governing medical advertising. Sunshine Coast woman Pia Marshall met a different Korean cosmetic surgery company in Melbourne last year at an expo similar to the one that was due to be held in Sydney. She said meeting patients at events like these appeared to be common practice, but after doing her own research, she decided to undergo the procedure with a different surgeon. The marketing specialist travelled to South Korea with her mother, Marion, for matching face lifts and documented their experiences online. The women, aged 41 and 69, travelled to Incheon, a city bordering Seoul, in June to undergo deep-plane face lifts, neck lifts and lower mid-face lifts. The procedures, performed under general anaesthetic, typically take several hours and involve repositioning the skin and underlying tissues to restore facial contours. The Australian Society of Plastic Surgeons (ASPS) confirmed wound infection and haematoma, when blood collects under the skin, were the most common face lift complications requiring operative intervention. The mother and daughter said South Korea's reputation for skin care, known as K-beauty, and the growing number of social media testimonials made it an "obvious choice", even though the face lifts themselves were not significantly different from procedures available in Australia. Pia Marshall spent 14 days in South Korea for the procedures. ( ABC News: Mark Leonardi ) Australia is now the second-highest-spending K-beauty market per capita globally , behind only South Korea, according to data from Future Market Insights. Pia was quoted $36,000 for the procedures, including accommodation and 14 days in South Korea. However, she negotiated a social media agreement with the company but could not disclose the details of the arrangement. Testimonial-style advertising for cosmetic surgery is prohibited when promoting a health service provided by an Australian-registered practitioner, but the same restrictions do not apply to overseas practitioners. A face lift in Australia typically starts at around $25,000, according to the ASPS, with the cost increasing depending on the surgeon, procedure and complexity. Pia said she found overseas cosmetic surgery options more accessible than those in Australia, due to Australia's strict advertising rules. Influencers are advertising the surgery. ( Graphic: ABC News ) While Pia said she did extensive research before her surgery, other influencers documenting their experiences have taken a more casual approach to discussing the risks. Ruby Tuesday Matthews is a 33-year-old Byron Bay content creator who specialises in lifestyle and luxury content and recently documented her own face lift.

events.title: Meta releases its first frontier model, Muse Wonder
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Meta’s Superintelligence Lab released a pair of new state-of-the-art models on Monday, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, representing the company’s first attempt at a frontier model. Where Muse Spark aimed to be a lightweight model that could perform at low latency, the Wonder models are larger and said to be more capable, with higher benchmark scores and better results on complex tasks like coding. According to Meta’s testing (presented in the model card ), Wonder and Wonder Full achieve comparable benchmark scores to Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra. “Together, they mark the next step on our scaling ladder and a major leap toward personal superintelligence,” Meta’s blog post about the models reads. That scale is reflected in the pricing: Accessed through the Meta Model API, Wonder will cost $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, making it roughly equivalent in cost to GPT-6 Sol or Opus 5.5. Notably, Wonder Full will only be available to Muse Code subscribers and will not be served through the API. Both models will also be used to power the Muse agent. In keeping with Meta’s interest in developing personal assistants that can perform tasks over a long period, the company placed particular emphasis on the new models’ ability to retain and synthesize information given by the user, a property Meta calls “active memory.” To achieve better recall, Meta highlighted the MemoryBench benchmark , which challenges continual learning and memory construction frameworks. According to the company’s testing, Muse Wonder now scores higher on MemoryBench than Fable, Opus, or Astra. “We put a tremendous amount of effort into making sure your model can remember what’s important to you over days, weeks, months, and beyond,” said research scientist Kavya Kopparapu in a video accompanying the launch. The new models are the first frontier model release since Scale AI founder Alexandr Wang restructured Meta’s AI efforts in August of last year . Since then, Meta has released its lightweight Muse Spark model and Muse agent but has avoided the kind of state-of-the-art model releases OpenAI and Anthropic are known for. According to the post, the models were trained at Meta’s Prometheus data center in central Ohio , which came online earlier this year. events.title: Zohran Mamdani orders use-of-force review for New York City police
events.summary: A city spokesperson says the calls for reform are not connected to the police response to an ICE shooting last week. Mayor Zohran Mamdani has ordered a review of the New York City Police Department’s use of force for the first time in a decade amid renewed pressure from his progressive base for law enforcement reform. On Monday, the city said it would introduce a “package of reforms” in addition to the review, to “strengthen accountability when police officers are accused of serious misconduct”. list 1 of 4 Mamdani, Irish PM play bingo, ‘split the G’ in New York list 2 of 4 New York Mayor Mamdani under fire for attending October 7 vigil list 3 of 4 ICE shooting of New York man in car with five-year-old sparks protests list 4 of 4 DHS defends ICE shooting in NYC, says officers believed they were in danger The New York Police Department (NYPD) is the largest police force in the United States. The reforms follow the retirement of a police officer involved in the shooting death of 19-year-old Win Rozario during a reported mental health crisis in 2024. “That officer retired before a disciplinary trial could take place,” the mayor’s office said in a statement. Among other measures Mamdani announced is $2.6m in additional funding for the Office of the Inspector General, which investigates NYPD policies and misconduct. Monday’s statement also calls for a new notification system to ensure disciplinary hearings are completed before an officer retires, and it includes a renewed push for the department to comply with state-level reporting requirements about police-involved deaths. The announcement comes amid pressure from Mamdani’s fellow progressives to enforce accountability at the city’s police department. Much of the focus has fallen on a division within the NYPD called the Strategic Response Group, a rapid-response unit that addresses protests, major events and “civil disorder”. Earlier this month, 17 state-level politicians and political nominees, including congressional candidates Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier, called for the group to be disbanded. Both Valdez and Chevalier were endorsed by Mamdani. In a statement, the politicians denounced the Strategic Response Group’s deployment during protests against a recent US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) operation. On October 8, an ICE officer shot 28-year-old Oscar Belgal while he was inside an SUV last week with his five-year-old son. The shooting, which took place in New York’s Marble Hill neighbourhood, sparked days of demonstrations against ICE’s tactics, as well as a police response. Chevalier wrote in a post on social media that she was “shoved to the ground by an officer” during the protests. She also claimed to have observed other instances of excessive violence. “When I was in Marble Hill last night I saw NYPD officers rapidly escalating violence,” Chevalier said. “I witnessed unmarked law enforcement cars hitting protesters as NYPD officers pushed people out of its path.” Mamdani condemned the shooting and called for Belgal’s release from federal custody. Critics have frequently pointed to such incidents as examples of why greater police oversight is necessary. Reported use of force within the NYPD has increased over the last decade, including physical force, the deployment of firearms, and the use of electrical weapons like tasers. There were 12,348 reported use-of-force incidents in 2025, compared with 4,087 in 2016, when the department first started collecting such statistics. Crime in New York City, however, has been on the downturn. Earlier this month, the city reported the “fewest shooting incidents, shooting victims, and murders” in the first nine months of the year and in the third quarter of the year, compared with any time in recorded history. Major crime, which includes murder, rape, felony assault and grand larceny, declined 9.4 percent in the third quarter and 6.6 percent compared with the same period last year. Still, Chevalier and other progressive politicians remained critical of the excess force authorised under the city’s police leadership. They have called on Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch, who was originally appointed by Mamdani’s predecessor, Eric Adams, to step down. The commissioner is appointed by the mayor. She can be removed either by the mayor or the governor of New York State. According to recent reporting from The Atlantic magazine, New York State Governor Kathy Hochul made retaining Tisch as police commissioner a condition of her endorsement for Mamdani in the 2024 mayoral election. In a statement to the magazine, Mamdani questioned that framing, saying Hochul’s support for keeping Tisch was “more of a recommendation” than a demand. A New York City Hall spokesperson told Al Jazeera that the use-of-force review was already in the works prior to the October 8 ICE shooting and the protests that followed.

events.title: Simulating student learning for better AI tutoring
events.summary: By Ke Yang , PhD Student Chenglong Wang , Senior Researcher Michel Galley , Senior Principal Research Manager Chandan Singh , Senior Researcher Jeevana Priya Inala , Senior Researcher ChengXiang Zhai , Professor, University of Illinois Department of Computer Science Jianfeng Gao , Technical Fellow & Corporate Vice President StudentSim is a research system for evaluating and improving AI tutors before they are tested with real learners; it is not a product, is not deployed in classrooms, and is not intended to replace teachers AI tutoring tools need feedback from students to improve, but collecting that feedback through human studies is slow, costly, and difficult to scale StudentSim trains personalized AI student simulators from publicly available, de-identified learner records, with one simulator adapted to each student The work evaluates simulators along two education-grounded dimensions: whether they respond like a specific student, and whether they update after tutor guidance Across chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics, StudentSim outperforms leading baselines and provides a useful feedback signal for training an AI tutor In research settings, teams are exploring how AI-powered tutoring systems can help explain a math problem, suggest an edit to a writing assignment, or guide a learner through a chess position. Yet the quality of teaching cannot be measured only from the tutor’s answer. A tutor needs to know what happens after the guidance reaches a student. Did the student correct the original mistake? Did the hint help them reason toward the answer, or did it give away too much? Would a different student need a different kind of support? In today’s AI tutor research, answering these questions often requires real learner studies. Those studies are valuable, but they are slow and costly to run, which makes it hard to use student feedback during fast model iteration. StudentSim is an AI system that creates personalized simulators of individual students, modeling how they answer questions and how their answers change after receiving a tutor’s guidance. The goal is to make student feedback more available during AI tutor development. This research also introduces StudentSimEval, a benchmark and evaluation protocol spanning chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics. Importantly, the goal is not to replace teachers or classroom learning. Instead, StudentSim helps researchers evaluate and improve AI tutoring systems during the research and development process before testing them with real learners. The research uses only publicly available learner datasets released for research use with de-identified records; no personally identifying information is used at any stage. Measuring what a student simulator needs to do A simple way to build a student simulator is to ask a large language model to role-play a learner. For example, a prompt might say, “You are an elementary-school student who struggles with math.” The model can change its tone and express uncertainty. The harder part is preserving the learner’s actual ability boundary. A model may speak in a young student’s voice while still relying on knowledge and reasoning far beyond that student’s level. For training an AI tutor, this can produce misleading feedback: the tutor may appear effective because the simulated student is too capable. Traditional student modeling approaches face a different limitation. Knowledge tracing and behavior prediction models are grounded in real learning records and can estimate a student’s current knowledge, skills, and learning habits. Many of these models, however, were not designed to take natural-language tutor guidance as input. They can help describe what a student has done, but they do not always tell us how a student would respond to a particular explanation, hint, or Socratic question. StudentSim defines the target through two dimensions inspired by education research. Educators often distinguish what a learner can do independently from what they can do with support. Vygotsky’s zone of proximal development captures this gap between current independent performance and performance with guidance. StudentSim turns this idea into two evaluation goals. Behavioral fidelity measures whether a simulator matches a specific student’s recorded responses on held-out problems. Guidance responsiveness measures whether the simulator updates its response after reading tutor guidance. These two goals are complementary. A simulator that only matches past student behavior may be useful for prediction, but it does not show whether a teaching intervention helped. A simulator that always follows the tutor may respond fluently, but it may fail to represent a particular student’s strengths, weaknesses, and likely mistakes. AI tutor training needs both signals: the learner’s starting point and how guidance affects the learner’s performance. Training personalized simulators from sparse student records StudentSimEval is built entirely from publicly available learner datasets that are released for research use with de-identified records. The records carry no personally identifying information, and each personalized simulator is trained only on the de-identified records of the student it represents. Real student data is often sparse at the individual level. A learner may contribute only a small number of essays, answers, or interactions. Training a separate simulator from scratch for each student would risk overfitting and would require each model to relearn common patterns in the domain. StudentSim uses a two-stage training pipeline. In the first stage, the model trains on records pooled across many students in the same domain. This stage learns common response formats, common errors, and common ways students revise after guidance. In the second stage, the model is specialized on one student’s own records, producing a personalized simulator for that student. The evaluation covers three domains with different response types. In chess, the simulator predicts a player’s next move and how that player may revise after coaching. In second-language English writing, it generates essays with error patterns matching a learner and predicts corrections after teacher feedback. In mathematics, it predicts a student’s multiple-choice answer and whether the student updates after an explanation. Across these domains, StudentSimEval uses the same principle: compare all methods on the same per-student training records and the same held-out evaluation records. StudentSim outperforms leading baselines across the three domains. In chess, for example, StudentSim reaches behavioral fidelity of 0.5150 and guidance responsiveness of 0.9067. GPT-5.4 reaches 0.2316 and 0.7186, respectively. Maia2, a chess-specific human move prediction model, reaches 0.4535 and 0.2721.

events.title: U.K. prime minister attributes plot against U.S. bomber base to Iran
events.summary: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the U.K. House of Commons Monday that Iran's Revolutionary Guard was "almost certainly" behind the suspected plot to attack the RAF Fairford base where U.S. bombers were stationed. Why it matters: This was the first time the U.K. officially blamed Iran for the alleged planned attack . What he's saying: "I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by the IRGC. We will not tolerate these threats on our soil," Burnham said. Driving the news: 10 days ago, the U.S. evacuated a dozen B-1 strategic bombers from RAF Fairford in response to intelligence indicating an Iranian drone attack. It would have been an unprecedented and brazen move by Iran against a U.S. base in Europe — with the potential to dramatically escalate the war in the Middle East. The decision to move the bombers came several days after British security forces arrested several dual British-Iranian citizens suspected of planning an attack on the base. It was unclear whether the people who were arrested were connected to the alleged planned drone attack or if they were planning a different attack. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel provided the U.K. with intelligence that pointed to a threat of an Iranian attack. State of play: British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said Monday that the Iranian ambassador was summoned to the foreign office in London to denounce the alleged Iranian plot. The other side: The Iranian ambassador to the UK, Seyed Ali Mousavi, told IRNA that Iran "categorically rejects" the allegations. After his meeting with the UK minister for the Middle East, Stephen Doty, Mousavi said Iran had no involvement in the incident and asked the British government to provide evidence to support its claims. He added that Iran is ready to cooperate with the British authorities in investigating the issue. events.title: Meta debuts Muse Wonder AI model in latest test of users' willingness to pay
events.summary: Meta debuted its latest AI model, Muse Wonder, and says it's the most advanced option for powering digital assistants. To access the model, users of the Muse app will need to sign up to for a monthly subscription plan of $20 or $100. The new model release underscores Meta's efforts to create AI-derived revenue sources outside of online ads. Meta debuted its latest artificial intelligence model, Muse Wonder, and says it's the most advanced option for powering digital assistants. But it doesn't come for free. To access the model, users of the Muse personal agent app will need to sign up for a monthly subscription of $20 or $100. The release underscores Meta's efforts to create new AI-derived revenue sources outside of its core online ad business . Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang said in an interview on Monday that the company developed Muse Wonder, codenamed Watermelon, to improve the capabilities of "personal and professional agents" so they don't stumble on tasks like booking dinner reservations and checking for availabilities. "When you do real-world tasks, you're going to get roadblocks and you're going to get things that come up or various setbacks," Wang said. "We specifically tried to train the model to be able to try other approaches instead of stalling and then checking back in with the user at any time." Meta said in a blog post that the latest model "offers our strongest safeguards to date" against "cyber misuse." Those protections only come with the paid model for now. Muse shot up to the top of Apple's App Store after Meta introduced the AI agent app last month. The app is free, with subscription plans available for more usage. Wang said Meta's AI team has been monitoring for agent-related "incidents or issues" with Muse in order to understand problems and resolve them. Some users have complained on social media that the agent accessed personal messages without authorization, which the company has disputed . Meta is trying to better inform people of how to use the app to avoid certain problems, Wang said. "I think there are certainly instances users have authorized various communications or whatnot earlier in a conversation, and then may have forgotten about that," Wang said. He added that the company is educating users on such matters "to ensure that consumers can trust the product going forward." Muse Wonder will also be available to coders who pay to access the company's related Meta Model API . Wang said that offering will cost more than the standard subscriptions because it is a "much larger model and at frontier level." He said it will still be priced "meaningfully below" leading models from OpenAI and Anthropic. An even more powerful variant of Meta's latest model, dubbed Muse Wonder Full, will only be available to developers who sign up to the company's software engineering focused Muse Code AI agent under a $50 or $200 a month subscription plan. events.title: When AI is subject to less regulation than your fridge, something is startlingly wrong | Richard Hermer
events.summary: When AI is subject to less regulation than your fridge, something is startlingly wrong Let’s be clear: the risk to humanity is unprecedented. Without an urgent public debate and robust use of international law, we will lose control of the future I n my two years as attorney general, I spent more time working on national security than any other issue. The range and gravity of the threats posed to our nation are multifold, from terrorism, armed conflicts and nuclear proliferation, to the impacts of financial insecurity and the climate crisis. All profound challenges, yet ones our superb intelligence and defence communities are well placed to counter. The risk from AI is of an altogether different magnitude, not only in scale, but also because there is a limited time window to address it. The risk is difficult to overestimate: it poses an existential risk to humanity. The lights are flashing red and we must act now before it’s too late. Although the extraordinary threats posed by AI have long been flagged by those closely involved in its creation, it was not until very recently, after the disclosure of the Hugging Face hack and the resignation of Jacob Coxon from Anthropic , that the issue at last started to gain traction in the public discourse. This moment is an opportunity, and to capitalise on it we desperately need increased urgency in international coordination to regulate frontier AI. There must also be meaningful public engagement with how AI should be shaped to benefit humanity, rather than entrench the power of a few. We cannot leave this to China, the US and big tech – we must all demand a voice in the debate. AI has enormous potential benefits for us all. It will be the source of mind-blowing advances in science and medicine, and offers hope for empowerment of some of the world’s most dispossessed people. Yet the risks we are now facing are truly staggering. I would put them in two very broad categories. The first is existential risk: quite literally the possibility that AI could kill billions, either because it enables terrible people to do terrible things – such as design and deploy biological weapons – or because AI itself determines it is more efficient to dispense with humans. The second category is existential challenge – that, left unchecked, the development of AI will deprive billions of us of meaningful agency over our lives, with utterly profound consequences for economies, national security and human happiness. As Bill Gates recently wrote , the AI era will herald “one of the most turbulent times in human history”, noting that it will either be the greatest equaliser ever invented or the worst source of injustice. He is right. On its current trajectory, it risks simultaneously revolutionising the meaning and availability of productive work, while placing unimaginable power in the hands of not only two states (the US and China) but also a small number of individuals who control the tech giants. The plain fact is that we really don’t know what the precise degree of risk is, or the full panorama of the challenge. Part of the problem is that AI is rapidly developing to a level that humans simply do not understand and will reach a point at which – even if they do – they will no longer have the means to control it. Recall that the 2008 financial crash was caused in part because no humans really understood the web of financial transactions that were leading inexorably to disaster. What we face today, though, is on a different scale in terms of the complexity of the systems and the human agency over them, as well as the level of devastation that might be wrought. The startling levels of risk we are discussing should be completely unacceptable to all of us. In today’s age it is unthinkable that the manufacturer of a toaster would be allowed to market a product with a 10% chance of electrocuting you. The case for slowing down frontier AI before we are clear that the risks can be managed is blindingly obvious. AI needs rigorous regulation now. There is more regulation governing the safety of your fridge than the work being undertaken by frontier AI labs that threaten to wipe out your family. It is ludicrous to suggest the industry can be left to regulate itself. The AI companies and the financial markets underpinning them are incentivised to develop new iterations as quickly as possible, all of this fuelled by the geopolitics of the race between China and the US for dominance. The sight of President Trump and Elon Musk on the White House Lawn brandishing a “ voluntary code ” provided little in the way of reassurance. It will be international law that matters. While the UK has shown sterling leadership (started by Rishi Sunak, embraced by Keir Starmer and now reflected in Andy Burnham’s promotion of Kanishka Narayan to cabinet ), the scale of the challenge requires international cooperation to have any effect.
