events.title: Why older Americans' wealth may be helping keep consumer spending strong
events.summary: CNBC Global Financial Wellness Advisory Board A new Principal Financial Group survey, provided exclusively to CNBC, finds baby boomers report greater confidence managing debt and greater satisfaction with their finances than younger generations. New JPMorganChase Institute research shows the share of individuals moving money from investments into checking accounts has more than doubled since 2019. Federal Reserve data shows families headed by someone age 75 or older saw their median net worth rise 37% from 2022 to 2025, while families under 35 experienced a 23% decline. American consumers have continued spending despite persistent pressure from housing costs , debt and everyday expenses . Economists have debated whether we're still in a "K-shaped economy" — where higher-income households' spending masks financial strain among lower- and middle-income Americans. Consumer spending resilience may be better explained by generations than by income differences, said economist Ed Yardeni, president and chief investment strategist of Yardeni Research. He calls it a "G-shaped economy" because it illustrates a generational divide. "If you look at the K economy, it's us versus them; it's the rich versus the poor," Yardeni said. The current economy, he said, "has a lot more to do with age." Yardeni said baby boomers are living longer, staying healthier and staying active longer — and spending more on themselves, their adult children and grandchildren. Plus, older Americans have investments, retirement savings and home equity that can provide greater spending power, he said. "There is an affordability crisis. It's for younger people. Older folks, seniors, have accumulated an enormous amount of net worth," he said. A new survey by Principal Financial Group, provided exclusively to CNBC, found that 53% of baby boomers said they felt able to manage their debt, compared with 42% of Generation X and millennials, and 39% of Generation Z. The findings come from a U.S. consumer survey fielded from April 17 to May 16 that included 1,000 respondents. The survey has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.1 percentage points. Here's a look at more stories on how to manage, grow and protect your money for the years ahead. Living abroad doesn't end U.S. tax obligations. What young expats need to know Inheriting a home can leave siblings with financial headaches — how to avoid mistakes Is the K-shaped economy ending? Finance pros weigh in SEC proposes investor exam to expand private-market access — how it could work You can't 'borrow your way out of debt,' expert says, but more people are trying Boomers also reported the highest satisfaction with their current financial situation, at 41%, compared with 29% of Gen X, 36% of millennials and 34% of Gen Z. And 52% of boomers said they had enough financial knowledge to make confident decisions, compared with 40% of Gen X, 42% of millennials and 36% of Gen Z. "Life stage can provide really important context and insight around how Americans, consumers, are feeling today and experiencing the economy," said Teresa Hassara, senior vice president of workplace savings and retirement solutions at Principal Financial Group. New Federal Reserve data underscores how Americans' wealth has fluctuated across generations. Families headed by someone age 75 or older experienced a 37% increase in inflation-adjusted median net worth between 2022 and 2025, according to the Fed's "Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2022 to 2025" report from the Survey of Consumer Finances, released Friday. Meanwhile, families headed by someone under age 35 saw their median net worth decline 23% over the same period. Other age groups experienced considerably smaller changes, the Fed found. Median net worth rose 5% among families ages 35 to 44 and 3% among those ages 55 to 64, while declining 6% among families ages 45 to 54 and 4% among those ages 65 to 74. According to the report, "retirement income growth seems to play a key role" in improving the net worth of the oldest households. The findings compare group medians across survey years, rather than tracking the same families over time. The Fed also found that median income rose 24% for families headed by someone age 75 or older between 2022 and 2025, compared with just 2% for families under 35. Research also shows older Americans, particularly those with substantial investment portfolios and retirement savings, are increasingly drawing on accumulated wealth to support spending. During the three months ending in April 2026, 8.2% of individuals moved money from investment holdings to their checking accounts, according to a September report from the JPMorganChase Institute. That's up from 4% during the same period in 2019. The economic think tank, which is part of JPMorgan Chase , examined more than 20 million de-identified Chase checking accounts. Investment withdrawals also represented a growing share of consumer spending, the report found.

events.title: Stellantis and Renault back UK to get EU car industry protection
events.summary: Bosses of Citroën owner and French carmaker also urge UK government to consider limiting imports from China Stellantis and Renault have backed the UK car industry for inclusion in proposed rules to protect EU industry, but urged the British government to consider limiting imports of Chinese cars. Emanuele Cappellano, who leads Stellantis’s European brands including Fiat, Citroën, Opel and Vauxhall, and François Provost, the chief executive of France’s Renault, said the UK should effectively be counted as one of the EU’s 27 member states for the purposes of the proposed “Made in Europe” legislation . The new rules aim to ensure EU subsidies and government procurement benefits Europe’s industry, rather than helping manufacturers from other countries. The executives were speaking at the Paris motor show, which was attended on Monday by the French president, Emmanuel Macron. Brands including Li Auto, GAC and Chery were among a host of Chinese manufacturers exhibiting in Paris with ambitious European expansion plans. Europe’s car industry is under enormous pressure as it copes with lower demand than before the coronavirus pandemic, while also investing tens of billions of euros in shifting production to electric vehicles (EVs). At the same time, Chinese carmakers’ market share has soared as the transition to EVs opens the door to new entrants. The EU confirmed on Monday it would limit the number of hybrid electric vehicles imported from China to 350,000 cars a year. The EU expects that the quota, which will come into force in December, will halve China’s market share, which now stands at 6% in a landmark four-year agreement made in Beijing last week. The Made in Europe rules are another plank of the EU’s response to the rise of China in key manufacturing industries such as carmaking and chemicals. Under the proposed Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), cars will have to be “made in Europe”, and contain enough European parts and materials, to continue to qualify for EV grants and to be bought by public bodies in the EU. However, automotive manufacturers and politicians are haggling over the details. If Brussels sticks to a strict definition of “European” as being only EU countries, Britain risks being left out – prompting intense lobbying from UK car industry and government to be included. Stellantis is among the manufacturers that still has a British factory, its facility in Ellesmere Port, Merseyside, which produces small vans. “I think that UK somehow needs to be equalised to the EU 27,” said Cappellano, referring to the bloc’s 27 member states. “We have a lot of relationship, we have footprint. Historically UK has been very close to the European market.” Europe’s main automotive lobby groups ACEA and Clepa have also put their weight behind the UK to be included. Some parts of European manufacturing, including France’s industry minister , had argued that the UK should be left out given Brexit. Provost said there was “no other choice” but a deal between the UK and EU. However, he said the UK would also have to stop allowing Chinese cars in without limits. “On your side, you have also to take decisions,” he said. “If the UK is willing to join the European ecosystem, this is to have an industrial ambition … to keep a strong automotive industry.” Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning He said this would be an industry that “is not closed to Chinese competitors, but … if you want to operate in Europe, you have to deeply invest in the whole value chain, final manufacturing, suppliers, R&D, technologies.” Provost added: “I’m not here to demand whatsoever, but I think if UK is willing to join this ecosystem of IAA, there is some open question about the level of imports.” London has so far rejected pressure to impose its own tariffs on Chinese imports, but the UK business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, this month said that decision was under review . Cappellano also said the UK should consider imposing tariffs on Chinese imports. “It’s very important that the UK defines what is the priority,” he said. “It’s very difficult to defend industrial footprint and at the same time let the market completely open to import. Either one or the other.” He expressed scepticism over whether other countries beyond the EU such as Japan, Turkey and Morocco should be included in the rules. “We don’t necessarily need to have a larger definition of European scope,” he said, pointing to proposals that carmakers be allowed to source 30% of their materials from outside the EU. He also argued for more time until 2030 for manufacturers to source batteries from within Europe. China is dominant in the global supply of batteries and Cappellano said it would take longer to build up the European industry.

events.title: Microsoft to expand Maia chip for the AI era
events.summary: Microsoft to expand Azure Maia system to multi-gigawatt deployments Oct 12, 2026 | Scott Guthrie - Executive Vice President, Cloud + AI Azure Maia 200 now in production; Azure Maia 300 coming in 2027 As we move into the era of Super Intelligence, Microsoft is entering a new phase of infrastructure. We will scale our Azure Maia family to multi-gigawatt deployments starting in 2027, making Maia the primary inference system for Microsoft products and services. The multigenerational Azure Maia program has become a foundational element of Microsoft’s AI infrastructure strategy. Maia 200 is now serving Microsoft production workloads, including Microsoft Copilot , and supporting the MAI team as they develop next-generation models, with GitHub Copilot and Microsoft Foundry to follow by end of year. Across these workloads, Maia 200 runs OpenAI models , Microsoft’s own MAI models and leading open-source model families. Insights from the scale of Microsoft’s AI services allow for unique co-design between hardware systems and software applications to optimize real-world use cases across enterprise applications and industry scenarios. Maia 300 is a complete intelligent system designed for the new types of AI workloads emerging today: Long-context reasoning, latency-sensitive conversational experiences and sustained, multi-step agentic tasks. By improving efficiency across the system, we expect Maia 300 to deliver 40% more tokens per megawatt compared to leading GPU-based systems. And in a full 96-accelerator configuration, it delivers up to 7x the rack-scale token throughput of Maia 200. Maia 200: Driving the workloads that Microsoft runs at scale The Azure Maia system is designed around the real-world workloads Microsoft runs at scale and the models we expect to build in the years ahead. Because silicon development takes years, our software and hardware teams collaborate early to anticipate architectures, scale and capabilities, translating those requirements into greater memory capacity, higher bandwidth and more accelerators operating as a single system. That co-engineering is already delivering measurable efficiency gains. Maia 200 is deploying across the United States, Europe and Australia and delivering up to 1.7x more tokens per watt for built-in AI capabilities in Microsoft Teams, Copilot and Cowork experiences compared with leading GPU infrastructure. Experience running our AI models and services on Maia 200 directly informed the design of Maia 300. Together, the two generations are designed to support a broad set of additional Microsoft’s AI services: multi-step agentic work that will help GitHub deliver coding experiences more efficiently; cloud-scale model serving that will help Microsoft Foundry support diverse architectures and deployment environments; inference and data generation for the MAI team; and latency-sensitive interactions that will help Dragon Copilot scale workflows and reduce clinicians’ administrative burden. Maia 300: Scaling more useful AI within every megawatt AI is becoming a foundational layer of every application, workflow and business process. As enterprises move beyond chat experiences to systems of agents that can reason, act and collaborate, AI infrastructure must deliver intelligence securely and efficiently at scale while continuously adapting as models and workloads evolve. As the third generation of our Azure Maia program, Maia 300 is designed with an inference-first architecture optimized for long-context, memory-intensive and decode-heavy AI workloads. This involves balancing compute, memory bandwidth, networking and power efficiency at cloud scale. Key capabilities of the Maia 300 system include: Less data movement, more useful compute: Moving data efficiently, rather than raw compute power, is increasingly the bottleneck in large inference systems. Maia 300’s software-defined dataflow architecture and AI-assisted kernel optimization work together to maximize locality, reduce data movement and improve utilization across compute, memory and networking resources. By treating dataflow as a first-class design principle, Maia 300 delivers a significant performance-per-watt advantage over traditional GPU architectures. Higher memory bandwidth within every watt: As AI workloads become increasingly context and memory-bound, Maia 300 delivers industry-leading HBM bandwidth per watt. Eight HBM4 stacks provide 18.0 TB/s of peak memory bandwidth within a 950-watt TDP, enabling efficient execution of large models and long-context workloads. Specialized kernel support uses on-die SRAM as a software-managed scratchpad, reducing pressure on HBM. Chiplet architecture for enhanced efficiency: A new multi-chiplet architecture separates compute, memory-controller and I/O functions, improving efficiency, scalability and cost structure. Compute chiplets are built on TSMC’s N2P process node to maximize performance-per-watt. Larger context, richer intelligence: By designing for advanced low-precision formats, including enhanced MXFP4, Maia 300 reduces memory and bandwidth requirements for both computation and KV-cache storage. The result is larger context windows, higher throughput and improved model efficiency within the same power envelope. Scale-up networking at datacenter scale: Maia 300 treats networking as a seamless extension of the software-defined dataflow architecture. Rather than moving data through separate communication layers, dataflow operations span compute, memory and network resources as a single system. High-bandwidth interconnects between Maia accelerators are optimized for tensor parallelism, while a custom AI transport delivers performant and reliable scale-up communication across accelerators and racks. The AI-optimized transport leverages Ethernet-based networking infrastructure to enable a unified topology that scales efficiently from a single rack to datacenter-scale deployments. Higher AI throughput from every rack: Maia 300 rack systems bring together 96 accelerators within a 167-kilowatt power envelope, delivering 27.6 TB of HBM capacity and 1.7 PB/s of aggregate HBM bandwidth across a high-speed scale-up domain. That density allows Microsoft to serve more simultaneous AI interactions and larger workloads from each rack, improving datacenter capacity and the economics of expanding AI services. Maia 300 will begin production deployments in 2027. For more information on Maia 300 architectural details, read our technical paper . Azure Maia is at the heart of our Frontier Transformation The future will not be defined by a single model or a single piece of silicon or a single innovation. Model and silicon choice are inherent in our vision for Frontier Transformation. events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. The U.S. Air Force will buy data collected by WindBorne Systems ‘ fleet of autonomous weather balloons under a new contract that could be worth nearly $50 million to the startup. WindBorne currently has about 700 weather balloons flying around the globe, collecting atmospheric sensor readings that the company sells to customers and also feeds into its own AI weather forecasting model. WindBorne, founded in 2015 and based in Redwood City, California, is one of the first organizations to directly feed empirical data into a deep-learning weather model. The company has worked closely with the U.S. government, particularly the National Weather Service and the U.S. Air Force and Navy, but this is the single-largest contract the company has participated in. The contract is worth up to $49 million, but the Air Force pays only as it needs data. It can place orders for specific regions at specific times. So far, it has ordered $1.7 million worth, and executives expect more orders to follow. “This is largely a vehicle through which continued growth of the constellation can be supported, as well as some work on research and development to continue to improve the hardware and performance of the balloons,” WindBorne co-founder and CTO Andrey Sushko told TechCrunch. He added that the contract, which was awarded without competitive bidding, is “a determination by the government that for this capability of collecting global data, we were the only company able to provide it in the way that met their needs for these operations.” WindBorne CEO John Dean told TechCrunch in August that the company had raised a $37 million Series B round to continue scaling its business. Earlier this summer, the company released the latest version of its forecasting model, WeatherMesh 6, which it says provides more accurate forecasts than the traditional model run by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), which simulates the atmosphere using the laws of physics. Since the arrival of transformer model architectures and the ECMWF’s release of a massive weather dataset a few years ago, AI weather forecasting has become one of the more productive uses of deep-learning technology. Meteorologists previously relied on expensive supercomputers running detailed equations that approximate how the atmosphere behaves. Now, end-to-end learning can ingest decades of weather data and issue predictions more quickly. Models built by frontier labs and government agencies are proving more accurate than traditional forecasts, although it is still a jagged frontier, with both types of forecasts required to enable useful understanding of the weather. Google DeepMind’s latest weather model offers important new capabilities, and its cyclone forecasting tools are becoming increasingly central to how the U.S. government responds to hurricane season. In August WindBorne became the first organization to send an unpowered flight system — one with no engine — to collect data in the eye of a typhoon . The company maneuvers its balloons by adjusting their altitude, bleeding air, or dropping sand carried as ballast, to send the vehicles into winds that take them where they need to go. “That’s a pretty novel step, and the two ingredients for that are one, having good wind and weather models, and knowing how to navigate them; and two, having a large enough constellation that you have balloons in the right places,” Sushko said. “It’s one of the first times that a deep-learning model was used for actual operational decisions.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Higher rates could be needed to avoid 'inflationary mindset' taking hold, says Fed's Hammack
events.summary: "When feasible, I generally think it's preferable to make smaller adjustments, and to do so relatively quickly, rather than to wait and risk needing a larger course correction," said Beth Hammack, president of the Cleveland Federal Reserve. Her comments come after Fed officials signaled in September meeting minutes that they could vote to raise rates again — but did not give a clear indication on when such a decision would come. Cleveland Federal Reserve President Beth Hammack said Monday that tighter monetary policy might be needed to bring down inflation and the central bank should make fast, incremental adjustments. "When feasible, I generally think it's preferable to make smaller adjustments, and to do so relatively quickly, rather than to wait and risk needing a larger course correction," Hammack, a voting member of the Fed's policymaking committee, said in prepared remarks delivered during the National Association of Business Economics annual gathering. "Considering all the inputs that factor into my reaction function, a restrictive monetary policy stance is appropriate to ensure a timely return to 2 percent inflation," Hammack added. Hammack's comments signal that more interest rate hikes could be on the horizon. Fed officials signaled in September meeting minutes that they could vote to raise rates again — but did not give a clear indication on when such a decision would come. The Fed last month voted to increase interest rates for the first time in three years. Traders priced in a more than 78% likelihood that the central bank keeps rates unchanged at its policy meeting later this month, according to CME's FedWatch tool. But they see a nearly 88% chance of a hike at the Fed's final meeting of the year in December. Sticky inflation poses challenges for consumers, businesses and monetary policymakers alike, Hammack said. The Cleveland Fed chief said that, with the "breadth" of current inflationary pressures, she expects it will take "some time" to get annual price growth down to the central bank's goal of 2%. The personal consumption expenditures price index came in at 3.4% year over year in August. The so-called core reading of the index, which strips out volatile food and energy costs and is favored by the Fed, registered at 3% compared with a year prior. "Long-run inflation expectations have stayed remarkably well anchored despite actual inflation being above target for more than five years," Hammack said. "But I'm not taking that for granted." "With each passing month, persistently elevated inflation raises the risks of an inflationary mindset becoming entrenched in the economy," she said.

events.title: Ukrainian soldiers are putting RPGs on robots for fights in the kill zone, a manufacturer says
events.summary: Ukrainian forces have used RPGs to fight Russia's invasion. Now, they're starting to put them on robots to attack. Roman Chop/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images Ukrainian troops are shifting another infantry weapon from soldiers to robots. RPGs are finding a new role as combat evolves and troops lean on emerging tech to mitigate risk. The change reflects how drones and robots are reshaping ground warfare. Ukrainian soldiers conducting operations in the kill zone have been putting anti-tank RPGs on ground robots, a robotic systems manufacturer told Business Insider, explaining that the battlefield has become too dangerous for troops to use the weapons the way they did earlier in the war. Rocket-propelled grenades are often used by infantry to defeat armored vehicles and weaken fortified positions, but the battlefield has changed, forcing new innovations. In the kill zone, "nobody knew how to use" an RPG "while staying safe himself," Oleg Fedoryshyn, the R&D director of Ukrainian robot maker DevDroid, told Business Insider. The kill zone along Ukraine's front is a perilous area, as deep as 50 kilometers in some areas, where drones are so heavily concentrated alongside other weaponry that any movement represents a significant risk. For many soldiers, simply getting within RPG range can be extremely difficult. The decision to move RPGs onto robots reflects a broader shift in the war. Early in Russia's full-scale invasion, RPGs were a common infantry weapon, used against Russian tanks and vehicles and to support infantry during fights in towns and cities. But cheap drones , in both surveillance and strike roles, have transformed ground combat, reducing the use of armored vehicles and changing infantry engagements. Ukraine's robot fleet can fire a growing array of weapons. Dmytro Smolienko/Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty Images DevDroid's ground robots aren't the only ones getting RPGs as the war evolves. Ukrainian UGV maker Temerland says its Gnom-VP ground robotic fire support platform carries two RPG-7 launchers, along with other weapons and mine-laying capabilities. Fedoryshyn said soldiers working with DevDroid started putting the RPGs on robots that were already armed with machine guns . The robots can drive close enough to targets and fire shorter-range weapons while keeping their operators much farther from danger. Fedoryshyn said a brigade came to the company and said they wanted to try putting RPGs on a robot, and they had "great" success using it. Now, the company is exploring "how to add support for this for everyone in the future," he said. Devdroid makes ground robots and a remote-controlled weapons station that allows operators to fire from safe distances, as well as electric triggers that allow operators to activate a weapon remotely. Requests from soldiers are often how Ukraine's new capabilities emerge . Arms makers work directly with front-line units, gathering feedback and rapidly modifying equipment. Fedoryshyn said DevDroid has 24/7 chat support available for every unit that uses its systems. He said that the company can design a new update, test it with a brigade, and roll it out across all deployed systems within a week. It designs its gear for easy updates, "like mobile phones or operating systems," he added. Robots have a growing role in Ukraine's fight against Russia's invasion. Oleksandr Klymenko/Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty Images The war is one of rapid innovation to field new capabilities and preserve the utility of older ones as the war changes. Mounting RPGs on ground robots is another sign of that evolution. Instead of discarding a weapon designed for a kind of fighting that is less common now, Ukrainian troops are changing who carries it to keep it in the fight. Other weapons, such as flamethrowers, grenade launchers, and machine guns, have also been mounted on robots. Fedoryshyn said his company is often surprised by how soldiers use its robots, including cases in which Russian soldiers have surrendered to them. Ukraine's experience, he said, shows Western militaries preparing for protracted wars should invest in large numbers of inexpensive, easily replaceable robots rather than relying solely on costly tanks and armored vehicles. events.title: Trump's Russia deal leaves GOP candidates with a Putin problem
events.summary: Republicans already saddled with Trump's unpopular policies in the midterms now face another awkward choice: whether to back his diesel deal with a dictator many of them despise. Why it matters: The agreement President Trump struck with Russian President Vladimir Putin Friday is designed to ease the cost of living for U.S. consumers. But Republicans who pleaded for help with fuel prices now face a fresh dispute over Russia, with energy analysts questioning whether the deal will deliver the relief Trump is promising. The big picture: With three weeks until Election Day, Republicans are trying to answer voter anger while keeping up with a president whose proposed fixes keep becoming political liabilities of their own. Trump's decision to lock arms with Putin adds another complication. Driving the news: Weeks after signing a sweeping Russia sanctions law, Trump announced Friday that Russia would supply diesel to U.S. and global markets. The next day, Trump blamed Ukraine for soaring diesel prices and called for President Volodymyr Zelensky to be replaced, even as Russia continued attacking Ukrainian cities. Republicans who just supported squeezing Moscow have three options in the final sprint for control of Congress: defend Trump's reversal, break with him or stay quiet. Zoom out: The diesel deal packs some of the GOP's biggest liabilities into one decision: the Iran war's economic fallout, the party's split over Russia and a president determined to make the election about himself. The deal also reverses Trump's own pressure campaign. Last year, he slapped an extra 25% tariff on India for buying Russian oil. On Oct. 2, he and other G7 leaders pledged to keep sanctions on Russia. Energy analysts also doubt the deal will do much for diesel prices, which averaged $6.28 a gallon Oct. 11, up 71% from a year earlier. What they're saying: The White House pushed back on criticism of Trump's record: "President Trump has consistently proven his doubters wrong," White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said. A senior administration official said Trump is "laser-focused on bringing down costs, whether it's diesel with the Russians or importing Argentine beef. Some people might not like it, but he's thinking of what Americans are paying and what he can do about it." Friction point: The internal pushback has been swift. Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.) vowed to force a House vote blocking the oil purchases. Reps. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) and Michael McCaul (R-Texas), along with Sens. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska), Susan Collins (R-Maine), Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) and John Curtis (R-Utah), already criticized the deal by Sunday. Tillis told NBC News' "Meet the Press" that Trump's deal may violate a law that requires the White House to notify Congress before lifting sanctions. Even MAGA ally Laura Loomer denounced the deal as not only funding Russia but indirectly helping Iran by putting "money back into the coffers of the Islamic regime of Iran." Yes, but: Some Republicans, like Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (Fla.) and Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso , backed the deal. How we got here: Farm-state Republicans have pleaded with the White House to deliver diesel relief. Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and others urged Trump to ban diesel exports, something the president embraced before the White House abruptly reversed and ruled out a ban. GOP candidates in key Senate races, like Iowa's Ashley Hinson and Michigan's Mike Rogers , have called for ending the Iran war after previously supporting it. Instead, Trump has defended it in vivid terms, saying Iran might have attacked Los Angeles and San Diego if not for his war. Between the lines: Trump's unpopular positions collide with voter sentiment as he touts the war with Iran, the rise of data centers and his own popularity. His efforts to give Republicans something to campaign on leave candidates exposed through big promises, about-faces and proposals that won't materialize before voters cast their ballots. Data centers: Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) has faced Democratic attacks over data centers, an issue the National Republican Senatorial Committee has identified as a vulnerability. Yet Trump used a Husted rally last week to defend the projects: "Look, there's so much money to be made for Ohio. You can't just turn them off. They'll go to China." Dividend checks: Voters have also rejected Trump's proposed $5,000 dividend checks that analysts say would cost $1.3 trillion . A September Reuters/Ipsos poll found 63% of Americans disapproved. Trump: Trump has insisted the midterms should be a referendum on his presidency, telling Republicans at last month's convention to "pretend that I'm on the ballot." But a Pew Research Centerpoll released Thursday found 44% of registered voters view their congressional vote as a vote against Trump, compared with 19% who see it as a vote for him. Texas Senate nominee Ken Paxton privately blamed oil prices, the Iran war and the midterm convention for falling poll numbers. The bottom line: For Republican candidates, the challenge isn't just selling Trump's record. It's keeping up with a president who continues to give them new decisions to defend.

events.title: Muse Wonder Puts Meta Back at the AI Frontier
events.summary: When Mark Zuckerberg rebooted his company’s artificial intelligence efforts last year, it seemed to be a very expensive gamble. Meta’s latest AI models, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, seem to show that the bet is finally paying off by putting the company back at the frontier of AI development. Muse Wonder Full boasts frontier capabilities, Meta says, meaning that it is among the most capable AI models in the world. “Together, they mark the next step on our scaling ladder and a major leap toward personal superintelligence,” the company said in a blog post today. The Muse Wonder models will be available though an API and through Muse Code, a tool for writing software with AI. Meta says the best version of the model will power features across its platforms, including its Muse personal agent . Zuckerberg overhauled his company’s AI research last year by sinking billions into the recently formed Meta Superintelligence Labs, and hiring the former Scale AI CEO Alexandr Wang to lead it. This effort has sometimes been rocky , with some researchers not sticking around for long. Meta was once a trailblazer in AI. Its Llama series of models were the first frontier open-weight offerings from a big lab. Llama, which could be downloaded and run on one’s own hardware, was widely adopted by researchers and startups. But the company fell behind after delivering several disappointing versions of the model, and as Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google rapidly introduced more capable models. Meta announced the first model from its new lab, Muse Spark , in April of this year. The company has also released a small open weight model called Muse Glimmer , and says it plans to release larger open-weight models in the future. It did not disclose details of how new Muse Wonder models were built or trained. Muse Wonder was built to compete with the very best, however. Meta says the largest version of the new model outperforms Anthropic’s second-best model, Claude Fable 5.1, and ranks just below its best, Claude Opus 5.5, on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , a widely used aggregated score of model capabilities. Meta says the model outperforms OpenAI’s best model, GPT-6 Astra, and both Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 on some specialized benchmarks, including ones that measure a model’s ability to work with legal documents and to build software. Benchmarks are not always a reliable measure of real-world performance, but this is still a significant step forward for Meta’s models. Muse Wonder also includes two novel features designed to help make agents more effective and less inclined to misbehave. The new features, called Active Memory and Active Focus, are designed to keep the model locked into a stated goal, and prevent it from becoming confused. This can be a challenge when AI performs complex research or builds a large software project, for example, and can lead to expensive mistakes or compounded errors. Meta says it has put significant effort into training Muse Wonder to refuse to generate dangerous outputs, such as recipes for building bioweapons or help with hacking. It says the company scores well on several benchmarks designed to measure how resilient models are to those prompts. A series of recent incidents involving rogue AI agents from Anthropic, OpenAI, and others, also shows how easily powerful AI models can stray when given open-ended commands. Meta did not disclose whether it has seen agents powered by Muse Wonder misbehave in testing or what it has done to mitigate this issue specifically. Zuckerberg said in a post on X last month that the company had delayed the release of its Muse models to work on safety. Meta also revealed a framework designed to ensure that it scales its models’ capabilities safely in a blog post earlier this month. Muse Wonder may add more fuel to an already furious race to develop more capable AI, however. It certainly suggests that Meta is once again competitive in the increasingly high-stakes AI race. events.title: The creepiest urban legend from every US state
events.summary: Bigfoot is the star of one of the most well-known urban legends in the US. Christy Rowe/Getty Images There are famous urban legends, including Bigfoot and the Loch Ness monster. However, there are also plenty of local myths that have not made it into mainstream pop culture. Keep reading to find out the creepiest urban legend that takes place in your state. Have you ever felt a chill as you walk down your street, or drive along a dark highway in your home state? You might want to check this list to see if your state's creepiest urban legend unfolded near you. Every country, state, and town has its own urban legends known to residents and fans of the paranormal. Some are attempts to explain mysterious phenomena or tragedies, while others are passed down due to our fascination with the dark and macabre. Some areas have capitalized on local urban legends to attract tourists and boost local economies. In the West Virginia city of Point Pleasant, for example, the legend of Mothman is integral to the community. The Mothman Festival is held every September and includes guest speakers, a street fair, bus tours, live music, food trucks, and more. There's even a Mothman museum. It's not for nothing. The Main Street Point Pleasant organization told The River Cities Tribune & Register in 2024 that it estimates the festival brings about $2 million to the city's economy every year. But not every urban legend is that well known. We chose the creepiest urban legend we could find in every state, from the little-known to the mainstays like Bigfoot and the Jersey Devil. ALABAMA: Hell's Gate Bridge The bridge. Google Maps The generally accepted story of Hell's Gate Bridge starts in the 1950s, according to the Oxford Paranormal Society ; a young couple driving over the bridge somehow drove their car off the bridge one night, and they both drowned. There are two legends associated with Hell's Gate Bridge: one is that if you drive your car out to the middle of the bridge and turn off the lights, the couple will magically appear in your car and leave a wet spot on the seat. The other, which is how the bridge got its name, is the belief that if you drive over the bridge and look over your shoulder halfway through, the scenery behind you turns into a portal to hell engulfed in flames. Potentially to curb ghost hunters and bored teenagers, Hell's Gate Bridge is closed to cars, according to The Anniston Star , and it is in such disrepair that walking across is strongly discouraged. ALASKA: The Kushtaka of the Alaskan Triangle David McNew/Getty Images Everyone knows the story of the Bermuda Triangle, but you might not know about the Alaskan Triangle. On average, five out of every 1,000 people go missing in Alaska, the Los Angeles Times reported in 2005, so even if there's nothing supernatural going on, it's easy to get lost in the Alaskan wilderness. The Tlingit tribe, who lives in Juneau, has their own explanation for the high number of missing people: evil spirits called the Kushtaka. According to books such as "In Search of the Kushtaka: Alaska's Other Bigfoot," the Kushtaka are shape-shifters (half-man, half-otter) who lure women and children to the water with fake cries in order to steal their human spirits and drown them. ARIZONA: The ghosts of Slaughterhouse Canyon The Chapel of the Holy Cross in Oak Creek Canyon, near Sedona, Arizona, April 1967 Slim Aarons/Hulton Archive/Getty Images The story of Slaughterhouse Canyon (not pictured), also called the less-frightening Luana's Canyon, takes place during the Gold Rush, according to The Miner. During the 1800s, there was a family who lived in the canyon. They were very poor, so the father would venture out for food for his family. One day, the father did not return, so his family slowly starved and descended into madness. The mother, unable to bear listening to her children's cries anymore, put on her wedding dress, murdered her children, and then threw them into a nearby river. The next day, she succumbed to starvation herself. The legend states that if you go down to Slaughterhouse Canyon at night, even now, you will hear the loud, anguished cries of the mother who lost her mind. ARKANSAS: The Boggy Creek Monster Caution. CineBlade/Shutterstock According to Atlas Obscura , the Boggy Creek Monster of Fouke is Arkansas' version of Sasquatch. He's commonly accepted to be around 7 or 8 feet tall and covered in hair. Legend says that he roams the creeks of rural Arkansas. He was first spotted in 1834 when people reported seeing a "wild man." These days, after people claim to spot the Boggy Creek Monster, the sightings are documented on the official Boggy Creek Monster's website . He has been the subject of at least five feature-length films, including 1972's "The Legend of Boggy Creek." CALIFORNIA: The Char-Man The Char-Man calls Ojai his home. David McNew/Getty Images The Char-Man's origin story, told in the journal "Western Folklore," is gruesome: A father and son were both caught in a house fire and horribly burned in 1948. After the fire, the son became so mentally unstable that he killed his father. When the police found the son, he was so unrecognizably burned that they didn't realize he was alive, so he ran away before they were able to arrest him for the murder of his father. The story goes that, ever since then, the Char-Man can be spotted wandering the woods surrounding Ojai, occasionally approaching tents of innocent campers or pretending to be a hitchhiker and attempting to attack them. COLORADO: The many legends of Riverdale Road A portion of Riverdale Road. Google Maps Riverdale Road is the site of not one, but  eight  creepy stories. Ranging from a "Hell Gate" to ghosts of slaves hanging from the trees, the stretch of road is decidedly spooky, as reported by local news affiliate Fox31. The creepiest story, though, is that of the phantom jogger. One day, there was a driver who hit a jogger and left him for dead. Now, it's said that if you park at the site of the crash, you'll hear disembodied footsteps getting closer and closer to your car. People have reported handprints on their windows and banging noises as if someone was kicking the outside. CONNECTICUT: Hannah Cranna You can visit Hannah Cranna's real grave. Hulton Archive/Getty Images Known as the "Wicked Witch of Monroe," per CT Insider , Hannah Cranna gained a reputation as a witch in the 19th century when her husband died by mysteriously falling off a cliff — and locals reportedly believed that she had bewitched him. People also believed that she would cast spells on people she didn't like. Hannah lived to the age of 77, but right before she died, she asked to be carried down to the cemetery in her coffin on foot, not by wagon. events.title: FAA warns U.S. airlines of safety risks over Saudi Arabia after attacks
events.summary: The FAA warned U.S. airlines about safety risks flying in or near Saudi Arabia after attacks on one of the country's biggest airports. Delta Air Lines is scheduled to launch its first nonstop flight between Atlanta and Riyadh later this month, but said it hasn't decided whether it will go ahead. The Federal Aviation Administration told U.S. airlines to exercise caution when flying in or around Saudi Arabia after deadly attacks claimed by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis, which have shut down the airport in the Saudi capital. King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, remains closed as of Monday after strikes that started last week. The attacks escalated Saturday, when a projectile struck a passenger terminal at the airport, officials said, killing at least 12 people and wounding more than 300. Airlines suspended flights to the airport, some for the rest of the week. The U.S., Australia and other countries advised citizens against travel to the region. The FAA late Sunday said pilots should "exercise caution" in or around Saudi Arabia "due to safety-of-flight risks associated with ongoing military activities" and navigation systems. It said the threats could be a potential risk "to aircraft at all altitudes." The FAA's warning is in effect until Dec. 10. Most U.S. airlines don't fly to Saudi Arabia, but the country's flights and passenger counts had climbed in recent years. The route between Riyadh to Jeddah in the country's west was the fifth-busiest in the world last year, according to aviation-data firm OAG. Delta Air Lines had been scheduled to launch its first nonstop flight from Atlanta to Riyadh on Oct. 23 but the carrier on Monday said it would delay that service until March. events.title: UnitedHealth shares are doing something unusual ahead of earnings
events.summary: The only thing more expensive than health insurance is perhaps the costs of insuring shares of health insurers. Case in point: UnitedHealth Group, which reports earnings Tuesday. Implied volatility is running at twice realized volatility ahead of the October 13 quarterly earnings release. In other words, options prices - the cost of insuring the underlying stock - are expensive, which sets up well for short premium strategies. In the case of UnitedHealth shares, traders can sell November premium to cut the cost of a longer-dated January call by more than half. UnitedHealth heads into Tuesday's report with much of the damage from its prior missteps already priced in. While rising healthcare costs always remain a headwind, management's 13% to 16% EPS growth target looks achievable. The stock has basically been flat over the last five years. By the way, according to the company, 90% of United's 52 million customers worldwide are in the U.S. By its own statistics, the company covers about 12% to 13.5% of the U.S. population. Growing enrollment is critical to EPS growth, but so too is underwriting margin. In the managed care and health insurance business, underwriting margin represents the core operational profitability generated directly from managing healthcare risk. It measures the financial return an insurer achieves strictly from collecting premiums and managing medical care. On the enrollment side, ACA marketplace-driven enrollment appears poised to decline, a headwind for revenue in a segment that had been a growth driver. Fortunately, it's a smaller piece of the enterprise than Medicare and Commercial. Commercial fee-based enrollment grew ~2.9% YoY between 2024 and 2025, while total Medicare enrollment grew 4.5%. The commercial segment growth may not look impressive as a headline number, but given the U.S. workforce grew ~1.4% over the same period, United appears to be gaining market share. At 17 times forward earnings, and with free cash flow at 5.7% of enterprise value and 6.5% of market cap, the stock isn't priced for any recovery. On the options side, the market is implying 40% volatility for a stock that's been realizing 20%. Granted. The 40% number captures this week's earnings, and it's likely elevated because the stock has had a couple of eye-watering earnings moves in the past 8 reported quarters. In January, the stock fell almost 20% following earnings, and April 2025 saw a similar sharp decline. As it stands, UNH is about 12-13% below the midpoint of the two-year high and low. The stock has traded lower in five of the last 8 earnings. Current options prices imply a 6.5% earnings move, according to Cboe LiveVol data. That's the second highest implied move in almost two years. Sell the November 340/420 strangle to help finance the purchase of the January 2027 400 call. Buying the Jan 400 call costs $18.20. Selling the Nov 420 call at $5.80 and the Nov 340 put at $4.80 brings in $10.60, for a net debit of about $7.60, cutting the call's cost by roughly 58%. If UNH finishes November between 340 and 420, both short legs expire worthless and the January call is held for $7.60, with a breakeven of $407.60 at January expiration. A rally through 420 is covered by the long 400 call. The real risk is below: a close under 340 means buying shares there, for an effective basis near $347.60 including the debit. events.title: Hackers force French supermarket fridges to heat up to 50C in ‘unprecedented’ cyber-attack
events.summary: Hundreds of Intermarché shops and Coopérative U outlets in France hit, with fears Dutch chains also affected Hackers have forced the temperature of many French supermarket fridges up to 50C overnight, in an “unprecedented” cyber-attack affecting several hundred stores across the country, with fires and food losses reported. The Paris prosecutor’s office said on Monday ⁠the large-scale attack was “affecting connected refrigerators ⁠in several ​major food retailers across France”. Reported damage included “food losses and fires”, it added. The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, instructed France’s national cybersecurity agency ANSSI to investigate, ⁠a person in his office said. France “was coordinating with its European counterparts, as other countries may also be affected”, while also investigating whether any other French ⁠firms were at risk, they said. Les Mousquetaires, which owns retailer Intermarché, said about 150 of its stores had been ​hit, with fridges heated up to 50C for six hours. ‌It had thrown all the food away to avoid any health risks, a spokesperson said. Dominique Schelcher, chief executive of Coopérative ‌U, said his supermarkets had also been hit by the attack. “Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is of extreme gravity and is unprecedented,” he wrote on X. Several other supermarket chains, including Carrefour, Monoprix and Auchan, did not respond to requests for comment. According to BFM TV, France’s largest supermarket chain E Leclerc was also affected, with hackers “managing to remotely trigger the forced defrosting of the refrigeration systems in numerous stores”. E Leclerc did not respond to a request for comment. The attack may not have been confined to France. The Dutch supermarket company ‌Ahold Delhaize said it was also dealing with a “security issue” in its network, and had taken several systems offline to protect them. Stores of its Albert Heijn chain, ​the largest supermarket chain in the Netherlands, which also has several stores in Belgium, remained open in both countries. But its online app and delivery system were down, while electronic price tags often displayed the wrong information. It was not clear if there was any link between the French supermarket attack and the ⁠problems flagged by Ahold Delhaize. Delhaize supermarkets, also part of Ahold Delhaize but operating ​in Belgium and Luxembourg, were ​also affected by the security issue, ​Belgian media reported. The source close to Lecornu said ANSSI had identified a vulnerability ​in software supplied by ‌the Danish company Danfoss. The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment Danfoss ​said it was “aware ​of incidents in France affecting a limited number of refrigeration management systems”. The affected units “were running outdated firmware”, Danfoss said, adding that it had “long advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware and to migrate legacy systems to current-generation solutions”. The incident comes against the background of growing concern over the potential havoc that can be caused in Europe in all sectors by cyber-attacks by malicious actors. The French president, Emmanuel Macron, a strong supporter of Ukraine in its fight against the Russian invasion, last month ordered measures to protect France’s critical infrastructure from Russian “hybrid attacks”.

events.title: I manage employees in 2 countries while caring for my mom with dementia. FMLA keeps me going.
events.summary: Vincia Gordon with her mom, Hyacinth Lynch. Courtesy of Vincia Gordon Vincia Gordon runs two call centers from her home, while caring for her 92-year-old mom. She supervises 40 members of staff and performs tasks such as administering medication. The mom of two takes 480 hours of FMLA annually to balance her career and personal life as a carer. This story is based on an interview with Vincia Gordon, 56, an operational manager for two call centers, living in Baltimore County, Maryland. It has been edited for length and clarity. My mom, Hyacinth Lynch, 92, lived in the US Virgin Islands , but constantly visited my family and me in Maryland, staying for months at a time. She lived by herself after my father died in 2020 at the age of 94. Longevity runs in our family. However, she started to show signs of decline in the summer of 2023. A physical exam confirmed she had high blood pressure and other issues, such as a hernia. What is your situation regarding long-term care for yourself or your loved ones? To share your story with a Business Insider reporter, please fill out this quick form . In September, one of our friends from the islands called to ask if there was something wrong with Mom. She had called her twice one morning, asking her the same thing. Gordon (second left) with her husband and two daughters. Courtesy of Cynthia Gordon It was the first sign of her dementia . Other friends were concerned, too. I told them to keep their eyes on her and report to me anything that was askew. I didn't like the idea of a care home She flew over for the holidays — and never left. Her mobility had gotten much worse, as well as the hernia. She had surgery in the Spring of 2024. The dementia progressed. Her long-term memory stayed intact — she could rattle on about looking after my daughters when they were young — but her short-term memory was a problem. I talked to her medical team, who put her on the drug donepezil. It helped slow things down and remove some of the brain fog. There was no question in my mind that she should stay at home with me. I didn't like the idea of a care home , because I compared them to overcrowded classrooms. You'd question your children's education if the teacher had 30 kids on any given day. How could Mom get the attention she needed without a specially designated aide? Gordon with her mom, husband, and daughter at her daughter's wedding. Courtesy of Vincia Gordon I contacted the senior living advisory, A Place for Mom , for help finding providers and other services. They put me in touch with some private carers, who usually visit between 11 a.m. and 1 p.m. They charge $44 an hour, and they mostly spend the time doing cognitive exercises. Mom has always been a word search queen and loves doing puzzles. We also have visits from other professionals, including a social worker and an occupational therapist. Meanwhile, I keep on top of things such as keeping her clean, monitoring her blood pressure , and administering her medication. I couldn't manage without FMLA I'm very accountable and write everything down in a copybook in case I need to consult a provider. People ask me how on earth I manage to run two call centers — one in the US and the other in the Philippines — while caring for my mother. My days are knee-deep in meetings and calls with staff. The answer is FMLA (the Family Medical Leave Act lets eligible workers take time off to care for a family member, without losing their job). I receive 480 hours a year, and my salary is not affected. I usually take it in increments of two or three hours, but it can extend into days if necessary. I also use my allotted PTO. It's always a balancing act, and the juggling is hard. Still, I wouldn't have it any other way. Mom is absolutely here to stay. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Photos: Protests over voter lists escalate in India’s capital
events.summary: India’s opposition parties have marched in New Delhi to protest a voter list purge they say favours PM Modi’s party. Thousands of protesters have marched in New Delhi, demanding the resignation of India’s top election official over alleged misconduct during a voter roll revision. The demonstrations on Monday marked the latest confrontation with authorities in the heavily fortified capital. Opposition parties and supporters of the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party protest movement have taken to the streets in recent days, defying a strict security clampdown to demand the government stop deleting voters from the rolls and calling for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. More than 133 million names have been removed from voter lists since last year, according to media reports. About 969 million people were eligible to vote in India’s 2024 polls. Critics say the large-scale revision of electoral rolls could benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). The Election Commission of India, which oversees the voting process in the world’s most populous nation, has denied any wrongdoing. Authorities deployed thousands of security personnel across central Delhi for a third straight day, erecting heavy metal barricades and closing key metro stations. Public attention has also focused on the police response, after a weekend in which thousands of protesters, including organisers, were detained , according to local media reports. Most of those detained, including three top leaders of the Cockroach movement , have since been released. Several journalists covering the protests said they were detained despite clearly displaying their press cards. The demonstrations have become a major political challenge for Modi, drawing together opposition parties, student groups and activists angered by the voter roll revision. Critics say the measure has disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims. Election authorities say the move was intended to eliminate duplicate, deceased and fraudulent names.

events.summary: Bitcoin buying is back. Corporate crypto heavyweight Strategy announced Monday that it bought over $21 million worth of Bitcoin last week, bringing its total holdings to roughly $70 billion. The company, led by flamboyant billionaire Michael Saylor , funded the purchase by selling more than 125,000 shares of its common stock and using $500,000 in cash. It also spent roughly $192 million to repurchase nearly 2 million shares of STRC, a type of preferred stock that makes regular payments to investors. The latest purchase extends Strategy’s return to Bitcoin buying, marking its fifth purchase since August. Bitcoin broke out of a prolonged trading lull in mid-August, climbing to around $77,000 for the first time since May. It has largely held above that level since and was trading at $82,600 Monday morning. The rebound followed a steep downturn that pushed Bitcoin from a high of $126,000 last October to a low of $58,000 in June. Amid the slump, Strategy—which holds roughly 4% of Bitcoin’s circulating supply—sold portions of its stockpile on four occasions. As Bitcoin’s price rebounded, Strategy stopped selling and returned to stockpiling. Strategy isn’t the only big player wading back into Bitcoin. Other companies have recently added crypto to their balance sheets, breathing life back into corporate crypto buying .  Earlier this month, Strive, the asset manager cofounded by billionaire Vivek Ramaswamy, announced a $169 million purchase of 2,000 Bitcoin, bringing its stockpile to roughly $2.4 billion. Robinhood, the crypto trading platform led by CEO Vlad Tenev, also joined the ranks of corporate Bitcoin buyers and recently disclosed a $25 million investment for its own balance sheet. Metaplanet, the Japanese investment firm and world’s second-largest publicly traded Bitcoin treasury company, announced this month that it sold 10,000 Bitcoin and bought 11,000 in the third quarter to demonstrate to credit markets that it could convert its holdings into cash when needed. But companies aren’t just stockpiling Bitcoin. Bitmine, a Bitcoin miner turned into an Ethereum treasury company, announced this month that it had added roughly $41 million worth of the cryptocurrency to its treasury. The purchase brought its holdings to about 6 million tokens—nearly 5% of Ether’s total supply. The renewed buying comes as Bitcoin’s recovery fuels hopes of further gains. The cryptocurrency has held up despite recent interest rate hikes in the United States and renewed tensions in the Middle East. Fortune previously reported that analysts expect Bitcoin to recover further by year-end, with one strategist predicting a summer bottom followed by a rebound toward $100,000. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

Fox reported Monday that the search was tied to a fraud investigation into Omar's immigration paperwork. The Somali native came to the U.S. in 1995 as a 12-year-old refugee. The intrigue: President Trump has made Minnesota's Somali community one of the most frequent targets of his anti-immigration rhetoric, and Omar the face of those attacks. Just last week, he called on Minnesotans to " fight back " against the state's Somalian population. He's also specifically demanded that Omar leave the country, or that she be deported . events.title: UK PM Andy Burnham vows to renegotiate post-Brexit trade deal with EU
events.summary: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham says renegotiating relationship with the EU could reverse some post-Brexit ‘damage’. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to push for closer relations with the European Union, confirming he will attend a bilateral summit in Brussels next month. Addressing parliament on Monday, Burnham said parts of the trade deal agreed with the EU after the UK voted to leave in 2016 would be renegotiated. list 1 of 3 The Burnham bounce: Is Labour gaining ground against Reform? list 2 of 3 Burnham, Macron talk border security and stronger Europe-UK ties list 3 of 3 UK PM Andy Burnham says it is ‘clear’ Russia interfered in 2016 Brexit vote Burnham said that the British public would be “the boss” at every stage of renegotiating Britain’s relationship with the EU and that he wanted “serious dialogue” about long-term ties. He told members of parliament that his focus at the summit would be boosting growth in the economy and controlling illegal immigration. Among the topics of discussion at November’s summit are cutting bureaucracy for British food exports and emissions trading, as well as a “new youth experience scheme” and deeper cooperation on immigration. The prime minister, who came into office in July, said the agreements could reverse some of the “damage” done to the post-Brexit British economy. He told MPs that Britain needed to “ take a calm, clear-eyed look at the world as it is today”. “Sticking to the status quo is not good enough,” he said, adding that “public opinion currently supports a pragmatic approach like the one I am suggesting”. After his address, the leader of the opposition, Kemi Badenoch , said Burnham would be unable to secure a better deal as the EU was ” tough negotiators” and warned that he had already “shown his hand”. In an interview released on Sunday, Burnham said it was “clear” that Russia interfered in the 2016 Brexit referendum and warned that French and German voters faced the same threat. His comments marked the first time that a UK Prime Minister acknowledged Russian interference in the referendum, but did not provide evidence to support the claim.

events.title: Tesla's robotaxis catch the eye of a US safety regulator — again
events.summary: Tesla's Model Y and Cybercab vehicles are facing a defect petition from the NHTSA. Aaron E. Martinez/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images NHTSA opened a safety inquiry about Tesla's self-driving Model Y robotaxis and Cybercabs. An unnamed petitioner alleged that the robotaxis were speeding in an active school zone. Tesla has faced growing regulatory scrutiny as it rolls out its all-important self-driving cars. Tesla's self-driving taxis are facing a fresh safety question: are they slowing down when kids are in school? On Monday, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration announced it had opened a defect-petition review into a claim that 2026 Tesla Model Y robotaxis and Cybercabs exceeded speed limits in school zones while their automated driving systems were active. An unnamed petitioner submitted three videos in support of the claim, according to the filing , which says the probe was opened on Friday. NHTSA said it will evaluate the complaint before deciding whether to grant or deny a formal investigation. The agency's filing lists no reported crashes or injuries, and estimates that about 1,000 vehicles could be affected. Tesla didn't immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. The scrutiny comes as Tesla pushes to turn robotaxis into a much bigger business. The electric automaker has expanded its self-driving services with the Model Y robotaxis beyond Austin into other Texas cities and Florida. In September, the company added its steering-wheel-free Cybercab to the Austin fleet . CEO Elon Musk has increasingly shifted Tesla's focus away from traditional vehicle sales toward self-driving, AI, and robotics. The self-driving rollout previously caught the attention of federal regulators. NHTSA opened an audit inquiry into the Cybercab's self-certification a few hours after the cars started offering services in Austin. School zones have also tripped up rival robotaxi companies. Last year, NHTSA opened a preliminary investigation into Waymo after reports that its vehicles passed stopped school buses in Austin and Atlanta. The Google-owned robotaxi company issued a voluntary recall in December. In January, a Waymo vehicle struck a child near an elementary school in Santa Monica, California. The child had "minor injuries" according to the NHTSA , and, in a statement published on its website, Waymo said the vehicle "braked hard, reducing speed from approximately 17 mph to under 6 mph before contact was made." events.title: Palmer Luckey says that executions should be 'public and brutal'
events.summary: Palmer Luckey called private executions "awful and dystopian." Bloomberg/Getty Images Palmer Luckey said that he was in favor of public executions. Luckey weighed in on the case of Nidal Hasan, who Pete Hegseth said would be executed on a livestream. Private executions are "awful and dystopian," Luckey wrote on X. Palmer Luckey wants to bring executions out from behind the curtain. The cofounder of Anduril weighed in on the case of Nidal Hasan , who was convicted of killing 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said that Hasan's execution would be livestreamed. President Donald Trump said he was still weighing the decision. Luckey said that he'd been "outspoken on wanting public executions for over a decade" — and that his position hadn't changed. "Executions should be public and brutal, not private and medicalized," Luckey wrote in a Sunday post on X . "They are the ultimate example of the state's monopoly on violence." Voters need to be confronted with the hard truth of these state killings in every instance, Luckey wrote, so that they can have appropriate "confidence or revulsion in the institution." It's not a new position; Luckey cites George Washington as an intellectual predecessor. Washington was a fierce disciplinarian who supported public hangings. Luckey's thoughts echo a French philosopher who lived two centuries after Washington. In "Discipline and Punish," Michel Foucault traced the spectacle of public executions to the private medicalization of executions behind prison doors. In his post, Luckey derided this shift toward private executions as "awful and dystopian." "It makes needless executions more likely, not less so," he wrote. "People who demean this as barbaric or yucky miss the whole point." Luckey had some sympathy for the pacifists who want to end the death penalty altogether. That argument is logically consistent, he wrote in response to another user. "If people don't want the Trump administration executing people in public, they definitely shouldn't want them doing it in private!" The post was certainly controversial. People on X called Luckey a " true psycho " and compared Silicon Valley to a psych ward . "Next they will be rationalising gladiatorial arenas for condemned prisoners," one user wrote. Others saw eye to eye with Luckey, including Palantir cofounder Joe Lonsdale , who wrote that he "agreed." "Palmer Luckey and George Washington are not barbaric," Lonsdale wrote. "Our society today is too soft in ways that cause our fellow citizens harm." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi counteroffensive is a proving ground for war robots
events.summary: Ground robots are being deployed in a variety of roles during Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi. Yevhen Titov/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images Ground robots are playing a key role in Operation Vivaldi, an ongoing Ukrainian counteroffensive. Ukrainian troops are using them to distract the Russians and carry out assaults behind enemy lines. Business Insider spoke with a commander whose unit is at the front of the robot operations. Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi is showcasing how ground robots are reshaping offensive warfare. In the opening stages of this complex operation, Ukrainian forces used uncrewed ground vehicles , or UGVs, as distractions. The robots drew Russian attention and exposed surveillance systems and firing positions while assault troops slipped through and seized key territory. Robots have also conducted airborne assaults, delivered explosives, attacked enemy command centers, and supported infantry operations amid this major counteroffensive in eastern Ukraine. NC13, a strike UGV unit within the Third Assault Brigade of the Third Army Corps, has played a leading role in Vivaldi. Mykola Zinkevych, the unit's commander, told Business Insider that his forces have used robots across a wide range of missions to inflict defeats on the Russians. Over the course of the operation, the robots evolved from diversions that enabled Ukrainian advances into armed strike platforms targeting Russian command posts, drone operators, and large troop concentrations in the rear. Ukraine is sending robots to distract and assault Russian positions. Yevhen Titov/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images Zinkevych, who goes by the call sign "Makar" and spoke through a translator, said these efforts disrupted Russian command and control and logistics, making it harder to bring in more soldiers and limiting Moscow's ability to conduct operations. Robots also carried out what the commander described as full-scale robotic assault operations , independently and in support of Ukrainian infantrymen. Most notably, NC13 used heavy bomber drones to carry armed robots over the front lines and drop them in enemy territory, surprising Russian troops and creating additional pressure, Zinkevych said. He added that it also affected their morale. Brig. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi, commander of Ukraine's Third Army Corps, revealed the use of this tactic in late September and said that his forces had become the "first in the world" to operationally air-drop robots from drones in combat. Beyond explosive-laden robots, NC13 also deployed robots armed with grenade launchers , Zinkevych said, adding that the unit was the first to do so in combat. He said the Russians apparently mistook the UGVs for an infantry assault, which led to confusion and disorientation. Broadly, robots are playing an increasingly important role in Ukrainian combat operations. ZUMA Press Wire via Reuters Connect These innovative tactics come amid broader efforts by Kyiv's forces to integrate ground robots into combat operations. Ukrainian officials have said they want machines to replace humans in dangerous front-line missions, particularly in logistics and casualty evacuation roles. Vivaldi, which Ukraine launched over the summer to halt Russian advances in the northern part of the Donetsk region, has already seen Kyiv retake control of dozens of square miles of territory, according to analysts at the Institute for the Study of War, a US think tank. Zinkevych attributed Vivaldi's success in part to strike robots, but he also credited Biletskyi's planning and coordination. Conventional weaponry, specifically artillery, has played a key role, too, according to Western analysts and the Ukrainian military. The Third Army Corps said last week that Ukrainian artillery fire has prevented Moscow from bringing up reserve forces, equipment, and ammunition to regain positions it had lost. Drones assessed damage and eliminated remaining targets. Artillery was responsible for a larger share of casualties in the war's early stages, but drones are now the biggest killer. ISW analysts wrote in an October 9 battlefield assessment that artillery remains relevant even in a drone-dominated fight. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Andrej Karpathy says this AI gap is widening
events.summary: AI researcher Andrej Karpathy said the gap in AI diffusion that he observed in April is widening. Michael Macor/The San Francisco Chronicle via Getty Images OpenAI cofounder Andrej Karpathy says most of the world is still barely using large language models. Karpathy said of those who do use LLMs, most regard AI as a Google-esque tool. That's not the only gap that is growing amid AI diffusion, Karpathy wrote. OpenAI cofounder Andrej Karpathy says the world still barely knows AI. "The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems," Karpathy wrote on X on Sunday. "When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot." Karpathy said he was following up on his April observation about a growing gap among AI users. Just over six months later, the renowned AI researcher who coined the term "vibe coding" sees the widening gap less as "two groups of people speaking past each other," as he phrased it in April, and more as a "sharp funnel." Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel. - Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come… https://t.co/79xGhQdf1n — Andrej Karpathy (@karpathy) October 11, 2026 The situation, Karpathy said, is that based on his estimate, roughly 75% of the world's population "have barely come in contact" with large language models at all. As for everyone else, Karpathy said around 1 to 2 billion people, "are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products." There's a bigger gap between the chatbot users and those who, Karpathy said, are using frontier models to code, a group that he estimates is around 20 million people or 0.2% of the population. This group, he wrote, sees "large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt." The smallest group, which Karpathy estimates is just 5,000 people, consists of those with inside access to frontier AI systems, likely due to their employment at one of the leading companies. Karpathy said the OpenAI Hugging Face breach showed what's on the horizon. "It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics," he wrote. "Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work." The pace of AI advancement is so rapid, Karpathy said, that humans are struggling to review the outputs fast enough. "For example, people are still involved in the 'archeology' of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago," he wrote. "Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while." Box CEO Aaron Levie said Karpathy's post was "a good way to understand how early we actually are in AI diffusion." "The vast majority of people are using AI as a chatbot for simple interactions that approximate next-generation search," he wrote. "This is super useful but dramatically underrepresents the full capability of AI." Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan said now is the moment to join the AI labs. "Be part of the 5000 today," he wrote on X. "It's amazing." Read the original article on Business Insider
