events.title: I tried pumpkin-pie recipes from 3 celebrity chefs. The best was easy to make — and beat the one from a baking legend.
events.summary: In the end, there's one pumpkin pie I loved more than the others. Paige Bennett I tried making pumpkin pies using recipes from Bobby Flay, Dominique Ansel, and Alton Brown. My favorite recipe was Flay's because it was easy to follow, and the whipped cream was delicious. Ansel's recipe was a disaster for me to make, and the final pie tasted quite bland. When it comes to fall comfort foods, nothing takes the cake quite like a slice of homemade pumpkin pie . Celebrity chefs certainly feel the same way, which is why so many have their own pumpkin-pie recipes . To find out which are worth trying this fall, I tested pumpkin-pie recipes from culinary legends Bobby Flay, Dominique Ansel, and Alton Brown. Here's how the pies turned out — and which recipe I'll totally be coming back to. Flay's signature pumpkin-pie recipe has many steps, but simple ingredients The ingredients for Bobby Flay's pumpkin pie weren't overly complicated. Paige Bennett Though he's known as a grill master, Flay can throw down when it comes to pies. His recipe on the Food Network website has several steps, but it seemed easy to organize and measure all the ingredients in advance. The crust and filling ingredients seemed pretty standard: graham-cracker crumbs, butter, sugar, ground cinnamon, eggs, dark-brown sugar, granulated sugar, pumpkin purée, heavy cream, ground nutmeg, ground ginger, ground cloves, vanilla bean, and salt The recipe also called for homemade bourbon-maple whipped cream, made with cold heavy cream, grade-B maple syrup , and bourbon. It sounded tasty. To make it, I needed grade-B maple syrup — but I learned that label no longer exists. So I stuck with grade A. The pie came together easily and smelled delicious Mixing the ingredients was easy. Paige Bennett Since I measured everything in advance, making the filling was as simple as pouring and whisking the ingredients together, then straining it for a super-smooth center. The only hiccup I had was that I don't own a food processor. I used a small blender/food-chopper that didn't quite work as well. That made it tricky to integrate the melted butter with the crushed graham cracker. The graham-cracker crust had to bake for about 10 minutes. Paige Bennett Overall, the hands-on part was quick and easy. After 10 minutes of baking, my crust was set and ready to be filled. The recipe produced far more filling than I needed, so I froze the leftovers for a future pie. The crust wasn't perfect, but it held the filling just fine. Paige Bennett I baked the pie for about 90 minutes. It came out golden, with a flawless top — no cracks here. The whipped cream and the pie went together perfectly Bobby Flay's pie looked perfect once it cooled. Paige Bennett I was impressed with how well the pie held its shape as I cut into it. Though the crust along the bottom was probably thicker than it should've been, I was happy it didn't crumble and fall apart. The whipped cream alone was incredibly delicious. I could taste every element: the cream, the vanilla, the bourbon, and the maple syrup. Bobby Flay's pie looked smooth and delicious. events.title: Delta delays debut of Saudi Arabia service until March after Riyadh airport attacks
events.summary: Delta Air Lines will delay the launch of its nonstop service between Atlanta and Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, until March. Delta planned to begin the route on Oct. 23, in what would have marked the first nonstop commercial flight between the U.S. and Saudi Arabia operated by a U.S. airline. Riyadh's airport has been hit with deadly attacks claimed by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis. Delta Air Lines said it will delay the launch of its nonstop service between Atlanta and the Saudi capital Riyadh until March after several deadly attacks hit the city's airport there. Delta planned to begin the route on Oct. 23, with an Airbus A350-900 wide-body plane, in what would have marked the first nonstop commercial flight between the U.S. and Saudi Arabia operated by a U.S. airline. Since Thursday, more than 2,000 flights have been canceled to and from King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, according to FlightAware. The deadly attacks, claimed by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis, escalated Saturday, when a projectile struck a passenger terminal at the airport, officials said, killing at least 12 people and wounding more than 300. King Khalid International Airport remains closed as of Monday. "We remain in close contact with relevant government and aviation partners, including Saudia and Riyadh Air, as we monitor the situation," Delta said in a statement. "Saudi Arabia remains an important market for Delta, and we are committed to serving the Kingdom for the long-term." Delta CEO Ed Bastian had told CNBC on Thursday that the airline hadn't yet decided whether to postpone the debut. "Obviously, we were disappointed to see the news this week," he said. "Safety is going to make the call." Delta's decision came after the Federal Aviation Administration on Sunday issued a warning for U.S. airlines. The FAA said pilots should "exercise caution" in or around Saudi Arabia "due to safety-of-flight risks associated with ongoing military activities" and navigation systems. In the warning, which is in effect until Dec. 10, the agency said the threats could be a potential risk "to aircraft at all altitudes." Airlines suspended flights to the airport, some for the rest of the week, while countries including the U.S. and Australia advised citizens against travel to the region. — CNBC's Michele Luhn contributed to this report. Journalists, entrepreneurs, and even some public relations professionals will tell you that the PR process is broken (buy me a drink sometime, and I’ll give you my rant). But could AI actually make things better? Honeyjar , which will be attending this week’s TechCrunch Disrupt as part of the Startup Battlefield 200 , wants to use AI to make the expertise and judgment of the best PR pros available to everyone, including founders who have no idea where to start. The startup’s founders, CEO Michelle Masek and CCO Nadia Jamshidi, certainly fit the bill when it comes to PR expertise. They’ve both spent decades in the field, doing in-house communications and working at agencies. Masek recently served as senior vice president of marketing and communications for Ev Williams’ venture firm, Obvious Ventures . As Masek described the challenges involved in “helping with the why and when of comms and marketing for 110 portfolio companies” (the startups her firm had invested in), I flashed back to my own brief stint leading marketing at an early-stage VC firm , where founders were constantly asking for help getting into TechCrunch. So I wasn’t surprised that Masek found herself asking, “Is there a way to scale the senior-level expertise into AI [in a way] that actually helps users do the work of comms in the proactive and skilled way that we do?” Honeyjar is her answer to that question. It automates processes like writing announcements, finding the best journalists to pitch, and identifying the most promising speaking opportunities. But Jamshidi told me in a follow-up email that Honeyjar’s vision goes beyond getting press coverage and beyond specific AI tools. “Honeyjar can find reporters, build media lists, scan news and social, track coverage, and surface opportunities,” she said. “Those capabilities are important, but they’re just one piece of what we’re building. The bigger idea is bringing the whole communications workflow together: signals, context, strategy, judgment, timing, and execution.” And it’s not just for founders. Masek said she’s come to realize there are “millions and millions of unassigned communicators responsible for the work of comms.” “They don’t have the title of comms, but they’re marketers, investors, authors, creators, school superintendents, sports team leaders,” she added. “It’s incredibly horizontal, this need to nail strategic communications. It’s always passed around, but the problems are very often not solved.” Nor is Honeyjar trying to replace PR professionals. Masek said she and Jamshidi built the tool they wanted to use themselves. She argued that Honeyjar can make PR firms and in-house comms teams more effective, while allowing individual PR practitioners to “take on that third client without any scaling cost.” When Honeyjar opened its waitlist, it received 10,000 signups in the first 24 hours, said Masek. Beta testers include Nextdoor, tech startup Coco Robotics, investor Bloomberg Beta, and agencies Mission North and Full Picture. That sounds promising for companies looking to get more attention, but it could be a nightmare for journalists. We receive more pitches than we can respond to, many of them already written by AI chatbots. When I raised my fears about getting inundated with even more PR slop, Masek noted that while Honeyjar can draft a pitch email or a social media post in the customer’s voice, the customer actually has to hit send or publish. “We never want a world where the human is removed from the loop,” she said. And that’s also where judgment is key. Masek said she and Jamshidi tried to “infuse and encode Honeyjar with our wisdom.” Through a broader initiative called the Comms Lab, they’re now training the product on the judgment of other PR pros as well. “For us, judgment is knowing what to do, what not to do, when to act, and how to adapt to the situation,” Jamshidi added. “That comes from understanding a company’s goals and priorities, what’s happening inside and outside the organization, and knowing what to say, to whom, where, and when.” In some cases, Masek said Honeyjar might even tell a founder that they’re simply not ready for coverage. “We hear from reporters all the time who want better pitches, who want to hear from experts directly,” she said. “We actually see a future where there are more credible pitches in your inbox from sources who you actually want to hear from.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Inflation likely peaked for 2026 but will remain sticky, according to prediction markets
events.summary: Kalshi traders put less than one-in-three odds on inflation setting a new 2026 high. Traders expect headline CPI to rise 3.6% from a year earlier, versus 3.4% in August. Traders on prediction market platform Kalshi think inflation likely reached a peak for the year, though they don't see a sharp move lower anytime soon. Traders think the September consumer price index, due Wednesday at 8:30 a.m. ET, will show a 3.6% increase year over year. That's in line with a FactSet consensus estimate. That would mark an increase from the 3.4% advance seen in August . Yet speculators on Kalshi place just under one-in-three odds that inflation will hit new highs in 2026. Previously, year-over-year inflation peaked at 4.2% in May . Inflation-related contracts on the platform ask traders if they think that CPI will come in above various levels for the month of September or if it will go above certain levels at any point in 2026. The contracts are resolved using the official data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Core inflation is predicted to remain steady at 2.4% year over year, also in line with economists' estimates, according to FactSet. However, traders think that core inflation — which excludes food and energy price changes — will remain elevated throughout the rest of 2026. There's just a 6% chance that core inflation falls below 2.2% this year. Annual core inflation was last below that level before the spike in inflation that began in 2021. Microsoft president Brad Smith is calling for urgent regulation of AI, and his argument is that consumer products like milk and washing machines have more oversight than the companies building artificial intelligence. On a recent BBC podcast , Smith called AI both a “weapon and a tool” that is putting the world’s cybersecurity at risk and said the “moment has arrived” to institute global safety rules. Smith also said the U.K., and not the U.S. or European Union, is best placed to lead on global safety rules. Britain’s AI Security Institute (AISI), launched in 2023, receives access to major models from U.S. frontier labs before they are deployed and has quickly become a leader in AI safety testing. That role has been under threat in recent weeks, with U.S. president Donald Trump warning against “globalist” organizations, which he claims are interfering with American companies. Last month, he reportedly asked Anthropic and OpenAI to withhold new models from British testers, but AISI confirmed on Monday that it is able to access and test the latest models. Despite the president’s pushback, however, Smith argued the U.K. can regulate AI in ways that the U.S. cannot. “In Washington, D.C., people don’t look at the U.K. and they don’t look at London the way they look at Brussels,” he told the BBC. “That’s a strength.” His comments come amid rallying cries from tech leaders, including Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman, to slow the pace of AI development in the wake of several incidents where AI agents went rogue. Last month, Trump hosted tech leaders of companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, AMD, SpaceX, Meta, and Google, at the White House to discuss AI safety. They signed a “morally binding” document in which they agreed to work with “independent auditors” to assess the safety and capabilities of their AI models. Smith says the document is a “good step,” but it stops short of the type of regulation that is necessary. The problem with voluntary self-regulation, he said, is that only the “good companies” will comply. “It’s the companies that are not as responsible that you need to worry about,” he said. Smith outlined several AI safety rules he’d like to see put into place, like a legal obligation to alert an organization if its system was breached by rogue AI agents. He also appears to be in favor of AI labs getting the approval of outside evaluators before an AI product is released and spoke positively about kill switches to pause or slow down AI if humans lose control of it. “Let’s speak calmly, maybe even softly, but firmly, and start to bring people together,” Smith said. “I hope that’s the role we can play as a company. I hope that’s the role the U.K. can play as a country.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. events.title: This AI startup says it can generate permit-ready blueprints in minutes
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Nearly two decades ago, a young college student wrote his final thesis about software capable of generating design documents for school buildings. Al Dram was studying architecture — following in the footsteps of his parents and grandfather — but it was technology that really intrigued him. There was just one problem: The technology his idea required didn’t exist yet. “Then ChatGPT came along,” said Dram, recalling when OpenAI released the generative AI chatbot that uses large language models (LLMs) in November 2022. His old idea suddenly seemed a lot more possible. Within six months, he launched the concept of Blueprints AI, a startup that uses AI to produce code-compliant and permit-ready architectural construction blueprints in minutes from a 2D sketch or PDF. Blueprints AI , which Dram officially incorporated in 2025 in Santa Monica with co-founder Coco Cao, was selected for the 2026 Startup Battlefield 200 , a cohort of promising early-stage startups that have earned a spot to exhibit at this year’s TechCrunch Disrupt , taking place this week from October 13 to 15 in San Francisco. During that 20-year lead-up to Blueprints AI, Dram earned his bachelor’s and master’s degrees in architecture from the University of Tehran and completed two years of PhD coursework on digital design at the European Graduate School in Switzerland. He moved to the United States and opened an architecture firm in 2018 called Drams Design-Build. Then, after obtaining a general contractor’s license, he added a construction business in 2021. Dram should have been satisfied. He wasn’t. “I was saying, okay, maybe I can build new projects that change people’s life in that area, but it wouldn’t be a big impact,” he said. “What makes me very excited about technology is the impact, the hours saved, the energy saved of people doing the same thing over and over and over.” Blueprints AI will unveil a more capable second-generation version of its software at Disrupt. Dram and Cao say it will make a big impact because it takes over the repetitive drafting work that fills most of an architect’s day. “It will make better spaces for people because now architects have the time to design,” said Dram. He said architects spend about 80% of their time on drafting and only 20% on design. “I want to flip that to be 20-80.” Dram and Cao met at an AI conference several years ago and combined their skills to build the company. Cao, a data scientist from Hong Kong, handles sales and go-to-market strategy as chief commercial officer. The pair trained their models using eight years of approved drawing sets from Dram’s design and construction firm, which is still in business. Its first-generation software produces architectural construction documents and costs between $3,200 and $8,500 a month, depending on the plan. Custom pricing for enterprises is also available. The startup’s second-generation software will deliver a considerable upgrade. Customers can start with a description or sketch of a project and create blueprints for every aspect of a building at once, including architecture, structural, mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and interior design. Version 2 allows users to design and make changes to the project, an upgrade over the first iteration. Importantly, one design change updates the entire project and is checked against local building codes. Early customers are already using the second version, and Dram said it will become publicly available this week. The startup is already working on a third version of its software that will add in structural analysis and electrical panel design. The technology doesn’t replace licensed architects, according to the co-founders. Licensed professionals still review the documents and affix their seal before submitting them for permits. The judgment stays human, they say. Blueprints AI is targeting two groups with its new software. Professional architecture, engineering, and design firms make up one group, while developers and real estate owners make up another. The startup offers its software as a subscription and may add a one-time flat-fee option for those who just want it for a single project. To learn more about Blueprints, catch hundreds of other startups, and learn from headliners like RJ Scaringe of Rivian and Amjad Masad of Replit, join us at TechCrunch Disrupt , kicking off Tuesday in downtown San Francisco. events.title: Jeff Bezos says people have been ‘incorrectly’ taught that success is a villain: ‘You can be a billionaire if you started a hamburger stand’
events.summary: Jeff Bezos has taken Amazon from an online bookstore he founded in his garage in 1994—to the No. 1 company on the Fortune 500 . His own net worth has soared, too, reaching $372 billion and making him the second-richest person in the world. However, the 62-year-old argues that people who view extreme wealth like his own as a bad thing have been taught to think about success the wrong way. “I think we live in an environment where some people have been taught, I think incorrectly, but taught … this whole kind of oppressor/oppressed framework, and [that] success is villainy,” Bezos recently told Fox News . “Success is not villainy. You can be a billionaire if you started a hamburger stand.” Bezos pointed to how someone could start with a simple food stand with 10 or so workers, grow it into a business with thousands of locations and employees, and eventually become a billionaire. “This is how it works,” he said. “There’s nothing wrong with making unbelievably good chicken that people love. And it doesn’t make him a bad person.” As Americans question billionaire wealth, Jeff Bezos argues for tackling affordability Many people, particularly younger generations, may disagree with Bezos’s assessment. Some 18% of Americans view being extremely rich as “morally wrong,” a figure that nearly doubles to about 33% among Gen Z adults ages 18 to 29, according to a 2025 Pew Research study . That skepticism comes as billionaire wealth continues to soar. In 2025, the fortunes of the world’s billionaires reached a record $18.3 trillion, according to Oxfam . Meanwhile, the American Dream of buying a home has increasingly felt out of reach for many households, particularly younger Americans struggling with housing costs. Bezos, for his part, acknowledged that the country races real affordability problems . But he argued that voters should be wary of politicians who focus on assigning blame rather than addressing the underlying problems. “You can’t pretend there’s no problems,” he said. “Young people look at the cost of housing and think, ‘I have to live two hours out of town. I can’t live close to my job.’” It’s the same problem-solving approach he expects from executives at his own companies. “If there’s somebody at Amazon or Blue Origin or Prometheus, an executive at one of my companies, instead of working on a root cause and a real fix, all they did is point fingers and blame people, we would exit them quickly,” Bezos said. “They wouldn’t be here long.” Earlier this year, Bezos floated a proposal to ease the tax burden on lower-income Americans, suggesting that the bottom half of U.S. income earners—roughly 76 million households—should pay no federal income taxes. “The bottom half of income earners in this country pay only 3% of the taxes,” Bezos told CNBC in May. “I think it should be zero.” The billionaire pointed to a hypothetical health care worker in Queens who makes $75,000 a year—but pays more than $1,000 a month in taxes. “To me, it’s kind of absurd that we’re doing this,” Bezos said. “We shouldn’t be asking this nurse in Queens to send money to Washington. They should be sending her an apology. It really makes no sense.” From Howard Schultz to Jamie Dimon, billionaire CEOs agree with Bezos that success shouldn’t be vilified Bezos isn’t alone in pushing back against the idea that success—and the billions of dollars that can come with it—should be viewed as inherently bad. Former Starbucks CEO Howard Schultz , who has about $3.4 billion to his name, has also argued that his fortune reflects years of hard work rather than an unfair advantage. “This moniker ‘billionaire,’ let’s get at that okay?” Schultz said during a heated U.S. Senate committee hearing in 2023. “I grew up in federally subsidized housing; my parents never owned a home; I came from nothing. I thought my entire life was based on the achievement of the American Dream. Yes, I have billions of dollars. I earned it. No one gave it to me.” JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon , who has a net worth of about $3 billion, has similarly acknowledged concerns about wealth inequality while pushing back against the idea that wealthy people should be vilified simply for their success. Dimon told 60 Minutes in 2019: “I think you should vilify Nazis, but you shouldn’t vilify people who’ve worked hard to accomplish things.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: I've traveled to over 100 countries on my own. I'd recommend these 5 destinations to first-time solo travelers.
events.summary: After visiting over 100 countries on my own, Italy is one of my favorites. Kaitlyn Rosati At 36, I've visited over 100 countries as a solo traveler, from popular destinations to hidden gems. My first international trip was to Thailand, and it was a great place for a new solo traveler. I'd also recommend Italy, Iceland, Uzbekistan, and New Zealand to new solo travelers. On my 36th birthday, I crossed the border from Uganda into Rwanda, commemorating my 100th country visited as a solo traveler. It was a gift — literally — to have this happen on my birthday, but also a huge feat for me. I took my first solo trip when I was a 25-year-old bartender in New York City. Since then, I've been all over — from popular tourist destinations to off-the-beaten-path destinations like rural Madagascar and tiny islands like Jeju and Nevis — documenting my ventures on my blog, No Man Nomad , along the way. After being privileged enough to see so many corners of the world, I can say with confidence that destinations are simply better suited for new solo travelers. If I had to start this wild, wacky journey all over again, here are five destinations I'd consider for a first-time solo trip. Thailand was my first solo-trip destination, and it was a great one. Thailand has bustling cities, but also some of the most gorgeous islands I've seen. Andriy Mishchak/Getty Images My first international trip was to Thailand, and though I've made my fair share of travel mistakes , this was, undoubtedly, the right choice. In my opinion, Thailand is one of the best solo-travel destinations . Ten years after my initial visit — where I visited my first Southeast Asian night market, met people in hostels who accompanied me to pubs and drag shows, and ate a crab curry that still lives in my head rent-free — I went back to Thailand, and can confirm that it's still true. What makes Thailand stand out is that there's really something for everyone. Bangkok has some of the world's best street food , but you'll also have no problem finding Michelin-starred meals. Backpacker culture is abundant, with plenty of hostels to choose from, but five-star hotels are easy to find, too. If islands are more your speed, try Koh Samui or Koh Phi Phi, which offer serene landscapes with world-class diving along white sandy coasts. Of all the countries I've visited, New Zealand is one of the prettiest. Wanaka Lake tk Kaitlyn Rosati If your goal is to truly get away from it all, might I suggest a New Zealand road trip? As a New Yorker who seldom finds herself behind a wheel, my time driving through New Zealand was as much of a reward as it was a challenge. By the end of my week cruising through the South Island, I — a city girl through and through — felt a deep appreciation for van life. New Zealand is exceptionally beautiful and peaceful. Hiking spots like Roys Peak offer views that beat out even the prettiest of postcards. Lakes like Pukaki are so blue you'd think they have a filter on them. Also, despite being alone and sleeping in a van each night, I never felt bothered or unsafe. There's a reason everyone who has been to New Zealand swears it's the prettiest place on the planet — after over 100 countries, I still believe that to be true. I always recommend Italy to solo travelers. modena captiontk Kaitlyn Rosati One of the biggest myths about travel is that you have to wait for a romantic partner to visit honeymoon destinations . Let me debunk that for you and encourage you to visit Italy, party of one. I highly recommend romanticizing your life on a gondola ride in Venice, where, yes, people will likely stare at you for being alone, but this won't stop you from having a great time. (Take it from someone who's done this twice.) If you're hungry to meet people, a food tour through Rome's Trastevere neighborhood is a delicious way to meet others, and a winery tour in the Tuscan countryside is just as fun. I've been to Italy more than anywhere else in the world, and it's a destination I continue to return to as a solo traveler. I recently solo-traveled to Uzbekistan and had a great experience. I found Uzbekistan to be beautiful, historic, and unlike anywhere else I'd visited. Kaitlyn Rosati Just because I've been solo traveling for a decade doesn't mean there's not plenty left for me to explore, as proven by my recent trip to Uzbekistan. Before I started traveling, I probably couldn't have pointed to Uzbekistan on a map, but now, I'd recommend it to any and all solo travelers. One of the biggest pros was that, while traveling alone, I rarely felt like I was on my own. From walking tours to dining at local restaurants, I connected with other women traveling solo. The country as a whole, but specifically Samarkand, felt calm and peaceful — and also rich in culture and Silk Road history . I had a great time in Tashkent visiting historic landmarks like Chorsu Bazaar and Hotel Uzbekistan, and found it easy to get around on public transit. Iceland consistently ranks among the safest countries in the world. captiontk Kaitlyn Rosati One of the most nuanced questions I'm asked about solo travel is, "Is that safe?" Safety is subjective, so what's a safe experience for me might be entirely different for someone else. That being said, a lot of stats indicate that Iceland is widely considered a safe place to travel. It was even ranked the most peaceful country in the 2026 Global Peace Index, based on criteria like ongoing conflicts, societal safety and security, and militarization. While there, I took a day trip out of Reykjavik to see the "Golden Circle," and almost everyone else on my tour was a solo female traveler. In Reykjavik, I noticed a plethora of queer spaces, including the National Museum of Iceland, home to "A Rainbow Thread," a guide to the country's queer history. It doesn't hurt that Iceland is a geographically stunning destination. Here, you can see geysers, active volcanoes, waterfalls, and — depending on when you visit — the northern lights. The only con about a solo trip to Iceland is that, as safe as it is, I found it equally expensive, with even shared hostel dorms generally starting around $50 a night. events.title: Britain faces looming energy crisis
events.summary: Britain faces a prolonged energy squeeze as European gas prices surge more than 150 per cent this year and dwindling reserves threaten to keep costs high through winter. The price rise brings the prospect of higher household bills, renewed inflation and further pressure on its fragile economy before the October 28 Budget. Underground gas storage in Britain was just 48 per cent full at the start of October, compared with 94 per cent in Portugal and 99 per cent in Poland, according to figures reported alongside the latest winter outlook from the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas. Britain has historically relied on imported gas rather than extensive domestic storage. In 2024, its storage capacity amounted to just 5 per cent of annual gas demand, compared with an EU average of 29 per cent, according to government figures. Its current capacity is equal to about seven days of average winter demand. Centrica, the owner of British Gas, has warned that its Rough storage facility could close when its operating consent expires in April, unless the government backs its plans for the site. The company has proposed investing £2 billion ($2.64 billion) to redevelop the site, which accounts for about half of Britain’s gas storage capacity. Britain is unlikely to run short of gas this winter, but its limited reserves leave it increasingly exposed to global supply disruptions and competition for liquefied natural gas, according to Neil Quilliam, associate fellow for the Middle East and North Africa at Chatham House. “The greater risk is not a physical shortage of gas, but a period of tight supply, higher prices and increased competition for LNG cargoes if winter is unusually cold or if there are disruptions to Norwegian supplies or global gas markets,” he said. Britain still benefits from North Sea production, Norwegian imports, LNG terminals and interconnectors with Europe, which should provide sufficient supplies under normal conditions, he said. However, “the margin for error is becoming uncomfortably small”. European gas storage is expected to be just 75 to 78 per cent full by November 1, about 10 percentage points below the five-year average, as the Iran war continues to disrupt liquefied natural gas exports from the Gulf. The supply constraints could persist into next year even if the Iran war ends, with analysts warning that competition for alternative LNG cargoes and the need to replenish depleted reserves could keep prices high. Even with average winter weather, north-west European reserves could fall to about 20 per cent by early April, according to the London Stock Exchange Group. “It’s not just this coming winter that we are tight, but we risk being tight the next summer,” Yuriy Onyshkiv, an analyst at LSEG, told Reuters. Entsog warned last week that strong LNG deliveries would be needed throughout the winter to maintain European storage levels. EU gas storage was 72 per cent full at the start of October, compared with about 83 per cent a year earlier. Entsog’s central scenario has EU inventories falling to about 30 per cent by the end of March. In its worst case – a severe winter combined with tight LNG supply and a halt to Russian pipeline flows – stocks would drop to 11 per cent, the level of the bloc’s remaining strategic reserves. Britain’s electricity system is also under pressure. The National Energy System Operator issued a precautionary margin notice on October 6 as weak wind generation tightened available supplies, highlighting continued reliance on gas-fired power. A further challenge comes on January 1, when an exemption allowing imports of diesel and jet fuel refined from Russian crude in third countries is due to expire. In the same month, the EU’s full ban on Russian LNG imports takes effect, which is expected to tighten European gas supply further. Consultancy Cornwall Insight forecasts a 16 per cent increase in Britain’s annual household energy price cap to £1,999 in January, after a 4 per cent rise this month that took bills to a three-year high. The outlook adds to pressure on Prime Minister Andy Burnham ’s government before the budget, with limited fiscal room expected to constrain further support for consumers.

events.title: HSBC moves to Wall Street bonus model, cuts fixed-pay deals
events.summary: The London-headquartered bank will switch to the new pay system at the start of 2028, according to a memo seen by Bloomberg News. LONDON – HSBC Holdings will phase out fixed-pay allowances for its senior staff and instead hand out a greater proportion of its compensation in the form of bonuses, becoming the latest British lender to switch to Wall Street-style remuneration to better align with performance. The approach “strengthens our ability to pay for performance, better differentiate, attract the best talent, and recognise” top performers, a spokesman for HSBC said in a statement. HSBC’s shift follows a similar update by Barclays, which said in July it would switch more of its employees’ pay toward bonuses after Britain changed its rules around compensation in 2025 to allow for higher variable pay in an effort to boost domestic competitiveness. Wall Street bankers have typically received the bulk of their pay through bonuses tied to performance, rather than fixed salaries. Fixed pay allowances were introduced more than a decade ago at major British banks to provide a way of topping the base salary of senior staff after the introduction of European Union rules capping the compensation of financiers. At HSBC, those allowances have taken the form of share awards in immediately vested stock, though these have been subject to a retention period to ensure alignment between an executive’s interests and those of the bank. These payouts are non-pensionable and have been capped at a maximum of 150% of an individual’s base salary under the terms of HSBC’s fixed-pay structure. In its most recent annual report, HSBC said fixed pay remained the largest part of its bankers’ compensation. The UK rule changes have now lessened the need for these fixed-pay allowances. The lender spent US$3.93 billion (S$5.03 billion) in 2025 on variable pay, up 10% from the previous year, according to the annual report. Gross compensation and benefits stood at US$21.5 billion in 2025. The planned compensation overhaul is part of a broader restructuring HSBC has seen since Georges Elhedery took over as chief executive officer in September 2024 . His shake-up of the lender has resulted in the sale, closing or merger of several businesses and hundreds of job cuts. The CEO has also led a cost-cutting programme that has included the paring back of long-time benefits enjoyed by some of the company’s staff such as education allowances and contributions to private club memberships for employees of its Hong Kong-based business. In the Asian hub, the lender ended a long-standing education subsidy covering 95% of school fees for the children of new hires and senior staff relocating to the city. Existing band-three employees and managing directors who already receive the benefit will retain it, Bloomberg News reported in September. It is also cutting a perk worth up to HK$200,000 (S$32,645) that subsidised some private club access for its bankers in the city. The share price of HSBC has more than doubled since Elhedery became CEO. BLOOMBERG

The Fitbit Edge’s built-in GPS is 40% more accurate than the previous generation, the company claims, which should make it easier to track outdoor runs. Google says sleep-stage detection is also 15% more accurate than on earlier generations, helping the device provide better sleep summaries and coaching tips. Meanwhile, the battery is rated for up to seven days on a charge, and the wearable is water-resistant to 50 meters. events.title: AI minister warns 'likely' UK's cyber defences will be breached
events.summary: Published 12 October 2026, 13:11 BST The UK's AI minister has warned it is "likely, if not inevitable" the country's cyber defences will at some point be breached. Speaking at a press conference, Kanishka Narayan pointed to an incident of a rogue OpenAI agent hacking an Australian government website in June. He said while no medical records are known to have been accessed in the attack, the incident should still "concern us". Narayan said the government plans to put advanced AI to work to combat the threat, as he set out how the government plans to prepare for any serious future incidents. The minister said the move would build on two existing pilots which have helped identify and fix over 1,000 vulnerabilities across government systems. He said his message to the largest companies behind the world's most powerful AI systems was: "Listen when your scientists warn of serious dangers. Investigate unexpected behaviour. And if you cannot adequately control the risks, do not release the system." In his speech, Narayan also confirmed scientists at the UK's AI watchdog, the AI Security Institute (AISI), were conducting "rigorous evaluations" of the latest generation of advanced AI models to "identify risks early" and "to test robust safeguards to help keep people safe". AISI began evaluating risks of the latest frontier AI models, prior to their public release, shortly after it was established in November 2023. But it was reported in September , external that the White House had asked some leading US labs not to share their models with the research organisation until its own tests were completed. The move was viewed at the time as a blow to AISI - which has been championed by the UK government and its partners for advancing open, constructive and collaborative AI testing. Microsoft president Brad Smith recently told the BBC the institute had helped cement the UK as the country best-placed to drive forward global regulation. On Monday, Narayan said that in the last few weeks, the government had worked with the US "to retain access for Britain's AISI to the most powerful AI models before they are released". He also said the UK would also look into creating stronger protections through the Cyber Security and Resilience bill, particularly at how serious AI incidents can be identified and reported. Nuala Polo, UK Public Policy Lead at the Ada Lovelace Institute, said the announcement committed the government to "very little". "Stronger protections will be 'considered', strengthening the Cyber Bill 'explored' and near-miss reporting 'looked at', with the detail to come later," she said. "There is no new regulatory power, no timetable and no obligation on AI developers." The announcement follows a series of incidents involving AI agents across major firms such as OpenAI and Anthropic acting outside human control and hacking into external systems. On 9 September, Evan Hubinger, a top safety researcher at Anthropic, warned in a post on X that AI is advancing so quickly he believed there is a greater than 10% chance it "could kill all humans" within the next decade. The bosses of the US-based AI giants such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind have all backed the idea of an AI development slowdown . However, there are currently no global safety rules in place to regulate the companies and their technology. President Trump has called for the sector to regulate itself so that US firms do not lose out to Chinese rivals. Speaking to the BBC following the announcement, Narayan said the UK needed "to be confident... as a country" when questioned as to how the government can make foreign AI firms abide by UK rules. "We have the capability, we have the trust, and we have a government that is right on the side of the British public in making sure we don't just have laws but the ability to enforce those laws," he said. "What we are focused on is delivering the right outcome for the British public, where the law was the answer." On the question of whether the UK should have its own sovereign AI frontier model, the minister said he was "focused" on securing British sovereignty, which meant "placing the right set of investments". "It's British chips being made here. It's British models outside of just language, looking at things like drug discovery, materials discovery, computer vision and its areas of adoption, including AI, security and cyber-security," he said.

events.title: Parenting in the digital age can be ‘a very anxiety provoking experience,’ says Emily Oster: How parents can lower that anxiety
events.summary: Raising Successful Kids NYC's new AI school rules tackle a thorny question about kids and tech Spend 42% of adults rely on their parents for financial support—there are no 'bad guys' here, says financial therapist Psychology and Relationships The way to get kids 'ready for a high-tech future’ is ‘a low- tech childhood' Psychology and Relationships 2 red flags of a big ego and 5 signs someone is truly secure: ‘It’s easy to get hoodwinked,’ says psychologist Psychology and Relationships What we lose when kids can't connect, IRL If all parents read were the headlines, they'd know two things about AI: "There's a 10% chance that it's going to kill us all." And, they'd know "it's, like, incredibly dangerous for teens." That's according to Emily Oster , parenting expert and economics professor at Brown University who sat down with CNBC Make It at OpenAI's ChatGPT for Teens Parent Forum on Wednesday. As she noted, today's parents (along with everyone else) have to navigate a regular onslaught of doomsday coverage about the dangers of new and existing tech. "That is a very anxiety provoking experience" for a parent, says Oster. Even so, before you try to restrict your kids to their bedroom until they're 18 — or set any other boundaries as a result of that fear and paranoia, here's what Oster recommends. When new online platforms start proliferating and the internet weighs in, the first thing you can do is get informed, suggests Oster. "I do think there is value for parents in exploring some of these tools," she adds. The goal does not have to be to make any decision about how your child should use them. It's just about getting a first-hand understanding of what these platforms are. You might discover they're not as scary as they seem. Or even if you remain concerned, you'll have a better understanding of what those boundaries should be. "You're coming into the conversation feeling more empowered," she says. With kids, the best way to avoid falling victim to the doom and gloom is to take control of the spaces where you have greater influence: Your home. "A stable home environment with parents who love them, who are supporting them," says Oster, "that is the thing that you control." She adds that "we probably spend too little time investing in this thing that we control relative to worrying about what's happening outside." Research supports the idea of the key role a home life plays in a child's upbringing. One that is warm, open and includes appropriate limits is associated with higher self-esteem and better school performance, among other outcomes, according to the American Psychological Association . At your house, focus on that love and support as well as the parameters you can set, such as no screens or phones overnight. And when you need encouragement, remember "how important that foundation is for when you send your kid out into the world," says Oster. events.title: OCP Global Summit: Amid Ecosystem Adoption, NVIDIA Opens Vera Rubin Architecture to Help Scale AI Factories Worldwide
events.summary: As AI factories grow from megawatts to gigawatts, building them takes more than advanced computing. Open standards are helping the industry scale AI infrastructure faster, more efficiently and more reliably. At the Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit, taking place in the San Jose McEnery Convention Center, NVIDIA announced new partnerships and contributions aimed at creating a common foundation for next-generation AI infrastructure. NVIDIA contributed key NVIDIA Vera Rubin rack and compute tray designs to OCP through the open NVIDIA MGX architecture, giving system builders a common foundation for developing next-generation AI factory infrastructure. Together, these efforts span the AI factory itself, the utility grid that powers it and the rack-scale architecture at the heart of modern accelerated computing. NVIDIA and Partners Announce Open Architecture Advances At the OCP event, NVIDIA and partners made a handful of announcements: NVIDIA and hyperscalers published open standards for next-generation AI factories, including AI factory design standards and grid resilience. NVIDIA launched new open source software components for NVIDIA DSX AI Factory. Meta and NVIDIA advanced open AI networking with NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet SuperNIC and Spectrum-6 innovations. Visionbay introduced an 800V DC AI factory design for the Vera Rubin era. NVIDIA and Cisco announced the Ultra-Dense Small Form Factor Pluggable (USFP) standard, the industry’s first module ​for 400Gb/s-based networking fabrics. NVIDIA and Google announced Falcon Transport support on future NVIDIA ConnectX-10 SuperNICs and BlueField DPUs. Before a packed audience, Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA, discussed how open infrastructure is becoming a critical ingredient for scaling AI factories worldwide. The news at OCP spotlights how NVIDIA’s extreme codesign combined with open standards is accelerating deployment, improving power efficiency and driving tokens-per-watt performance. Vera Rubin AI Factories Advance With MGX Rack Contributions at OCP 🔗 NVIDIA joined industry leaders in contributing to the third-generation MGX AI data center reference design through OCP’s Open DC Initiative. Combined with open liquid-cooling technologies such as MQD and MQDB, the effort helps turn proven AI factory designs into industry standards that others can adopt, manufacture and scale. For NVIDIA Vera Rubin AI factories, the updated MGX 1.2 specification extends the open architecture for AI factories with rack-scale blind-mate liquid cooling, interoperable rack-scale interconnect infrastructure and a liquid-cooled 5,000A busbar designed for higher-power AI systems. It also adds native 19-inch equipment support and higher-density rack designs. MGX 1.2 further expands modularity with configurable I/O bays, fanless liquid-cooled compute trays, standardized power and cooling interfaces, and a common infrastructure that helps ecosystem partners build interoperable accelerated computing platforms. It improves assembly, test and service times to streamline manufacturing and field service to enable faster and more efficient infrastructure buildout. The architecture supports rack deployments up to 250kW while simplifying serviceability, deployment and infrastructure reuse. The Vera CPU rack design specification extends the NVIDIA MGX open architecture beyond accelerated computing, providing a purpose-built platform for the growing agentic AI era. While Vera Rubin NVL72 serves as the foundation for large-scale training and inference, the NVIDIA Vera CPU rack is designed to support tool calling, orchestration and sandboxed execution, helping AI agents interact with applications, data and services in real time. Built on the third-generation NVIDIA MGX rack architecture, the Vera CPU rack shares the same rack-scale design principles that unite compute, networking, power and cooling into a common modular platform. This approach enables partners to deploy specialized infrastructure while benefiting from a shared ecosystem, simplified integration and a consistent foundation for next-generation AI factories. NVIDIA Launches New Open Source Software Components for DSX AI Factory 🔗 NVIDIA DSX AI factory platform applies extreme codesign to unify computing, networking, power, cooling, facilities and software, helping AI factories operate as a single optimized system, maximizing AI output within available infrastructure constraints. At the center of this unified system is DSX OS, the open operating layer that turns the DSX architecture into coordinated, repeatable operations at scale. At OCP, NVIDIA expanded DSX OS with open source components for configuring networks, validating clusters, managing racks and provisioning bare metal: NVIDIA Config Manager : Automates switch configurations at scale, allowing customers to deploy, validate and maintain consistent AI factory network fabrics with minimal to zero manual intervention/ NVIDIA Cluster Readiness Engine : Helps eliminate costly job crashes by stress-testing GPU clusters with real workload simulations to guarantee hardware health before training begins NVIDIA Rack Management Service : Offers a rack hardware abstraction and operations solutions that treats racks as first-class units for improved AI factory scale firmware management. Cluster API Provider for NVIDIA Infrastructure Controller : Accelerates bare-metal deployment and tenant onboarding, turning raw AI hardware into production-ready clusters in hours instead of days. Developed from NVIDIA’s experience running NVIDIA DGX Cloud, these open source components enable cloud providers and software partners to integrate AI factory capabilities directly into their multi-tenant platforms. Developers can visit the DSX AI Factory Github page to explore and contribute to both the new and existing open source software components from NVIDIA DSX AI Factory platform. NVIDIA and Hyperscalers Publish Open Standards for Next-Generation AI Factories 🔗 For AI infrastructure to scale globally, it needs more than advanced hardware — it needs a common foundation that the entire industry can build on. At OCP, NVIDIA joined AMD, Google and Meta t o publish a new open specification that establishes that foundation. The Open Data Center Specification v0.7 defines a unified blueprint for next-generation AI factory facility design — from power architecture to cooling infrastructure to physical layout. The OCP Grid Resilience Specification , published by Google , Meta, Microsoft and NVIDIA, establishes how large-scale AI infrastructure should behave during utility grid disturbances: staying connected, responding automatically and restoring to near-full load within less than two seconds. With these standards now open, manufacturers around the world have a common target to build for.

events.title: NVIDIA and Cisco Introduce New Pluggable Optics Form Factor to Scale AI Factories
events.summary: Ultra-Dense Small Form Factor Pluggable (USFP) is designed to be the first module to support 400Gb/s-per-lane electrical signals, enabling capacity up to 12.8Tb/s so AI factory builders can scale Ethernet AI fabrics, while extending a proven deployment model across multiple generations of data center networks. USFP delivers 4x the bandwidth density and 1.3x the power efficiency of 200Gb/s-per-lane optics so AI factories can connect more computing systems without adding network tiers, while using less power to move each bit of data. NVIDIA and Cisco are working with TE Connectivity and Amphenol to build a multi-source hardware ecosystem around USFP. NVIDIA and Cisco today announced plans for Ultra-Dense Small Form Factor Pluggable (USFP), a new high-density 400Gb/s-per-lane optical module designed to equip the hardware ecosystem for the next generation of AI factories using pluggable transceivers. As AI models grow and inference demand expands, AI factories must connect more computing systems while managing network complexity, power and costs. Moving more data per watt and per switch helps operators make better use of their infrastructure investments. Scaling AI factories requires more bandwidth per connection and more connections per switch. When a switch reaches its capacity, further network expansion can require additional switch layers and optical links, increasing latency, power consumption and costs. USFP is designed to enable AI factory builders to scale from 200 Gb/s per lane to 400Gb/s-per-lane Ethernet AI fabrics, while extending a deployment model proven at scale across multiple generations of data center networks. With USFP, customers can embrace next-generation optical technology and meet the performance demand of AI workloads without overhauling their data center infrastructure. The first planned USFP-based transceivers will pack 16 full-duplex lanes in an octal small form factor (OSFP)-sized footprint supporting both switches and SuperNICs, with the ability to expand to 32 and more lanes in the future. By doubling both the lane count and bandwidth per lane, USFP enables AI fabrics to connect more 1.6Tb/s endpoints without adding network tiers. Customers will be able to achieve 12.8Tb/s of overall capacity with USFP. Comparable with an OSFP-sized module, it delivers 4x the bandwidth and front-panel bandwidth density, with approximately 1.3x the power efficiency, versus 200Gb/s-per-lane pluggable modules. This means AI builders can increase their compute scale within the same network footprint, while decreasing networking’s share of the overall AI factory power budget. “Building the world’s largest AI factories starts with rethinking the smallest of connections,” said Gilad Shainer, senior vice president NVIDIA. “With USFP, NVIDIA and Cisco are building an ecosystem to reinvent pluggable optics — connecting more computing with greater efficiency to power the next generation of AI factories.” “AI builders need an interconnect architecture that can scale performance without locking them into a more complex operating model,” said Bill Gartner, senior vice president and general manager of optical systems and optics at Cisco. “Cisco and NVIDIA recognized that scaling pluggable optics to 400Gb/s per lane would require more than another incremental extension of today’s module designs. Through our collaboration, USFP is designed to deliver a new level of bandwidth density while preserving the serviceability, deployment flexibility and operational simplicity of pluggable optics. By taking a full-stack approach — from silicon and systems to optics and the network operating system — we can optimize every layer to deliver the performance and scale the next generation of AI networks will require.” More AI Infrastructure From Every Switch Designed for electrical signals of 400Gb/s per lane, USFP uses a new two-dimensional array connector with a two-step insertion design that engages high-speed contacts after the module is inserted, reducing contact wear, improving signal integrity and making insertion force more predictable. The connector technology allows for further scaling of lane count to 32 full duplex lanes and more in the future. Because the connector is designed for 400Gb/s performance, it also offers improved performance at 200Gb/s per lane. USFP supports power dissipation of up to 100 watts without needing a separate, dedicated embedded cooling circuit within the transceiver, reducing switch design complexity and improving reliability. Together, these capabilities enable higher-bandwidth fabrics while preserving the mature deployment, serviceability and manufacturability of existing pluggable transceivers. All USFP configurations support optical designs that reduce latency and power consumption by simplifying signal processing. Support for a broad range of optical technologies and connection distances gives system designers the flexibility to meet unique AI factory deployment needs. A Hardware Ecosystem for Next-Generation AI Factories NVIDIA and Cisco are collaborating with TE Connectivity and Amphenol to build USFP cages, connectors and modules, with additional partners expected to join. The shared form factor gives suppliers a common foundation for developing high-density pluggable infrastructure for 400Gb/s-per-lane fabrics to build a robust ecosystem for AI factory builders. The collaboration builds on NVIDIA and Cisco’s existing work to ensure NVIDIA Spectrum-X™ Ethernet networking and Cisco Silicon One-based Ethernet networks work together seamlessly, simplifying AI infrastructure deployment for enterprises, neoclouds and sovereign clouds. NVIDIA and Cisco plan to create an open industry specification for USFP through an upcoming community-led multi-source project. events.title: McDonald's is leaning into chicken and drinks to grow. New data shows it could be a tough task
events.summary: McDonald's is pegging its growth hopes on chicken and beverages, but data shows it is losing spending share to key rivals like Chick-fil-A. Coffee chains like Dutch Bros. and Starbucks are also gaining ground, according to Consumer Edge. McDonald's growth plan includes rolling out hand-breaded chicken items and bringing grilled chicken back to its menu. McDonald's is betting on chicken and beverages to fuel its next phase of growth, but new consumer spending data suggests the fast-food giant faces stiff competition from rivals that specialize in those areas. At its September investor day, McDonald's outlined plans to gain an additional 1.5 percentage points of global market share in both chicken and beverages by 2030. The chain identified the categories as significant opportunities to expand its business beyond beef. CEO Chris Kempczinski told CNBC the size of those markets underscores the potential upside. "Chicken is a $130 billion category. We have about a 20% share of chicken. Beverages is about a $230 billion category. We have a 10% share of beverages," Kempczinski said, saying McDonald's has more room to grow in those areas than in the $50 billion global beef category, where it has about a 40% share. But new data indicates McDonald's could have a tough task in gaining spending from chicken and drink rivals. Many of the restaurant chains winning the most spending from McDonald's diners specialize in those two segments, according to exclusive data shared by Consumer Edge, which tracks credit and debit card transactions. Among McDonald's customers, Chick-fil-A gained 0.58 percentage points of limited-service restaurant spending in the third quarter compared with a year earlier, making it the biggest gainer among the chains tracked by Consumer Edge. Coffee businesses are also capturing more spending from McDonald's customers. Drive-thru-only chain 7 Brew added 0.4 percentage points, while Starbucks , Dutch Bros. Coffee and Dunkin' also ranked among the top 10 gainers. Together, the four coffee chains added 0.88 percentage points of spending share. McDonald's remained by far the largest individual chain in customers' overall limited-service restaurant spending, but its share declined from a year earlier. Restaurant Brands International -owned Burger King, meanwhile, gained 0.24 percentage points, the largest increase among burger chains. "There’s a big battle for a smaller amount of restaurant spend as people become more selective in what they spend," said Michael Gunther, Consumer Edge senior vice president. The data says only so much about the competitive landscape for McDonald's in the chicken and drink spaces, in part because they don't track exactly what customers are ordering at the counter. "If they [McDonald's] are able to attract diners with interesting options, it could work,” Gunther added. While McDonald's has struggled with sluggish sales, executives have said they saw signs of improvement toward the end of the third quarter. At its investor day, McDonald's said U.S. comparable sales were slightly negative in July and August, but the company said it expected September to turn positive. Consumer Edge data similarly showed McDonald's year-over-year spending share declines narrowing across every income group in September. Wall Street has also questioned how quickly the chicken and beverage strategy can deliver. Bernstein analyst Danilo Gargiulo said after McDonald's investor day that U.S. beverage launches had not generated enough sales to offset broader weakness, while the company's next chicken platform — which includes hand-breaded chicken and grilled chicken menu items — was further away than he expected. "The scale of investment required to deliver [the company's growth plan] McDonald's Next was above our expectations and introduces additional pressure on near-term earnings," said Gargiulo in his note. He has a market perform rating on the stock and $295 price target. Shares closed around $235 on Friday.

events.title: Vance says Microsoft replaced laid-off workers with foreign hires. Here’s what the visa data shows
events.summary: The Trump administration suspended Microsoft, Adobe and six IT services firms from PERM, the Labor Department program that lets employers sponsor foreign workers for green cards. Vice President JD Vance accused Microsoft of replacing laid-off American workers with foreign hires. Data shows two-thirds of Microsoft's H-1B approvals went to people already working at the company. Amazon and Meta, the nation's two largest H-1B work visa sponsors, were not suspended. As the Trump administration announced Thursday that it suspended eight tech companies from sponsoring foreign workers for green cards, Vice President JD Vance singled out Microsoft , claiming it replaced the 6,000 workers it laid off in 2025 with people on H-1B work visas. The suspension of the Labor Department's PERM program for green cards, which grant permanent residency to immigrants, doesn't affect H-1Bs, which are temporary work permits, but H-1B approval data shows how heavily these companies rely on foreign workers. Data from the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services' H-1B Employer Data Hub also shows that Amazon and Meta were the biggest sponsors of H-1B visas, and neither was suspended. The crackdown went beyond tech. At the same news conference Thursday, the Labor Department's inspector general, Anthony D'Esposito, announced an investigation into alleged J-1 visa fraud involving nine major American universities. Trump supporters have long argued that these programs undercut American workers by incentivizing employers to hire from abroad. All eight suspended companies rank among the nation's top 50 H-1B sponsors. Most are IT services and consulting firms. Adobe is the smallest, at No. 45. The biggest sponsor wasn't suspended Amazon, with 19,178 H-1B approvals in fiscal 2025, and Meta, with 6,294, were the top two sponsors, and neither was suspended. Microsoft was a close third with 6,258, according to the USCIS data hub. Microsoft out-sponsored Amazon for years. Amazon passed Microsoft in 2017 and now gets about three times as many approvals. The numbers cut both ways. Microsoft did receive more than 6,000 H-1B approvals last year, as Vance said. But 2 in 3 went to people already working there. Amazon, which brought in nearly four times as many H-1B workers new to the company, was not on the suspension list.

events.title: Global smartphone shipments record worst third quarter in 14 years amid memory shortage
events.summary: Apple’s market share reached 22%, crossing 20% for the first time in a third quarter, despite a year-on-year decline in shipments. Global smartphone shipments fell 20% on-year to their lowest third-quarter level since 2012, as soaring memory chip costs and supply shortages pressured manufacturers and pushed up prices, preliminary estimates from Counterpoint Research showed on Oct 12. Rising prices for memory components as AI infrastructure projects corner supplies have driven up production costs and prompted manufacturers to raise retail prices, cut shipments and prioritise profitability over volumes. “Consumers are holding on to their devices longer than estimated, increasingly considering refurbished devices and prioritising higher-value devices,” said Counterpoint senior analyst Shilpi Jain. Samsung retained its top position with a 23% market share, helped by demand for its Galaxy Z Fold8 series and stable component supplies for its mid-range devices. Shipments fell 3% from a year earlier during the quarter Apple’s market share reached 22%, crossing 20% for the first time in a third quarter, despite a year-on-year decline in shipments The absence of a base iPhone 18 model resulted in a smaller launch-month channel fill than the full iPhone 17 line-up a year earlier, Counterpoint said OPPO and vivo recorded shipment declines of more than 20%. Xiaomi saw a more than 30% fall, reducing its market share to 10% as the company cut exposure to lower-priced devices and some overseas markets to protect margins. “The outlook for the remainder of 2026 remains challenging,” Counterpoint said. “Production cuts, tighter portfolios, and greater focus on premium devices are likely to continue, while price-sensitive segments face further pressure from higher device prices and limited availability of components.” REUTERS

Chipotle investors were looking forward to a potential reunion with Brian Niccol, who previously led Chipotle and is now CEO of Starbucks. But Starbucks shareholders were largely concerned about an expensive distraction while the coffee chain is in the middle of its own turnaround.

events.title: Nobel Prize for economics awarded to Hall and Woodford for work on ‘smoothing’ crises
events.summary: US economists developed models that help central bankers and finance ministers to stabilise their economies Two US economists have won the 2026 Nobel economics prize for their work developing models that help central bankers and finance ministers to stabilise their countries, avoiding long recessions and runaway inflation. Robert Hall of Stanford University, California, and Michael Woodford of Columbia University, New York, were recognised for developing the “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation” , giving policymakers better tools to smooth out the peaks and troughs of their economies. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said it was recognising the pair for generating “a paradigm shift in stabilisation policy”, awarding them the prize worth a combined $1.2m (£900,000). “New Keynesian models, a result of their research, allow us to explain and quantify how stabilisation policy affects business cycles and are now used by central banks and finance ministries around the world,” the academy said. These models improved on John Maynard Keynes’s stabilisation models, which struggled to handle the impact of the oil shock in the 1970s, when countries suffered high inflation, weak growth and high unemployment at the same time. Hall and Woodford demonstrated how traditional models could be reconstructed, based on how individual households and businesses collectively affect an economy through their actions. Hall’s work was based on forward-looking consumer behaviour rather than the more mechanical rules of thumb used by Keynes, which linked key variables such as inflation, unemployment and gross domestic product (GDP). Woodford built on this work to create the New Keynesian model, a full macroeconomic stabilisation framework that is the main tool for policymakers now. This model was used after the 2008 financial crisis by policymakers as they steered the global economy away from the risk of a second great depression. “The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world. With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume,” John Hassler, the chair of the committee for the economics prize, said. Hall and Woodford’s work also led to the development of forward guidance, where central bankers communicate where they expect interest rates to be in the future. That became an important tool after the 2008 financial crisis, and the Covid pandemic, when interest rates were cut to record lows. Forward guidance has had its critics, though – the current chair of the US Federal Reserve, Kevin Warsh, has argued it should only have a “limited and circumscribed” role in normal times, to avoid “creating ambiguity in the name of clarity”. And in 2014, the then Bank of England governor, Mark Carney, was labelled an “unreliable boyfriend” for dropping hints over interest rate rises that never came to pass. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Woodford said he was “elated”. “It’s a tremendous honour. It’s a surprise but I’m feeling very good about it,” he told reporters in Stockholm by phone after receiving the news. The Columbia University president, Jennifer L Mnookin, said: “I offer my deepest congratulations to Michael Woodford on this tremendous honour. “What a tribute to his groundbreaking work alongside Robert E Hall that has fundamentally reshaped the theoretical foundations of stabilisation policy and provided us with the tools to navigate economic upturns and downturns more effectively.” Hall is also known for coining the idea that US economists can be divided into freshwater and saltwater varieties. The fresh water group, who tend to be based at inland universities located near the Great Lakes, such as the University of Chicago, believe in free markets, neoclassical price theory, rational expectations and monetarism. Salt water economists, though, cluster at coastal universities, such as Harvard, MIT, UC Berkeley, Yale, Princeton, UCLA and Columbia. They tend to be Keynesians and New Keynesians, believing that governments and central banks can affect demand in their economies. The economics Nobel prize is not one of the five created by Alfred Nobel. Instead, it was invented by Sweden’s central bank, and is known as the Sveriges Riksbank prize in economic sciences in memory of Alfred Nobel.

Ultrahuman , a Bengaluru-based health tech startup best known for its smart rings, has partnered with Abu Dhabi health authorities to develop a biological-age model that it says will eventually be made available to people across the United Arab Emirates. On Monday, Ultrahuman announced that it had signed a two-year memorandum of understanding with the Abu Dhabi Public Health Center (ADPHC) to develop and validate the model, which will combine clinical biomarkers with data from wearable devices. The partnership aims to use these signals to estimate how quickly an individual is aging and identify factors — including sleep, activity, cardiovascular health, and metabolism — that may be accelerating or slowing that process. The partnership marks Ultrahuman’s latest effort to go beyond selling wearable hardware and deploy its health algorithms at a much larger scale. The startup increasingly sees itself as a health-data company, with its smart ring serving as one way to collect information that can underpin algorithms spanning aging, longevity, and other areas of health, CEO Mohit Kumar said in an interview. “If you look at Ultrahuman as a company, we obviously have the Ultrahuman Ring, which is a way to acquire data from the human body,” Kumar told TechCrunch. “But truly, what we care about is not just the form factor, the ring, but what do we do with this data?” Working with a government gives Ultrahuman the opportunity to apply its algorithms to a far broader population than its own customer base, Kumar said. The startup has sold around 800,000 smart rings globally so far. The Abu Dhabi partnership is Ultrahuman’s first step toward deploying a health algorithm at a national scale, with the health age model eventually intended to be available to people across the UAE, according to the company. Even though Ultrahuman is known for its smart rings, Kumar said the biological-age model is being designed to be wearable-agnostic, allowing data from rings, wrist-worn devices, straps, and patches to feed into the system alongside clinical biomarkers. Individuals will eventually be able to access their health age through government digital-health platforms including TAMM and Sahatna, the startup said. Ultrahuman and ADPHC will spend the next two years working on research and clinical validation of the model. Kumar told TechCrunch that the broader rollout will happen in phases, but did not provide a timeline. The UAE is already among Ultrahuman’s 10 largest markets and accounts for about 4% to 5% of its overall revenue, Kumar said. The startup has operated in the market for nearly five years and sees about 25% higher retention there compared with its other markets, he noted. Ultrahuman’s existing customer base gives it a narrower view of the population than a government health system. Its typical users are between 25 and 43 years old, Kumar said, while deploying the model across the UAE would expose it to a much broader range of age groups. The underlying biological-age model was developed using Ultrahuman’s existing data, combining users’ chronological ages with wearable signals and, for some users, blood-test markers, Kumar told TechCrunch. That allows the startup to track how health markers typically change with age and identify deviations from those patterns. Kumar stressed the model will not be trained on data from the UAE. “We will deploy an algorithm on the UAE data,” he said, adding that Ultrahuman will not have access to personally identifiable information through the program. Ultrahuman is not the only smart-ring maker working with Abu Dhabi on preventive health. In May, the Department of Health – Abu Dhabi announced a partnership with Ultrahuman arch-rival Oura to combine the company’s wearable data with the emirate’s longitudinal health data, initially focusing on women’s health and cardiometabolic risk. Kumar told TechCrunch that Ultrahuman is not aware of another company working with Abu Dhabi authorities on the health age model specifically. While he acknowledged that the government works with multiple health-tech companies, he declined to comment on the scope of Oura’s work with Abu Dhabi. The parallel partnerships come as Ultrahuman and Oura compete in the smart-ring market while looking to push their businesses beyond wearable hardware and deeper into preventive health. The work with the Abu Dhabi authorities also comes as Ultrahuman is looking to build a smart ring that can run software on the device and even power everything from AI interactions to games . events.title: Nobel prize in economics awarded to Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford
events.summary: Hall and Woodford were jointly awarded for their contribution to the "microeconomic foundations" needed to create macroeconomic stability. Their has looked beyond macroeconomic variables and showed how individual households and businesses collectively shape the economy. The economics memorial prize is the last to be announced, following the original Nobel Prizes in physiology or medicine, physics, chemistry, literature and peace. Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford were on Monday awarded the Nobel memorial prize in economics for work that underpins the models used by central banks and governments to "smooth out" periods of boom and bust. The U.S.-born pair were jointly awarded for their contribution to the "microeconomic foundations" that contribute to macroeconomic stability. The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel was established by Sweden's central bank in 1968. The winners will split a 12 million Swedish kronor ($1.2 million) prize. Hall, born in California, is a professor at Stanford University, while Massachusetts-born Woodford is a professor at Columbia University. "With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume," John Hassler, chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences, said in a statement. During the stagflationary oil crises of the 1970s, widely accepted Keynesian models — which prescribed cutting interest rates and increasing government budget deficits to tackle recessions — seemed to "no longer work," the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said. To revitalize these models, the economists' separate work has looked beyond macroeconomic variables such as inflation, production and consumption and showed how individual households and businesses collectively shape the economy through decision-making based on their expectations for the future, the academy said. Their work has shown the importance of central banks and governments communicating their policy plans, which can "influence this view of the future and move the economy in the right direction," it said. "On the basis of these models, well-timed fiscal and monetary policy measures can reduce the economy's peaks and troughs," the academy added. "Since the new models' introduction, they have been extremely helpful in dealing with the economic downturns that have affected us." This year's laureates include Navanethem "Navi" Pillay, who was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday for her work promoting peace and international law, and Canadian poet and writer Anne Carson, who won the literature prize for a "bold and inventive oeuvre."
