events.title: UAE wealth set to hit $6 trillion in 2030 despite short-term war volatility
events.summary: Net wealth in the UAE is set to jump to $6 trillion by the end of this decade despite the short-term volatility caused by conflict in the Middle East , a new report has found. In the five years to the end of 2030, net wealth in the Emirates is set to increase by more than $2.3 trillion, at annual growth of 10.6 per cent, the report by global advisory firm Boston Consulting Group said. The sharp projected increase, driven by a rise in real assets and financial wealth, “points to the UAE's long-term wealth creation potential”, BCG said in its Global Wealth Report 2026: The Great Reordering report on Monday. Last year alone, net wealth in the Arab world’s second-largest economy grew by almost 13 per cent on an annual basis to reach $3.6 trillion. Real, or physical, assets with intrinsic value such as property portfolios reached $2.4 trillion in 2025, jumping from $2.2 trillion at the end of the previous year. Financial wealth grew to $1.4 trillion in 2025, rising from $1.2 trillion a year earlier, while liabilities for the same period rose from $210 billion to $220 billion. The report estimates liabilities to rise to $340 billion by 2030. The Iran war has introduced “short-term volatility across Middle Eastern markets, with investor sentiment shaped by geopolitical uncertainty and oil-price movements”, said Lukasz Rey, managing director and partner at BCG. “While we anticipate slightly lower growth over the next one to two years, a rebound is expected towards the latter part of the decade.” Sovereign wealth strength, economic diversification agendas, family-business liquidity events and private capital activity will all help drive wealth creation in the country, Mr Rey said. Caution to prevail BCG, he said, expects wealth managers to remain cautious in the near term. However, “the region's wealth development story remains structurally resilient over the five-year projection horizon”, Mr Rey added. The Iran war, which began on February 28, has led to increased economic uncertainty across the Middle East. Despite a halt in all-out hostilities since early April, several attempts to reach a permanent deal to end the conflict have failed. The World Bank last week said Gulf economies would contract by an average of 4.3 per cent this year, a downwards revision of 5.7 percentage points from its forecast in April. The International Monetary Fund also expects economies in the region to contract this year but anticipates a sharp expansion next year once the conflict settles, managing director Kristalina Georgieva said. Despite the geopolitical uncertainty and economic headwinds, wealth generation and flow of new money to the UAE continues. The country remains a magnet for the ultra-wealthy , as well as global wealth managers and trillion-dollar asset managers. A base in the country offers global investors and money managers opportunities to expand regional operations and work with some of the world's largest sovereign wealth funds, as well as family offices and institutional partners. Concentration of wealth The UAE’s financial wealth remains concentrated among high-net-worth individuals, with “the composition of wealth expected to evolve by 2030 as more wealth accumulates within the lower high-net-worth segment”, the BCG report said. The country had about 500 ultra-high-net-worth individuals – those with assets in excess of $100 million – in 2025. That number is expected to jump to about 800 by the end of the decade, while their share of total financial wealth will rise marginally from 26.3 per cent to 26.5 per cent. The upper high-net-worth segment, featuring people with assets of $20 million to $100 million, is forecast to grow from about 2,700 to 4,200 individuals, with their share of wealth broadly stable, rising from 7.4 per cent in 2025 to 7.6 per cent in 2030. Meanwhile, the group of 200,000 lower high-net-worth individuals, with an asset range of $1 million to $20 million, are estimated to increase their share of financial wealth from 29.3 per cent in 2025 to 31.5 per cent in 2030. The affluent segment with assets worth $1 million is expected to expand from about 500,000 to 600,000 individuals in 2030. However, its share of wealth will decline from 15.5 per cent to 14.6 per cent, BCG data found. Centre of choice The UAE also continues to strengthen its position as a global wealth booking centre, with cross-border wealth belonging to international clients and booked in the country jumping more than 11 per cent to $721 billion last year. Currency and deposits, valued at $471.8 billion in 2025, are projected to rise more than 10 per cent annually to $778.9 billion by 2030. Bonds are estimated to grow almost 12 per cent on an annual basis to $27.8 billion, while equities are expected to reach jump to $591.9 billion by 2030, from $419.4 billion last year, BCG found.

events.title: American professors Hall and Woodford win Nobel economics prize
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Americans Robert E Hall and Michael Woodford win Nobel memorial prize in economics Robert E Hall (left) and Michael Woodford shared the economics award. ( Reuters: Anders Wiklund ) American professors Robert E Hall and Michael Woodford have won the Nobel memorial prize in economics. They were honoured for their groundbreaking work on the micro-economic foundations of macro-economic stabilisation. The will receive around $900,000 each for winning an award that began in 1968. American-born economists Robert E Hall and Michael Woodford have won the Nobel memorial prize in economics for their work on the micro-economic foundations of macro-economic stabilisation. Professor Hall, 83, is professor of economics with Stanford University in California, and 71-year-old Professor Woodford is the John Bates Clark Professor of Political Economy at Columbia University in New York. The award was announced by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm. "The laureates' work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world," John Hassler, chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences, said. "With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume." Last year, three researchers who study business innovation won for explaining how new products and inventions promote economic growth and human welfare , even as they leave older companies in the dust. The Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences was first awarded in 1968. ( Reuters: Tom Little ) The economics prize is formally known as the Bank of Sweden Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel. The central bank established it in 1968 as a memorial to Nobel, the 19th-century Swedish businessman and chemist who invented dynamite and established the five Nobel prizes. Nobel purists stress that the economics prize is technically not a Nobel prize, but it is always presented together with the others on December 10, the anniversary of Nobel's death in 1896. The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.8 million), whether for an individual, small group of laureates or organisation, so they will receive around $900,000 each. Journalists in Stockholm were able to interview co-winner Michael Woodford on the telephone from the US. ( AFP: Jonathan Nackstrand ) "It's a surprise, but I'm feeling very good about it," Professor Woodford told reporters via phone during the announcement of the prize, saying he felt "elated" over receiving "a tremendous honour". The US imposes sanctions on the International Criminal Court hours after one of its former judges is given the Nobel Peace Prize. A concrete example of his work implemented in practice was when the 2008 financial crisis created a situation where "traditional tools of monetary policy were not really adequate to deal with the problem of restoring economic activity," he said, noting that interest rates were already lowered to zero in many countries. One of the new approaches employed by central banks was to start making "more explicit statements" on where they believed guiding interest rates were headed in the future, which continues to this day. The majority of previous economics laureates have been from the US. Only three women have ever won, most recently Claudia Goldin in 2023 for work on how gender has affected pay and employment over time in the United States. Nobel prizes for the categories of medicine , physics , chemistry , literature and peace were announced last week. events.title: HMV to close Oxford Street store after three years
events.summary: HMV says it is looking for a new site in London's West End HMV has said it will shut its flagship Oxford Street store three years after it reopened the site, blaming a proposed doubling of the rent for the closure. The entertainment chain said it would leave the shop in March 2027, in a move affecting more than 50 staff. It said it was looking for a new site in London's West End district for its flagship shop and said it planned to maintain a "significant presence" in the capital. Phil Halliday, managing director of HMV, said it was "frustrating" that the Oxford Street shop was "commercially unviable". He said: "This is a special store, it's where we began 100 years ago and bringing it back to life in 2023 was a big moment in our recent history. "We are looking ahead, and our focus is now on what we do to make exciting steps for HMV in 2027." HMV shut its Oxford Street store in 2019 after it went into administration The group said its landlords had proposed doubling the rent on the site at 363 Oxford Street, and it was also facing a bill for "substantial" renovation works at the store, which together would make the shop "commercially unsustainable". HMV said it would look to transfer affected workers to its two other London stores and head office while it looked for a new site. The chain reopened its historic Oxford Street store in November 2023 after a four-year absence following a deal secured with landlords. It first opened the Oxford Street site in 1921. HMV has 113 stores across the UK, including six sites under the Fopp brand, as well as another eight in Europe. The group said it remained committed to high street stores. events.title: Tanzania seeks investment to tackle youth job pressure
events.summary: The News Tanzania is counting on increased investment to accelerate industrialization and create jobs for its young population, the prime minister said. The government has targeted $15 billion in annual foreign direct investment, roughly triple last year’s figure, as part of its long-term economic plans . Mwigulu Nchemba, speaking on the sidelines of an investment forum in London, said the government had put money into rail and port infrastructure, as well as expanding power generation to create an industrial base. This was on top of cutting the cost of doing business, and strengthening supply chains. Nchemba said increased industrialization would boost local processing of natural resources leading to more employment opportunities. Tanzania, like many African countries, has a rapidly expanding population. The UN estimates 42% of people are aged 14 or under . The prime minister said the path to creating work for all the country’s school leavers rests on developing the private sector through investment. “There is no way you can absorb all those graduates,” the prime minister told reporters. “The only way you can solve the issue of job creation is by empowering the private sector to create those vacancies for our youth.” Know More Tanzania has large offshore gas resources and deposits of minerals needed for the energy transition and digital infrastructure — such as copper, lithium, and cobalt — as well as precious metals and stones, including gold and diamonds. In August, the country commissioned a 2,115 MW hydropower plant that more than doubled its electricity generation capacity and ​created a surplus that officials said could support power exports and industrial growth. Tanzania, like governments across the continent, is looking for ways to add value locally instead of raw minerals exports. In neighboring Kenya, President William Ruto has focused on job creation through industrialization as a key plank in his campaign to secure a second term in next year’s election. Notable Liquefied natural gas development offers Tanzania its most obvious means of monetizing its giant gas reserves after the wars in Ukraine and Iran upended global energy markets, wrote Neil Ford in African Business.

events.title: Sheng Siong, OCBC, SGX receive analysts’ downgrades
events.summary: New challenges are emerging for Sheng Siong, while its previous competitive advantage might be fading, says an analyst. SINGAPORE – A few Singapore stocks received downgrades by analysts recently, including OCBC, Sheng Siong and the Singapore Exchange (SGX). Maybank analyst Hussaini Saifee downgraded the supermarket’s stock to “hold”, leading to the stock sliding more than 2% on Oct 12. Hussaini said Sheng Siong remains a high-quality operator, but its “strong share price re-rating now prices in much of it”. He added that Sheng Siong has benefited from resilient consumption, market share gains and targeted vouchers that channelled spending directly to supermarkets, but that support is weakening as assistance is shifting to GST vouchers and cash payments. “Supermarket growth has already eased to low single digits,” he said, adding that growth will track underlying income and population trends, instead of repeating the “unusually favourable” conditions of recent years. He added that new challenges are emerging for the supermarket brand, while its previous competitive advantage might be fading. Previously, Sheng Siong captured displaced demand when Giant and Cold Storage shut some stores. Hussaini also noted that people may be crossing the border into Malaysia to shop, given the upcoming Johor Bahru-Singapore Rapid Transit System Link, or going online to get groceries, which might pose challenges to Sheng Siong. “While neither appears disruptive enough to reshape the industry in the near term, both point to a less favourable backdrop than in recent years,” he added. He downgraded the target price to $3.12, from the $3.22 he previously aimed for. Meanwhile, Citi analyst Tan Yong Hong downgraded OCBC to “sell” and reiterated his call to sell UOB. However, he kept DBS at a “buy” call. He said analysts see downside earnings risks to the third-quarter forecasted results, based on “market misplaced optimism on Singapore dollar rates and after an exceptional first-half wealth-related income”. This is particularly the case with OCBC, which he said is trading at the tightest dividend yield spread over bond yield, followed by UOB and DBS. This means that the market is pricing in most aggressive growth, he noted. “Singapore banks have enjoyed a three-year re-rating cycle from 2024, starting from capital management hopes from 2024, wealth management growth from 2025, and recently crowding positionings amid the Equity Market Development Programme and ‘anti-AI’ trade,” Tan said. The programme refers to a $6.5 billion initiative launched by the Monetary Authority of Singapore to boost the liquidity and vibrancy of the local equities market. Tan also said there are risks that forecasters have been mispricing net interest income upside by assuming higher rates because of the resurgence in loans growth. Higher Singapore dollar funding costs is a key risk to that, alongside fixed-rate loans repricing lower, he noted. However, JP Morgan analysts recommended trimming OCBC and DBS, while relatively preferring UOB. They noted that banks in the region may be impacted by the ongoing sharp increase in long bond yields. All three banks saw share price gains on Oct 12 despite the downgrades. DBS rose 0.8% to hit $73.94 on Oct 12, while OCBC rose 0.2% to $29.06. UOB gained 1.4% to close at $40.50. Separately, SGX was also downgraded by Macquarie analysts a week ago. It was labelled as “underperform”, down from “neutral”, as analysts noted its monthly statistics were starting to wane. Citi analysts noted that the SGX acts as a proxy to the Singapore market. If there is an improved economic outlook, SGX will see upsides. But if there is news of a slowdown, it could imply downside risks for the exchange. The analysts also noted that turnover of securities and derivatives on the local bourse has been volatile, among other factors. SGX closed 3% higher at $21.35 on Oct 12. Sue-Ann Tan is a business correspondent at The Straits Times, covering capital markets and sustainable finance.

events.title: Dangote's Kenya refinery triggers political battle
events.summary: The News The $16 billion project to build Aliko Dangote’s refinery on the Kenyan coast is at the center of a high-stakes political battle ahead of elections in 10 months. President William Ruto is hinging his second-term bid on a series of major infrastructure developments. He has argued that the refinery could raise Kenya’s annual gross domestic product by 12%. Additional expected benefits include 500MW added to the national grid and thousands of new jobs. But mounting litigation, some initiated by his political rivals, is threatening to delay its construction, scheduled to be completed by 2030. Groups behind the legal action allege that the project is only the latest in a series of “secretive deals” signed by Ruto and his administration. The government’s refusal to make public key agreements related to the refinery has been criticized by opposition leaders, including one of Ruto’s main challengers, Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna. He has launched a bid in parliament for the documents, including the refinery contract, to be released. Unanswered questions remain over the impact on the environment, the community living near the refinery, and taxpayers. The president and his allies have warned that legal hurdles and uncertainty affecting key projects could dampen investor confidence. Ruto’s government is no stranger to court challenges to its financial deals. Its plan to privatize the country’s fuel pipeline company was eventually approved after various cases were dismissed. Last month, the $1.6 billion sale of a government stake in telecoms company Safaricom to UK’s Vodafone was declared illegal by the courts — the administration has launched an appeal. Both deals are meant to fund Ruto’s infrastructure push, according to government documents. Know More Ekuru Aukot, leader of the opposition Thirdway Alliance,told Semafor he would “definitely file a suit” if the government failed to meet an Oct. 23 deadline in his access to information request seeking more details about the refinery including the names of those who stand to benefit. “We are not opposed to investment. What we are saying is follow the law, follow the constitution,” he said. “The era of secretive deals negotiated in the dark will end when we kick this current regime out and return our country back to the rule of law,” Sifuna said on social media , adding that Ruto was frustrating his parliamentary push for more details. He insisted that the disclosure was “a constitutional imperative.” The threat of protracted litigation also looms over a suit launched by more than 100 Lamu residents arguing that the site of the refinery is part of their ancestral lands, with a court halting construction until the matter is heard. In addition, campaign groups have raised the alarm over the government’s failure to publish the environmental impact report, with Greenpeace threatening legal action . Last year, its five-year effort to block the construction of a $2 billion coal plant in Lamu ended in success for the activists. Despite the legal cases, Dangote and Ruto, who broke ground on the refinery project on Sept. 30, have expressed confidence that the project will overcome the legal hurdles. Step Back Seen as the candidate for the young and downtrodden in the last election, Ruto’s popularity has waned especially among the youth after the deadly 2024 Gen Z-led protests in which dozens of demonstrators were killed by police. Instead, Ruto is now leaning heavily on his infrastructure plans and the promised opportunities to shore up support for his re-election campaign. He has promised to move Kenya “from third world to first world” within 10 years, and unveiled a $38 billion infrastructure fund meant to finance various projects. The View From Nigeria Dangote is taking the objections in his stride. Speaking to investors in Nairobi ahead of the groundbreaking ceremony, Dangote said legal challenges were “normal for us in Africa. In fact, this is small.” He drew parallels with concerns over his cement plant in Senegal , which faced delays over land-related legal disputes. “They stopped our factory for one year. We went up to the Supreme Court to get a judgment,” he said. Notable Kenya’s Capital Markets Authority approved the Dangote IPO , enabling local investors to participate on the Nairobi Securities Exchange.

events.title: Why Trump’s Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire may offer oil markets little relief
events.summary: US President Donald Trump's declaration of an " energy ceasefire " between Russia and Ukraine has raised questions over its validity, after Moscow offered no confirmation about the truce and Russian strikes hit Ukrainian power plants within hours of the announcement. The move sent oil and diesel prices into decline early on Monday, but analysts cautioned that even a sustained halt to attacks on energy infrastructure would offer limited relief to global fuel markets, with much of Russia's refining capacity offline after months of Ukrainian drone strikes. Brent fell 1.3 per cent to $103.35 a barrel in early trading, while West Texas Intermediate declined 1.4 per cent to $90.55 a barrel. ICE gas oil futures, a benchmark for diesel, dropped about 3 per cent. The oil benchmarks pared losses by midday, with Brent trading 1.10 per cent higher at $105.87 a barrel by 1.55pm UAE time, while WTI was up 1.13 per cent at $92.89 a barrel. “Effective immediately, there is an energy ceasefire in the war between Russia and Ukraine,” Mr Trump wrote on Truth Social on Sunday. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv supported a ceasefire but was awaiting details from Washington. A similar announcement by Mr Trump in September failed to produce a lasting halt to strikes. “Only time will tell how durable it proves to be,” said Giovanni Staunovo, commodity analyst at Swiss bank UBS. “We have seen similar commitments in the past that ultimately failed to hold.” Diesel squeeze The announcement follows a US Treasury decision on October 9 to temporarily ease sanctions on Russian diesel transactions until April 7, 2027, after Mr Trump said Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release additional fuel into global markets. But the volumes are modest relative to the scale of the disruption. The proposed 300,000 tonnes for the rest of this month equates to about 100,000 barrels a day, Mr Staunovo said. That “would only partially offset the decline in seaborne diesel exports, which in September were around 1.3 million barrels per day below the levels seen at the start of the year”, he said. Francesco Sassi, assistant professor of energy geopolitics at the University of Oslo, said Washington's decision to suspend sanctions on Russian diesel for six months marked a significant shift in energy geopolitics that threatened to undermine western unity against Moscow. He described the move as the clearest failure yet of efforts to isolate Russia through energy sanctions. “What remains unsaid regarding the guarantees that Russia had from the US for supplying diesel is far more important than the few details we know so far about the energy ceasefire,” Mr Sassi said. Ukraine's response would also be a test of its relationship with Washington, potentially increasing pressure on the European Union to sustain support for Kyiv without US backing, he added. Russia's capacity to deliver the additional fuel is also in doubt. Its diesel exports fell from about 706,000 bpd in January to 47,000 bpd in August and almost nothing last month, according to Kpler data, as Ukrainian drone attacks damaged refineries and curtailed fuel production. Total Russian oil exports declined to about 6.8 million bpd in September from 8 million bpd in May. Shipments to India , Russia's biggest buyer, have more than halved since June to 1.2 million bpd, the data showed. The drop highlights the difficulty of restoring Russian fuel supplies without first repairing damaged infrastructure, a process that could take months even if attacks cease. S&P Global Commodity Insights said the announcement could weigh on diesel refining margins but only if Russian exports increase. “We see the immediate market impact as limited,” analysts James Bambino and Richard Joswick said. Additional Russian shipments would cover only about 10 per cent of the global shortfall in diesel exports, assuming they represent new supply rather than cargoes diverted from existing buyers, S&P Global said. About half of Russia's refining capacity is offline and repairs could take months, limiting the scope for a rapid recovery. Any additional cargoes are likely to remain in the Atlantic Basin, potentially reaching the US East Coast or Brazil and freeing up US Gulf Coast supplies for Europe. That could put downwards pressure on diesel margins in north-west Europe and the US but only “as long as a ceasefire holds”, the analysts said. Middle East risks persist Even if Russian fuel exports recover, the broader oil market remains exposed to disruption in the Middle East, where the Iran war has restricted supplies and forced major changes to established shipping routes. Crude has largely remained above $100 a barrel in recent weeks as attacks on infrastructure and shipping continue to threaten supplies from the Gulf. Goldman Sachs raised its December Brent forecast to $90 a barrel from $85, saying Gulf supply disruption was likely to ease more slowly than previously expected. The bank estimates geopolitical tension is adding slightly more than $20 a barrel to prices and does not assume a quick resolution to the US-Iran conflict. “Potential renewed escalation still poses significant net upside risk,” the bank's analysts said.

events.title: AI set to continue growing, but how it unlocks value is the question: TikTok, Broadcom, Intel CEOs
events.summary: TikTok chief executive officer Chew Shou Zi speaking at the DBS Asia Future Forward Conference at Suntec Convention and Exhibition Centre on Oct 12. AI will keep growing and may beat some human skills, but leaders said its real value depends on human judgement, creativity and safe use. TikTok’s Chew Shou Zi warned about alignment and cybersecurity risks, and said people still value authenticity as AI-made content remains low. Broadcom and Intel CEOs said AI demand for compute will stay strong for three to five years, but growth depends on supply, ROI, costs and talent. SINGAPORE – Artificial intelligence is set to continue its growth and may even surpass some human capabilities, but what matters is how it can unlock value for businesses and society, said the chief executives of three major tech companies. TikTok CEO Chew Shou Zi said there is a “non-zero chance” that AI could surpass humans in certain ways in the future, but he also noted the importance of human judgment and creativity even as AI becomes more widely used . Meanwhile, in response to a question by DBS CEO Tan Su Shan on whether the world is “overbuilding” AI infrastructure , Broadcom CEO Hock Tan and Intel CEO Tan Lip-Bu said the demand for AI infrastructure will continue to grow in the next three to five years, limited mainly by supply constraints. They were speaking on panels at the inaugural DBS Asia Future Forward Conference held at Suntec Singapore Convention and Exhibition Centre on Oct 12. Organised by DBS, the new flagship event brings together global leaders across technology, business and investment to examine the forces shaping the region’s future. Chew said AI models might currently be unable to do certain things that humans can, such as rapid visual learning or long-term memory retrieval. But he added: “The technology is evolving, (and) you can see a world where silicon is just superior to carbon. “You can see a world where it will last longer. It’s more scalable. It finds it easier to connect information together than us human beings.” But Chew also said there is a place for human judgment in AI usage. He noted that there are some extreme examples of how machines can behave without human alignment, such as the “paper clip analogy”, where a machine is asked to produce paperclips and goes completely overweight on paperclip production at the expense of everything else. “My view is that in the next two to three years, we’re going to have a real scientific breakthrough: physics, biotech, chemistry, material science, because of AI. It’s very, very, very possible,” he said. “And if that happens, then you know the question will be: How do you align the models? How do you align the machines to be doing things that are obvious to us as human beings?” These include moral and ethical boundaries that humans recognise, but AI models may not. “I don’t think we have an answer, to be honest, at this moment in time. I think it really is a very complex issue, but it will matter in the age of AI,” Chew said. Human creativity is also a very relevant question, especially for TikTok, he added. He noted that AI -generated content has not totally taken off yet, with views in the low single-digit percentages. “I think people still value authenticity when they see a video and it’s very obviously... artificially generated. I think there’s still a little bit of pushback in terms of consumption. So I agree that human creativity will continue to be important,” he said. Chew added that in the long term, AI agents might be able to do more things autonomously, especially as the trust and guard rails are built. But in the short term, referring to the next two to three years, Chew said that what matters is developing skills to be able to use AI effectively. “I think that’s probably the most important thing for us internally. We are encouraging not just our engineers, but also our lawyers and people working in corporate functions to have more first-hand experience,” he said. “If you don’t use these products yourself, you cannot figure out exactly what it can or cannot do just by reading about it.” He added that users should be curious and hands-on while understanding the boundaries of this technology. Education is also important, Chew said, especially as AI also poses cybersecurity risks . This is particularly the case when users give agents permission to do things for them, like making purchases using credit cards , without fully understanding what the technology does. Intel CEO Tan Lip-Bu (right) and Broadcom president and CEO Hock Tan (left) participating in a panel discussion moderated by DBS Bank CEO Tan Su Shan during the DBS Asia Future Forward Conference at Suntec Convention and Exhibition Centre on Oct 12. At a separate panel, the Broadcom and Intel CEOs were grilled by DBS’ Tan on whether AI will end. Broadcom’s Hock Tan said: “My presumption is this might continue. This would probably continue till 2029 and probably into 2030.

events.title: Obama cuts ad in Mississippi Senate race
events.summary: Former President Barack Obama has cut an ad for Mississippi Senate candidate Scott Colom, the latest sign of Democrats putting real effort behind boosting their candidate in the deep red state as they eye a potential upset next month. The Colom campaign will run the 30-second spot on digital and radio statewide in Mississippi as part of a seven-figure media buy in Mississippi, according to details shared first with Semafor. In the ad, Obama tells voters: “Mississippi, it’s time for a change.” “You need to send Scott Colom to the US Senate,” Obama continues in the ad . “Scott made his community safer, prosecuting violent crimes as a district attorney and fighting corruption.” Colom is running against Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, a conservative GOP senator who blocked Colom’s nomination to a federal judgeship under then-President Joe Biden. Colom currently serves as a district attorney in Mississippi. The race to defeat Hyde-Smith is not a must-win for Democrats to retake the Senate and Colom remains an underdog in deep red Mississippi. But national Democrats have been eying the race for months due to the state’s large Black population, and Obama’s ad is a clear effort to juice turnout. Sen. Raphael Warnock, D-Ga., will appear with Colom on Wednesday in Jackson and Democratic Sens. Cory Booker of New Jersey, Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, and Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware have also previously campaigned with the Democratic candidate.Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has also listed Mississippi as a target for Democrats. Democrats tried to beat Hyde-Smith in the past and failed. She defeated former Democratic Rep. Mike Espy by 7 points in 2018 and a wider margin in a 2020 rematch. But most Senate Democrats think Colom, a young father, is a stronger candidate in a tough environment for Republicans.

events.title: Learning to Play Like a Pro: Adaptive Motion Planning and Tracking for Humanoid Robots
events.summary: This White Paper provides roboticists and control engineers with a comprehensive overview of how motion planning and motion tracking can be decoupled to preserve professional athletic style in humanoid robots, and why adaptive, speed-aware control is essential for closing the gap between simulation and real-world deployment. What you will learn about: Why combining a professional athlete’s motion style with reliable task performance remains an open challenge in humanoid ball-sports robotics, and how separating a high-level planner from a low-level tracker addresses this trade-off. How motion data extracted from broadcast video and motion-capture recordings can be reconstructed, retargeted, and physically corrected into reference motions a humanoid robot can safely track. Why the sim-to-real transition introduces compounding tracking errors, and how training a tracker on randomized execution speeds, paired with a learned motion-speed adapter in the planner, improves robustness on physical hardware. events.title: UAE approves 2027-2029 budget with Dh292.5bn in spending
events.summary: The UAE Cabinet has approved its federal budget for 2027 to 2029 with spending of Dh292.5 billion ($79.64 billion). The allocation marks an increase of 28.3 per cent compared to the previous three years, Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai said on Monday. The Cabinet also approved the 2027 budget with expenditure of Dh90.1 billion. Main sectors covered by the new federal budget include community protection and safety, the economy of the future, future-orientated education, employment and empowerment, health and quality of life, leadership, government affairs and international relations, the UAE Government Media Office said in a statement. The budget will also focus on industry, technology, energy, infrastructure, culture, media and sports. “Our priorities remain fixed and unchanged … Education, health, housing, social services, and the quality of life and stability of the citizen,” Sheikh Mohammed said in a post on X. The UAE last year launched its 2027-2029 budget cycle , focusing on sustainability, artificial intelligence and efficiency. It followed four consecutive cycles during which the total federal budget reached about Dh900 billion ($245 billion), officials said in July last year, adding that the cycle focuses on sectors such as education, health care, social welfare and core government services. Mohammed bin Rashid: Today, we approved the UAE Federal Government’s general budget for 2027 to 2029, with total expenditure of AED 292.5 billion, up 28.3% compared with the previous 3 years. We also approved the 2027 budget, with total expenditure of AED 90.1 billion. Our… pic.twitter.com/0vkaH0AljA — Dubai Media Office (@DXBMediaOffice) October 12, 2026 The UAE's economy grew 0.4 per cent annually to Dh961.9 billion in the first half of 2026, driven by non-oil business activity, despite the impact of the Iran war . The non-oil sector's contribution to the country's gross domestic product during the six-month period increased by 1.8 per cent to 79.2 per cent, the Federal Competitiveness and Statistics Centre said last week. The Iran war has tipped the Middle East into one of its worst geopolitical crises in decades. The conflict, which began on February 28, led to Iranian strikes on its Arab neighbours and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The UAE, the Arab world's second-largest economy, continues to grow despite the conflict. Ratings agency Fitch said on Monday that the UAE non-oil growth model is broadly resilient to the war baseline. The non-oil growth model of the UAE has leveraged a role as a hub between Asia and Europe “backed by a favourable operating environment, supportive government policy, and the ability to attract and retain foreign labour and visitors”, it said in a report. It added that it expects further measures to “improve the operating environment along with a smoothing of administrative procedures” for corporates and residents, backed by higher spending and other sources of financial support at the sovereign and government-related entity level. “Fitch sees structural strengths that will support the resilience of the non-oil economy. However, a persistent period of regional insecurity will call into question logistical advantages and perceptions of the country as a commercial and financial centre and tourism destination,” said Paul Gamble, senior director at Fitch Ratings. The approval of the budget confirms the UAE government’s “keenness to achieve a balance between current development requirements and investment in future opportunities, and to establish a government financial system characterised by flexibility, efficiency and sustainability”, the media office said on Monday. It enhances the UAE’s position among the most advanced and prosperous countries in the world, it added. Budget breakdown for 2027: Dh34.6 billion (38.4 per cent) – Social development and social benefits Dh29.1 billion (32.3 per cent) – Government affairs Dh17.8 billion (19.7 per cent) – Federal expenses Dh5.6 billion (6.2 per cent) – Financial assets and investments Dh3 billion (3.4 per cent) – Infrastructure and economic resources

events.title: Mars may be a hellhole, but the moon is not far behind
events.summary: Welcome to the second space race. You can be forgiven for experiencing déjà vu. Last time, it was the Soviet Union and the United States vying to be the first to plant some flags. Now it’s a sprint to the lunar surface between America and China—alongside a host of varyingly friendly and rival nations—plus a cornucopia of private spaceflight companies. And this time it looks like they’re getting ready to set up camp. There will be, the contenders say, bases on the moon, permanently inhabited castles under the stars. The notion of a moon base, fanciful as it might sound, isn’t new. But this year, under the leadership of Administrator Jared Isaacman, NASA has been flooding the zone with bold announcements . If all goes according to plan—a plan that will likely cost tens of billions of dollars to start—there will be drones , robotic landers, communication satellites , and a nuclear power plant ; there will be plant terrariums and moonquake sensors; there will be mechanized scouts exploring craters for water. Initial astronaut missions to the lunar surface, which the US is currently planning to start in 2028, will be focused on exploration and technological experimentation. But the idea is that we will—some time in the 2030s—get to a point where there will be habitation quarters for long-term stays, surrounded by a network of scientific research stations, resource mining and processing plants, and landing pads for spaceships. “It’s going to be an expanse,” says Carlos García-Galán, NASA’s moon base program manager—one that will add up to “hundreds of square miles.” The effort is undoubtedly being fueled by nationalistic competition. China has near-identical plans to build its own base on the moon. And being first matters, because the “victor” gets to define the terms. What is the moon, exactly? Is it a militarized outpost? Is it a manufacturing hub? Is it a wilderness to be studied and preserved? But there are also other reasons to go. Earth’s companion contains primeval rocks that hold clues to the formation of the entire solar system. The lunar surface, with virtually no atmosphere in the way, is an ideal place to put telescopes that could examine the most ancient epochs of the cosmos. The far side of the moon would be “a fantastic place to explore the further universe,” says Josef Aschbacher, the European Space Agency’s director general. And it’s way more energy efficient to launch rockets from the low-gravity lunar surface than it is from Earth, meaning sending astronauts—or robotic spacecraft—farther into the solar system will become much less difficult. “The moon is critical. It will be a stepping stone for going further—that means to Mars and beyond,” says Aschbacher. SELMAN DESIGN But if these bold visions are to become reality, there’s a daunting amount of work to be done. A sprawling moon base must be safe for its astronaut inhabitants—protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings. It also must be somewhat self-sustaining, so that it can weather changing political fortunes and not cost ruinous amounts of money to maintain. For that, we’ll need to find a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating—and ideally generating revenue. And we’ll need autonomous robots that can build, maintain, and expand the base even when their human masters aren’t present. “It’s almost like starting civilization from scratch,” says Simon Middleburgh, co-director of the Nuclear Futures Institute at Bangor University in Wales. Assuming we can overcome these starting challenges, decades from now—let’s say, by the year 2100—our initial moon bases could grow from barely visible structures into luminous cities, perhaps not too dissimilar from those dreamed up by authors and screenwriters the world over. “It’s like science fiction today that we really want to turn into a reality,” says García-Galán. Will anyone succeed? The moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp. In general, daytime temperatures can reach more than 250 °F; at night, they can plummet to less than –200 °F. Exposed to the vacuum of space, the surface is constantly showered in carcinogenic radiation and frequently hit by meteoroids. And its volcanic dust is sticky and corrosive, a destroyer of equipment and choker of lungs.  Sadly, the lunar south pole—the area NASA is targeting—is even harsher. NASA wants to build a base there because its permanently shadowed craters are thought to harbor caches of water ice, which would be more precious than gold. Purify it, and you can water crops and hydrate astronauts; split it into oxygen and hydrogen, and you have breathable air and rocket propellant. But the temperature in those craters can be lower than –410 °F, making them some of the coldest places in the known universe. On the surface outside those pits, astronauts would be bathed in the scorching sun for 14 days before experiencing an equally long frigid night. But there is only so much money we can spend on safety. “What it comes down to is acceptable risk of death,” Philip Metzger , a spaceflight engineering researcher at the Florida Space Institute, said while pondering some of the dangers. “What can we reasonably survive without breaking the bank?” Temperature is one of the easiest problems to handle. Materials science has come a long way, and there are myriad metals, ceramics, plastics, compounds, and alloys that can resist wild temperature swings. Radiators keep things cool; heaters keep batteries from dying prematurely. Astronauts survive just fine too, with their fancy spacesuits—but that technology has proved itself only during brief excursions. It’s not yet clear how long this equipment could operate under such tempestuous conditions. The temperature in the moon’s south pole craters can be lower than –410 °F, making them some of the coldest places in the known universe. Outside those pits, astronauts would be bathed in the scorching sun for 14 days before experiencing an equally long frigid night. Space radiation, which can wreak havoc on electronics and trigger a cancerous division of cells, is far more pernicious. And as Stuart George, a physicist at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, explains, it comes in two unpleasant forms.  The first is galactic cosmic rays , which rain down on the moon almost constantly. “They’re made by supernovas and neutron star mergers—all these kinds of things,” says George. And because the atomic nuclei, protons, and electrons that make them up are moving at significant fractions of the speed of light, these cosmic rays have oodles of kinetic energy, meaning they can punch through thin shielding (say, a metal wall) with ease. “They also have this habit where the heavier ions are fragmenting in that shielding and making secondary particles,” says George. That means if your shield is too thin, the astronauts behind it will be blasted with a surprisingly large dose of radiation.

events.title: Starbucks Korea regains coffee chain lead five months after ‘Tank Day’ controversy
events.summary: Starbucks regained the top spot in South Korean sales after four months in second place. Starbucks Korea regained the No. 1 sales spot in September, with estimated card payments of 121 billion won, overtaking A Twosome Place after four months. Its sales recovery followed backlash over the “Tank Day” promotion, which caused public anger, a CEO dismissal, an apology, and history education for staff. Other chains fell in September, but the data only covers card spending, so it does not prove full revenue or a full recovery in customer trust. SEOUL – Starbucks Korea regained the top spot in sales among South Korean coffee chains in September, overtaking A Twosome Place after four months in second place following a public backlash over its controversial “Tank Day” promotion . According to estimated credit and debit card spending data released on Oct 11 by Mobile Index, a market intelligence platform operated by IGAWorks, Starbucks recorded an estimated 121 billion won (S$116 million) in card payments in September, up 4.3% from August. Monthly card spending fell to 100.39 billion won in June before rising for three consecutive months. Meanwhile, A Twosome Place recorded 110.5 billion won in September, down 6.4% from 117.99 billion won a month earlier. The gap between the two chains narrowed from approximately 7 billion won in July to 1.9 billion won in August. Starbucks then pulled ahead by 10.58 billion won in September. The figures indicate a weakening of negative sentiment against Starbucks, which came under fire for using phrases such as “Tank Day” to promote its tumbler discount on May 18, the anniversary of the 1980 Gwangju Democratic Uprising. The campaign drew public criticism for evoking the military crackdown on pro-democracy protestors, prompting Shinsegae Group to dismiss Starbucks Korea’s chief executive, issue an apology and introduce history education for employees. The coffee chain also suspended product launches and promotions before gradually resuming them in July. Other major coffee chains recorded declines. Mega MGC Coffee’s estimated card payments fell 3.2% to 94.75 billion won, while Paik’s Coffee posted a 6.4% decrease to 22.94 billion won. The figures exclude prepaid cards, mobile gift vouchers and other payment methods, meaning they do not represent total revenue or establish whether consumer confidence has recovered. THE KOREA HERALD/ASIA NEWS NETWORK

events.title: How to avoid getting stung if you miss credit card payments
events.summary: Published 12 October 2026, 00:19 BST An increasing number of people are missing credit card repayments as finances are stretched by rising bills, according to the Bank of England. Lenders also told the Bank they expected the number of unpaid credit card debts to keep going up this autumn. This could lead to more demand for advice on how to deal with debts – but, if you are struggling and need help, there are some traps to avoid. And it is worth remembering that impartial advice is available free of charge from debt charities. So here's what to think about. If you find yourself with money troubles, it can be tempting to seize any opportunity to get things back on track. Social media and internet search pages are full of supposed quick-fix debt solutions. Cold calls and WhatsApp messages also promise debt help. But they may well come with upfront fees, unrealistic claims about writing off debt, and pressure to make a quick decision. Suggestions on the best way to find help include: Impartial, authorised debt advice comes free. You can find a provider on the government-backed Moneyhelper website , external Check whether a firm offering debt help is authorised by the regulator, the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). You should cross-check the authorisation details they give with the FCA's Firm Checker , external Anyone unhappy with the service from an authorised firm can complain and, if you are still not happy, go to the independent Financial Ombudsman Service. Alison Walters, director of consumer finance at the FCA, said: "Anyone struggling with debt deserves advice that puts their interests first. "Free, impartial debt advice is available to everyone, and no one should be pressured or misled into paying for a debt solution that may not be right for them." The FCA says that some unregulated firms collect people's details, through cold calling or online adverts, sometimes impersonating debt advice charities or debt collectors, and pass this information on to firms offering debt solutions that you pay for. A quick search online will throw up lots of businesses offering ways to clear your debt, not all of which are trustworthy, according to charities. Warning signs of unscrupulous firms include pressure tactics, such as repeated contact, often in messages and on the phone, pushing people to agree to a debt solution, the FCA says. Some people have been encouraged to change financial details on lenders' paperwork, or are "coached" in ways to respond. Sometimes people are steered towards a fee-charging debt solution, such as Individual Voluntary Arrangements (IVAs) or some debt management plans, without alternative options being properly explained or offered first. And, do you know who you are talking to? Ask them who they work for, and check if their details match the firm's official details. "Before making any decisions around how to deal with your debts, it's always worth getting full, free and impartial debt advice first, exploring all options to clear your debt in the safest and most sustainable way," said Vikki Brownridge, chief executive at debt charity StepChange. events.title: The ecologist revealing the invisible networks that revive rainforests
events.summary: In a research station in central Panama, you can walk through a century of forest time, watching scrubby plots of adolescent trees give way to cathedral-­like canopies of mature growth. Forest ecologist Daisy Dent, a senior scientist at ETH Zurich, oversees this sequence of plots across the Barro Colorado Nature Monument, some of which date as far back as the 19th century. Not one of the trees she surveys was planted by human hands. She maps, measures, and tracks each trunk that emerges, revealing how waves of tree life rise from bare earth.  Tropical forests like these are our planet’s biggest terrestrial carbon sink, accounting for around 40% of carbon stored on land . As part of an international network of researchers, Dent is deciphering the networks of animal and plant interactions that enable some forests to recover after destruction. The goal is a low-cost, high-impact alternative to typical carbon-­crediting schemes, which plant huge areas with a single species of tree. For over a decade, her research has built a body of evidence that such large “monocrop” programs could be expensive mistakes—and that more resilient forests can rebound naturally in just a few decades, re-creating ecosystems that suck up vast quantities of carbon dioxide. Few places are better to demonstrate this than Barro Colorado, a reserve covering the forested peninsulas and islands that formed when construction of the Panama Canal flooded the area in 1914. Under the management of the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute, generations of ecologists have amassed more than a century of records.  That means Dent can trace why some plots rebound after clear-cutting for farming and forestry while others falter. Fruit-eating animals—including spider monkeys, bats, and parrots—are responsible for planting more than 70% of trees in tropical forests, and Dent’s dataset can tell which built each patch of trees by depositing seeds in their nutrient-rich droppings. Many of these creatures worked together to plant a diverse 70-year-old patch whose canopy is approaching the stunning structure and richness of an ancient jungle. In contrast, a patch of similar age populated by narrow trunks of a single long-lived species, Gustavia superba , hints that tropical rodents called agoutis are more or less the sole animal architects behind this more homogeneous forest.  The data she collects helps write a playbook for when to let ecosystems regenerate and when to give them a helping hand. One 2024 estimate in Nature found that some 215 million hectares of forest worldwide (an area larger than Mexico) could regenerate naturally. “Tropical forests are underpinned by this massive network of interactions,” Dent says—interactions between life-forms like the fungi that help trees take up nutrients, as well as pollinators and seed-distributors. Supporting those relationships is key to growing forests that lock up carbon and help sustain local communities and wildlife.  Filling in the gaps Just over a decade ago, as the landmark Paris Agreement was being codified in 2015, forest recovery seized global attention as a solution to the climate crisis. Global leaders rallied behind plans to regrow a trillion trees , after the ecologist Thomas Crowther highlighted their potential to capture a decade’s worth of global carbon emissions. But the biggest question has lingered: How, exactly, do you regrow two trees for every star in the Milky Way? While startups have proposed seed-spraying drones and nutrient-coated seed bombs , Dent has spent two decades studying what happens when we let forests rebuild themselves. As a PhD student around the turn of the millennium, she researched old-growth forests in northern Borneo but felt hopeless watching entire landscapes felled for palm oil plantations. Rather than despair, she turned to restoration. Then, as a postdoc in 2005, she joined Panama’s Prorena, a joint initiative between the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute and the Yale School of Forestry and Environmental Studies, which aimed at determining how best to establish diverse native forests on clear-cut land. Back then, secondary forests—ones that grow naturally after the original forest was lost—had been “a bit of a niche research area,” Dent says. But as farming and human infrastructure have driven deforestation, resurgent forests now account for some 70% of all tropical canopies. Prorena initially followed the usual playbook of transplanting nursery trees to rangelands, but Dent began to question whether planting was necessary. In 2009, she published an encouraging paper showing that animal populations rebound quickly as forests naturally regrow. In 2010, she began working in Barro Colorado on the plots established by the pioneering American ecologist Julie Denslow. In 1994, Denslow identified plots that had been regenerating naturally for 20 to 100 years, and Dent would add younger ones to continue the sequence.  The site provides not just general data on forest regrowth but in-depth demographic information over time, says Robin Chazdon, a professor emeritus of ecology and evolutionary biology at the University of Connecticut who collaborated with Denslow when she established the plots. “It tells you more about the actual processes that are happening in the site,” she says.  For example, previous research had shown that fast-growing “pioneer trees,” the first to thrive in the damaged land, are eventually overtaken by larger carbon-storing trees. Dent’s research helped fill in gaps about the mechanics of how this happens—or doesn’t happen—in individual cases. In the Gustavia -dominated patch, for instance, stubborn grasses planted by cattle ranchers smothered most other trees before they could take root. These trees can hang around, crowding out the light, for 150 years, blocking the second wave of large-trunked trees.  To plant or not to plant Dent found herself well placed for the massive influx of interest in reforestation that began in 2015. She’d already become a principal investigator for 2ndFor, an international research network aiming to learn how best to manage secondary forests. Using data gathered from the Barro Colorado plots, the team authored a 2016 paper in Nature showing that a hectare of naturally regenerated secondary forest can capture 11 times as much carbon each year as an old-growth one, with young trees absorbing it quickly as they compete to grow toward the sun. ( ABC News: Xavier Martin ) The Bureau of Meteorology says "severe thunderstorms" have brought heavy rains and damaging winds to Alice Springs. The Hilton DoubleTree is among the properties damaged, with parts of its roof collapsing in during the storm. The weather bureau says more storms are possible through the week and emergency services are urging locals to remain vigilant. Thousands of homes are without power after a surprise storm brought wind speeds of almost 100km/h to Central Australia, pulling down trees and damaging properties. According to the Bureau of Meteorology (BOM), heavy rain and hail fell on Alice Springs at 3:30pm this afternoon and wind gusts of 96km/h were recorded locally at 3:44pm. It's the second storm to rock Alice Springs in just a few short days. ( Supplied: Damien Ryan ) "A surface trough coincides with a warm and unstable air mass in southern parts of the Territory, which has resulted in the development of severe thunderstorms," the weather bureau said. The short-lived storm cell pushed trees onto roads, powerlines and roofs. The Alice Springs Hilton DoubleTree was among the properties to suffer significant damage. The Alice Springs Hilton DoubleTree sustained damage to its ceiling. ( ABC News: Xavier Martin ) In a statement released on Monday afternoon, Power and Water Corporation said "approximately 9,000 properties" had lost power "due to damage caused by a sudden storm cell". "Our crews are assessing the damage and will work to restore services as quickly as is safely possible," the statement said. "The communities of Arumbera, Burt Plain, Ilparpa, Simpson, Hermannsburg, Hugh, Namatjira and Wallace Rockhole have also been affected. Territorians can check power outages via Power and Water's online tracker . Cars parked outside the hospital in Alice Springs were damaged in the storm. ( ABC News: Xavier Martin ) The BOM's Robert Urbaniak said Centralians were "not out of the woods yet", warning another similar storm cell was predicted for Tuesday afternoon and evening. "Unfortunately another day of it, but after that should settle down somewhat." NT Emergency Services (NTES) said it had received 47 calls for assistance since the storm hit. Adam White from NTES said Alice Springs residents would need to remain vigilant in the coming few days and urged people to keep an eye on SecureNT for updates . "I've got some reports of multiple trees down, some damage from the hail and the winds," he said. It was the second storm to hit Alice Springs in less than a week. Two cells are moving east over parts of Central Australia and the Barkly region, according to the BOM, which are likely to persist through this evening. events.title: Healey faces £35bn Budget challenge to meet spending pledges, says think tank
events.summary: Published 12 October 2026, 00:04 BST Chancellor John Healey faces having to find £35bn to avoid cuts to public spending while meeting defence promises in his first Budget, an influential think tank has warned. The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said that if the government wants to raise defence spending to 3% of national income by 2030 and lift health spending without squeezing other departments, it will need a "top-up" of billions of pounds. Higher inflation, caused by the Iran war, could eat into what the government hoped to spend on public services, meaning Healey will have to choose between spending cuts, tax rises, or a mixture of both, the IFS said. The government is under growing pressure to show financial markets that it has a tight grip on finances as the cost of borrowing rises. The IFS said that Healey must set out "credible" spending plans in the Budget, which will take place on 28 October. "A 'steady-as-she-goes' Budget is not an option available to the chancellor," said IFS director Helen Miller. "Choosing to stay the course with the inherited tax and spending plans would mean allowing inflation to blow departments' spending plans off course. "Simply pencilling in implicit cuts that he has no intention of delivering would make the Budget a work of fiction," she added. Speaking ahead of the annual International Monetary Fund meeting this week, Healey said: "The consequences of conflict in the Middle East and Europe are hitting countries worldwide, leading to higher prices at the pumps and more expensive mortgages at home. "But Britain and our allies can face up to these challenges together." He said his Budget "will build on this approach with fiscal discipline helping to deliver economic resilience" and give people "breathing space". Miller told the BBC's Today programme that Healey had inherited spending plans for government departments where spending growth would slow in the coming years. "[It] already looked likely that he would have to make spending cuts just to live within those," she said. "Now, along comes the Middle East war, inflation goes up and those spending plans look very tight indeed." Added to that, the chancellor has said he wants to get defence spending up to 3% of national income. Under Keir Starmer's leadership, Healey resigned as defence secretary in June in a battle with the Treasury over military spending. Miller said: "You put all that together, if he wanted to do all of that within current spending plans he's looking at having to cut some other services by something like £35bn." She said the government would have a "tough time" if it wanted to raise taxes to stop cuts to departments and fund defence spending. Former chancellor Rachel Reeves announced billions of pounds in tax rises. Meanwhile, Labour pledged in its manifesto "not increase taxes on working people", ruling out rises to National Insurance, income tax or VAT. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will stick to that promise. Miller said: "You'd really have to be scaping around and doing lots of small things to get up to big sums." The chancellor does not have to address spending totals in this Budget, and may choose to leave such decisions until future events - for example, next year's Spring Statement or Spending Review - by which time the outlook for the economy could look very different. But the IFS warned not addressing it would cast doubt on the credibility of the government's plans. Previous chancellors have relied on a similar strategy of pencilling in unrealistic future spending plans to ensure that they meet the fiscal rules on the day - only to change the plans further down the line. Miller said Healey's focus on fiscal discipline was a "good first start but what he needs to do is not just say he's going to cut borrowing in coming years but actually deliver on those plans." The US-Israel war against Iran and Russia's invasion of Ukraine have together helped drive up energy prices around the world. These higher costs have been passed to customers via higher prices on shelves and at the pumps. The wars have also contributed to a rise in the cost of UK government debt interest payments, adding to the pressure on Healey. Although higher inflation will boost tax revenues, it will also eat into the value of departments' cash budgets, the IFS said. Like other analysts, the IFS thinks recent turbulence on bond markets and higher inflation will add around £10bn to forecasts for the government's borrowing costs in 2029-30. However, it still expects the government to meet its self-imposed fiscal rules - that it will only borrow for investment projects by the financial year 2029-30 and also be reducing debt as a percentage of GDP - not least as inflation pushes up tax revenues. But it expects those rules to be met by a smaller buffer - known as "headroom" - of around £20bn.

events.title: Saudi Arabia says oil supply to continue to flow despite Riyadh attacks
events.summary: Saudi Arabia sought to reassure the world’s energy industry that escalating attacks on the kingdom would not disrupt its role as a major oil supplier. “The word ‘fear’ in the Saudi dictionary does not exist,” Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said on Monday at the opening of the WPC Energy Congress . “We, as Saudis, are fearless, combatant and determined people.” The remarks came after King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh was struck four times in five days, emphasising the growing security risks facing the world’s biggest crude exporter amid the Iran war. A missile attack on the airport on Saturday killed 12 people and injured 309, Saudi authorities said. Another projectile struck the airport on Sunday evening, killing one person and injuring 11. The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen blamed the Iran-backed Houthi rebels for Saturday’s attack. But Riyadh is to press ahead with a week of high-level energy meetings, including Sunday’s International Energy Forum ministerial talks and the WPC congress, which the kingdom is hosting for the first time. “Riyadh is the capital of energy security and your presence here today proves that,” Prince Abdulaziz told delegates. “Our gathering today does not mean that risks have disappeared.” The attacks have sharpened focus on Saudi Arabia’s ability to keep oil flowing during periods of conflict, particularly as threats mount around the Strait of Hormuz and Bab Al Mandeb strait, two of the world’s most important energy chokepoints. Prince Abdulaziz said Saudi Arabia’s ability to withstand disruption was the result of decades of investment in storage, redundancy and alternative export routes. “Resilience is built before a crisis begins,” he added. He referred to the kingdom’s East-West pipeline , which carries crude from eastern oilfields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, allowing exports to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. The flow was halted after Houthi attacks in September, before recovering to about 5.8 million barrels per day by October 6, compared with capacity of about seven million bpd. The disruption showed the importance of restoring operations quickly, Prince Abdulaziz said. Resilience depends not only on infrastructure but also on domestic expertise, he added. “Pipelines do not repair themselves. Our systems do not restore themselves. Facilities do not restart themselves. People do,” he said. At Sunday’s IEF meeting, he pledged that Saudi Arabia would continue to supply domestic and international customers “regardless of circumstances”. The gathering took place against an increasingly volatile market backdrop. Brent crude hovered at about $104 a barrel on Monday as the Riyadh attacks and strikes on two tankers near the Strait of Hormuz and Oman added to geopolitical risks. “The events of recent weeks are serious,” Prince Abdulaziz said. “Our response must be equally serious.”

events.title: Vikrom Kromadit built his industrial park empire in Thailand and Vietnam. Laos is next
events.summary: Thai real estate developer Amata Corporation says Laos will become its “largest focus” in the years to come, CEO Vikrom Kromadit tells Fortune . “Laos will become our largest focus because of the land bank that they have,” Kromadit tells Fortune . “They also have lots of green energy—that’s why they’re called the battery of Southeast Asia.” Amata expanded into Laos in 2022, starting with Amata City Namor, which covers 31.5 square kilometers and sits beside a station on the China-Laos Railway. The company says its long-term Laos vision could reach 200 square kilometers . Kromadit’s company built its fortunes in Thailand and Vietnam. Amata Corporation, founded in 1989, built industrial parks across Thailand’s Rayong and Chon Buri provinces . It was also an early backer of Vietnam, building its first facility there in 1994, early in the Southeast Asian country’s reform program. Laos, however, offers an opportunity for Amata to capture Chinese manufacturers expanding to new manufacturing hubs in Southeast Asia.  Laos, Southeast Asia’s only landlocked country, boasts a huge energy surplus, as its rivers and mountainous terrain supported a government-led push to build hydroelectric dams as a core economic pillar. The country currently exports about 80% of its electricity to other Asian countries like Thailand, China, and Singapore.  “They have plenty of land and a lot of water,” Kromadit says, adding that it has “the best natural conditions” for industrial development. (While Laos generates over 12 GW of capacity from over 80 hydro plants, most cross-border transmission lines bypass local communities, sticking consumers with frequent blackouts.) To Kromadit, Laos’s potential is also backed by China, long the country’s top foreign investor. In 2025, China pumped $18 billion into Laos’s economy , primarily toward industry, mining, and agriculture, according to the Vientiane Times , a local newspaper. Laos has been slotted into “ China plus one ” supply chains, where both Chinese and global manufacturers move some—or all—of their production to other countries, both to reduce cost and avoid tariffs on Chinese-origin products. “China is the largest manufacturer of all products, so they can’t just keep building only within their country,” Kromadit explains. “They’re also being hit by political pressure from the U.S.” After graduating from National Taiwan University with a degree in mechanical engineering, he returned to Thailand in 1975 and founded V&K Enterprise, an import-export business that focused on agricultural products, minerals, and seafood. But by the 1980s, he was frustrated with being “just a middleman.” “I wanted to make more money,” Kromadit confesses. “When I was in the food business, even though I was the one who created all the channels and brought in business, once companies achieved success, they kicked me out.” In 1988, he cofounded the Bang Pakong Industrial Estate on the eastern coast of Bangkok, then established Amata Corporation in 1989. Amata’s first industrial facility, Amata City Chon Buri, opened that same year. After Kromadit visited Vietnam in 1990, he decided to make the country Amata’s first overseas market. “I found that the Vietnamese were focused, capable, and smart,” he says. “I thought that Vietnam, in the future, would compete with Thailand for industrial investments.” Amata launched Amata City Bien Hoa in Dong Nai province in 1994. His prediction has largely come true: Vietnam is now Southeast Asia’s fastest-growing economy, with Q3 GDP growth of 9.95%. Hanoi wants to have Vietnam reach high-income status by 2045 . Amata today hosts more than 1,500 factories in 12 locations across Thailand, Vietnam, and Laos. It briefly attempted an expansion into Myanmar in 2019, with a facility in Yangon, the country’s commercial center. Plans were halted in early 2021 following a military coup and resulting civil war. Amata positions its facilities as industrial cities that include not just factories but also housing, schools, hospitals, and shopping malls. The company’s flagship Chon Buri campus, for instance, houses the massive 38,000-square-meter Lotus Plus Mall , which includes a hypermarket, retail stores, banks, restaurants, and an international cinema. The company’s facilities include kindergartens, schools, and technical training institutes, with more on the way. “We’re now looking to build a university,” Kromadit says. Asked whether Amata might expand into other Southeast Asian markets, like Indonesia or Cambodia, Kromadit says the company already has enough land to occupy him for the rest of his life. “The land that we have on hand is around 700 square kilometers,” he says. “It’s big enough to make me busy until I go to heaven.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Oman aims to launch new international financial centre by 2027
events.summary: Oman plans to launch full licensing at its new international financial centre by 2027 and is to begin registering companies later this year. IFC Oman, the plans for which were first revealed in January, is currently working on its legal framework, rule book and registry system, it said in a statement on Monday. A package of laws for business registration and licensing, financial services regulation and an independent dispute resolution framework are to be issued shortly, the financial centre said. They will provide the legal basis for IFC Oman’s authorities to adopt an initial package of regulations and rules. A registry system, which will enable businesses to submit their applications online, is to move into the testing phase soon, the statement added. “IFC Oman is accelerating towards opening its doors, with its legal, regulatory and digital infrastructure moving into place," said Mahmood Al Aweini, chairman of the IFC Oman Authority Board. "The centre will offer global businesses and investors a stable and competitive place to do business." IFC Oman will join other existing financial centres in the Gulf, including Abu Dhabi's international financial centre ADGM, the Dubai International Financial Centre and the King Abdullah Financial District in Riyadh, as well as the Qatar Financial Centre. The financial centre has started boosting its international outreach to engage prospective businesses, investors and professional services firms around the world, the statement said. Oman has been taking steps to diversify its economy away from oil , with investments in sectors such as logistics, manufacturing and property helping to expand its non-oil economic base. Under its economic and social reforms programme, Oman aims to reduce its dependence on oil income from about 30 per cent to 16 per cent by 2030 and 8.4 per cent by 2040. The sultanate has also announced the introduction of personal income tax starting in 2028, with a 5 per cent rate of tax on annual income exceeding 42,000 Omani rials ($109,134). Muscat also unveiled a golden visa programme in August to attract more foreign investment into the country. It also has plans to build a new economic area centred on developing its artificial intelligence capabilities, as it aims to accelerate its technology sector to strengthen its economy. Last month, S&P Global Ratings boosted the economic growth forecast for Oman to 3.5 per cent on the back of favourable trade logistics amid the Iran war. The outlook is more than double the previous 1.6 per cent real GDP growth estimate for the sultanate. It is also higher than the 2.3 per cent growth posted by Oman last year.
