events.title: Campaigners claim minister attempting to undermine 'Holiday Hunger Bill'
events.summary: Paul Givan has now proposed amendments which would give him discretion to decide when the payments would take effect Published 12 October 2026, 06:23 BST Campaigners have accused the education minister of attempting to undermine a proposed Stormont law which would help poorer families with the cost of food. The Democratic Unionist Party's (DUP) Paul Givan has been consistently critical of the legislation which is being brought forward by Sinn Féin assembly member Danny Baker. Givan has warned it would immediately cost his department £20m a year at a time when it is already struggling to balance its budget. The Holiday Meals Payment Bill , external would create a new payment for families whose children receive free school meals which would be made during school holidays to help with the cost of food. The matter is due to be discussed in the assembly on Monday. Givan has now proposed amendments which would give him the power to delay implementation. He will need support from other parties for the amendments to be accepted. It is not clear if he will get that support, although the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) has expressed reservations about the proposal. The payment would be made during school holidays to help with the cost of food As it is based on school meals, the cost of the scheme would be on the Department of Education. It is modelled on the School Holiday Food Grant scheme introduced during the pandemic, which paid qualifying families £27 per child every fortnight. In April, Givan warned MLAs that his department did not have funding for the scheme, so they would be voting to cut education spending if they supported it. He has now proposed amendments which would give him discretion to decide when the payments would take effect. A coalition of campaign groups, including the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children (NSPCC) and Save the Children, say the amendments would mean "no guarantees about when, if ever, payments might begin". They added: "We are calling on all political parties and all MLAs to reject the amendments tabled by the education minister and support the bill as it currently stands." Baker has said the education minister is attempting to "obstruct" the implementation of the bill. "His proposals would give him control over when, if ever, holiday hunger payments begin. "This is an attempt to delay and undermine legislation that has the support of the majority of parties in the assembly." A Department of Education spokesperson said the minister's amendments "do not seek to delay or block the Bill". "They reflect the Department's duty to manage its budget responsibly, taking account of financial pressures, competing priorities and the impact of new spending on existing services, particularly at a time when education faces significant financial challenges across the system," they added. "The amendments fulfil that duty while preserving the Bill's intended purpose. The Bill's key provisions remain unchanged, including eligibility, payment levels, holiday coverage and the Education Authority's responsibilities." events.title: MAS introduces enhanced safeguards around public events by financial institutions
events.summary: Under the enhanced safeguards, financial institutions are expected to conduct public prospecting activities only within designated areas at commercial premises. SINGAPORE – The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) on Oct 12 announced more safeguards around public prospecting activities by financial institutions. This comes as these activities, including roadshows, allow financial institutions and their representatives to engage consumers and market financial products and services in public places, and may cause “concerns” when conducted inappropriately. Such inappropriate conduct includes instances when consumers are subjected to unsolicited or “persistent solicitation”, said the authority. Under the enhanced safeguards, financial institutions are expected to conduct public prospecting activities only within designated areas at commercial premises, and appoint “suitably qualified individuals” to oversee their representatives’ conduct at such events. Representatives must clearly inform consumers at the outset that they intend to market financial products or services, and obtain consumers’ consent before proceeding with the engagement. Street canvassing and door-to-door prospecting will also remain prohibited. The enhanced safeguards follow a public consultation by the authority on proposals to strengthen standards of conduct in this area. Lim Tuang Lee, assistant managing director for capital markets at MAS, said consumers should not feel “pressured or caught off guard” when approached about financial products and services. He added that the enhanced safeguards assist in ensuring that consumers are treated “fairly and professionally”, while allowing financial institutions to continue engaging consumers through appropriate channels. MAS will issue the updated guidelines in 2027, and financial institutions will be given a nine-month transition period to implement the enhanced safeguards thereafter. THE BUSINESS TIMES

events.title: 'I just live on noodles': Report reveals scale of NT cost-of-living crisis
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Territorians 'in crisis' as report shines light on skyrocketing cost of living over past decade Four generations of Shirley Napurrula Miller's family in Central Australia are supporting each other to try to make ends meet. ( ABC News: Xavier Martin ) New data has revealed the rising cost of essentials is making it harder for people to meet their basic needs in the Northern Territory compared to a decade ago. The report by the NT Council of Social Service examines the changes in the cost of living between 2016 and 2026 across key spending areas of housing, utilities, transport and food. The community sector peak body is recommending federal government welfare payments be increased along with the remote area allowance for people in isolated areas. For an Alice Springs grandmother who receives a disability pension, the struggle to afford groceries between pay cheques is constant, with the cost of food "too high". Shirley Napurrula Miller is among the nearly 50 per cent of the Northern Territory's population who experienced food insecurity because of rising prices in 2025, according to a new report. "Sometimes I can't buy groceries, or meat, or anything," she said. Shirley Napurrula Miller says she struggles to afford the basics for herself and her family. ( ABC News: Xavier Martin ) The report by the NT Council of Social Service (NTCOSS), released today, examines changes in the cost of living between 2016 and 2026 across key spending areas of housing, utilities, transport and food. It shows every day, across all spending areas, many Territorians are having to make impossible money decisions and weigh up what they must prioritise to live. Hunger relief charity Foodbank Australia estimates that 46 per cent of NT households experienced food insecurity in 2025, above the national average of 33 per cent, according to the NTCOSS report. The report found that while incomes have increased in real terms in the past 10 years, the cost of essentials has too. ( ABC News: Xavier Martin ) In remote areas, the cost of food is even more prohibitive than in urban centres such as Darwin and Alice Springs, where prices have also risen substantially. "In 2023, the average cost of a healthy food basket was 40 per cent more in remote stores than in a supermarket," the report states. The 10-year comparison report found that while incomes have increased in real terms, the cost of essentials has too, making it harder for everyone — especially those on low incomes — to meet basic needs. Power costs have risen 18 per cent and those on prepaid plans, predominantly First Nations people in urban and remote public housing, are having their electricity cut off more frequently, with 2,284 more disconnections per month on average last year than in 2019-2020. The report found there were 103,648 involuntary self-disconnections in major centres in the NT last year. ( ABC News: Xavier Martin ) Further compounding cost pressures for those already on the poverty line, the report states the prepaid electricity price is higher than for standard postpaid billing to account for customers not paying a fixed daily charge. According to the report, there were 103,648 involuntary self-disconnections in major centres in the NT last year. "Affordability challenges are a key driver of such disconnections," the report states. Ms Miller said she had faced disconnection many times and Aboriginal families often lent on each other to share their limited incomes and keep the power on, particularly in the heat over summer. Linda Lechleitner says her electricity bill alone is more than her Centrelink payment. ( ABC News: Xavier Martin ) Her daughter, Linda Lechleitner, who lives between Alice Springs and a remote Aboriginal homeland near the community of Papunya, about a 3-hour drive away, said she worried about electricity costs amid a heating climate. "It's more than the government payment that they give you, the Centrelink payment doesn't carry people through fortnightly," she said. "Every little dollar counts … it's not carrying through to the next fortnight or the next week, they're having to borrow money from family and then pay that back. The report reveals rents have skyrocketed 55 per cent over the past decade. Meanwhile, the NT's social housing stock only increased by 4 per cent between 2017 and 2025, while social housing applications increased by 37 per cent over the same period. The report shows transport costs have also shot up, with an 80-litre tank of diesel now costing $28 more in Darwin and an extra $88 in Alice Springs.

events.title: AI is less regulated than milk, says Microsoft president
events.summary: Microsoft boss: 'If a company builds AI agents and they break loose, there should be a legal obligation to tell the victim' Published 12 October 2026, 00:07 BST Milk and washing machines are currently more regulated than AI, the president of Microsoft has said. Brad Smith said there needed to be global safety rules in place, including a legal obligation to tell a "victim" if their system is breached by a rogue AI agent as well as deciding when outside evaluators should sign off on an AI product before it is released. His comments put him at odds with President Donald Trump, who said the sector should regulate itself so US firms don't lose out to Chinese rivals. But Smith said: "Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI. Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection." Demands for laws and rules to control AI have grown after experts in the sector said they believed the technology is a threat to humanity. The bosses of the US-based AI giants such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind have all backed the idea of an AI development slowdown , but Trump has pushed against this. Speaking to the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast, Smith called AI both a "tool and a weapon" that urgently needed to be regulated. "Let's get started today," he said. He said firms need "emergency brakes" – often known in the industry as 'kill switches' – to pause or slowdown AI if it got out of control in some way. He also said there should be a legal requirement for firms to write "incident reports" and tell victims if the technology goes rogue. He also suggested that independent government evaluators should vet new AI technology. "We know how to do this for other products," Smith said. "We should build on that knowledge and think about how to apply it to AI." Smith said the UK was best placed to drive forward these global rules for AI because of its AI Security Institute , external , launched during former prime minister Rishi Sunak's government as the AI Safety Institute. "In the world of technology, in the tech sector, most people that I know would say, if you ask them, name the country that is the leader in having this technical capability, they would say, it's very simple. It's the United Kingdom. They are the best." Smith's views are very different to those of his president, who believes the US should be going full-steam ahead on AI. Trump has repeatedly said that "whoever wins AI, wins". However, Smith does not believe the US government would be as opposed to UK-led AI regulations as Trump's comments make it seem, suggesting the US would be more accepting of the UK making standards than the EU. "In Washington DC, people don't look at the UK and they don't look at London the way they look at Brussels – that's a strength," he said. "When you look at AI agents that have escaped human control, when you look at models that are so powerful that they're putting the world's cybersecurity at risk. I would say: The moment has arrived. "Let's speak calmly, maybe even softly, but firmly, and start to bring people together. I hope that's the role we can play as a company. I hope that's the role the UK can play as a country." Big Boss Interview: Microsoft's Brad Smith The president of the tech giant calls for global rules on AI, and says the UK is in the "best position" to lead the charge. At the end of last month, Trump hosted the leaders of US tech giants OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, SpaceX, Meta, and Google at the White House where the executives signed a "morally binding" document . The companies agreed to work with "independent auditors" to assess whether their AI systems are working as intended and make sure they do not "hack or access technical systems in unintended ways". Smith said he applauds the statement and Microsoft is "happy to sign it". "It's a good step, it's a necessary step... But I don't think it's sufficient any longer." He added that the challenge for any "self-regulatory regime" is that "the good companies will do what you want". "It's the companies that are not as responsible that you need to worry about." events.title: AI investment boom offsets energy shock to keep global growth at 3%, IMF chief says
events.summary: Strong investment ⁠in AI infrastructure is keeping global growth at about 3 per cent, yielding major ​benefits for many Asian economies that supply the hardware, such as Thailand, International Monetary Fund managing director Kristalina Georgieva said on Monday. The artificial ⁠intelligence investment boom was already delivering a “demand shock, an investment shock” that could boost growth in advanced Asian economies by a half to one full percentage point, and emerging Asian economies by 0.2 to 0.8 percentage point, she said. “AI, love it, hate it. It's already here,” Ms Georgieva said. “That ⁠shift into higher gear is what is keeping the world economy growing at around 3 per cent, despite the fact we are ​being dragged down ⁠by the energy supply shock,” she told ‌hundreds of participants on the first day of a week-long series of meetings of the IMF and World Bank in the ​Thai capital. The IMF in July forecast global growth at 3 per cent in 2026. It will release an updated outlook on Tuesday. About 18,000 people are expected to attend the meetings this week, including finance officials from the IMF's 191 members. Several ministers will skip the meeting to focus on domestic priorities, including US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Spanish Finance Minister Arcadi Espana, sources said. Profound consequences Ms Georgieva said AI amounted to a “slow-moving tsunami” that would have profound consequences for jobs, growth, education and even how governments generate revenue through taxation, given the expected shift from labour to capital. The IMF estimates that AI could lead to 40 per cent of jobs being augmented, downgraded or eliminated, over time, she said. An initial study showed that 10 per cent of jobs in the US already required AI skills. While routine, repetitive jobs were shrinking, low-paying jobs were increasing in two lower-paying sectors, construction and data centres. “It is a transformative technology . It so completely changes how we work, how we live,” she said, noting that an AI assistant now gave her a ​30-second message about her schedule each day. The US, China and India are the most important ‌producers in the AI supply chain, but many of ⁠the firms building the needed infrastructure are in Asia , Ms Georgieva ​said, referring to Thailand, host of this year's annual meetings. Impact on entry-level jobs World Bank President Ajay Banga, who ​has made jobs ‌a central focus of his presidency, said the development bank was focused on leveraging “small AI”, which is not dependent on large language models, to generate ⁠enormous productivity gains for farmers, healthcare systems, educators and others in emerging markets. Singapore's President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, speaking at the same event, ⁠said governments should address how AI was reducing job opportunities for graduates. “There is a particular problem that we have to address very soon … and that is that, the first rung in employment, your first job upon graduation, is now seeing less demand,” he said. Mr Shanmugaratnam said the world should also guard against AI resulting in a “new divergence” in growth and job creation between ​developing and advanced economies. “AI is going to widen the divergence if we are too passive about it,” he said. “So we've got to do everything we can to first use AI to create good jobs and to create jobs that can be done well by human beings, can allow them to ride up a career ladder despite AI.”

events.title: Human judgment and intentional outcomes are vital in AI use: DBS CEO
events.summary: DBS Bank CEO Tan Su Shan during the DBS Asia Future Forward Conference at Suntec Convention and Exhibition Centre on Oct 12. DBS CEO Tan Su Shan said AI must be used for clear business and work goals, not just added on. She called this “AI lipstick” and urged firms to redesign workflows. DBS’s new AI report said advantage now depends on solving real problems, building trust, and linking intelligence to real outcomes. It also said businesses should start with the intended result. Tan said Asia must stay connected through trade and cooperation to avoid AI supply chain blockages. She stressed that human judgment, wisdom and creativity are vital to guide AI well. SINGAPORE – Applying artificial intelligence is not enough – it has to be harnessed for intentional business and work outcomes, said DBS chief executive Tan Su Shan on Oct 12. She was speaking at the inaugural DBS Asia Future Forward Conference at Suntec Singapore Convention and Exhibition Centre. Organised by DBS, the new flagship event brings together global leaders in technology, business and investment to examine the forces shaping the region’s future. In this first edition, the focus was on AI and how such technology is transforming industries, business models and the nature of work. Tan spoke about Asia’s emergence as a region and how it has proved that AI can be brought to everyday use cases, from enterprises to solving health issues to supporting finance. “I think Asia’s proven and shown that we are able to use AI for good business outcomes and good human outcomes – whether it’s to help the elderly at home, whether it’s to redesign workflows,” she said during her opening address. She added that simply applying AI is not good enough. “We call that AI lipstick. That’s not going to work,” she said. “What we have to do is we really have to rethink our workflows and our work processes so that we can truly unlock our potential. So just adding AI in it might help marginally, but it’s not going to change the way we work.” Tan made these remarks in conjunction with the release of a DBS report on AI outcomes. The report noted that as AI capability becomes more widely available, technical advantage becomes harder to sustain. “Competitive advantage increasingly depends on identifying important problems, earning the trust required for adoption and connecting intelligence to real-world outcomes,” it said. The report said that businesses can start with the intended outcome. “Redesign workflows, partnerships and operating systems around that outcome, then demonstrate that it improves organisational performance and delivers measurable value for customers,” it said. It added that for Asia, the challenge is to turn regional strengths into shared advantage. Tan also said in her speech that countries need to be better connected with one another, and mentioned agreements such as the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership, signed by 15 Asia-Pacific countries, and the Future of Investment and Trade Partnership, which was co-convened by New Zealand, Singapore, Switzerland and the United Arab Emirates. Better connections have to be made, even while countries become increasingly protectionist, Tan said. She noted that AI depends on everyone trading with one another, because each country has its own niche area. For instance, Taiwan has the semiconductor foundries, South Korea has the memory components, and the raw materials come from China and South-east Asia. “So if we don’t cooperate, we will continue to have blockages in our AI supply chain. Even if we want sovereignty, you need to have some trade cooperation,” Tan added. “So stay connected, but keep your sovereignty with your models or data. We have sovereignty, but we also stay connected.” She added that AI has created both visions of a dystopian future where technology takes over or a utopia where AI helps to solve many issues. “What we need now is for humans to exercise good judgment, good wisdom, good creativity to ensure that this AI journey that we take together as a human race will take us up the right path,” Tan said. Sue-Ann Tan is a business correspondent at The Straits Times, covering capital markets and sustainable finance.

events.title: China’s domestic car sales downturn continues, exports retain momentum
events.summary: Chery and Leapmotor vehicles at a Chinese auto show in Buenos Aires, Argentina, on Oct 2. BEIJING – China’s domestic car sales extended their decline for a 12th successive month, while exports remained a key growth driver as automakers looked overseas to cushion the impact of a sluggish home market. Passenger vehicle sales fell 28.1% from a year earlier to 1.63 million units in September, worsening from a 23.7% decline in August, data from the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA) showed on Monday. Annual car exports jumped 73.2% to 923,000 vehicles last month, versus a 77.5% rise in August. Sales of battery electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids at home slid 16.7% from the year before to 1.08 million units, compared with a 10.1% fall in August. The segment’s export growth quickened to 163.5% from August’s 154.7%. Any curbs on plug-in hybrid exports are unlikely to significantly affect overall new energy vehicle exports, given the dominant role of pure EVs, said CPCA secretary-general Cui Dongshu. China and the EU have reached a deal that could halve Chinese hybrid vehicle exports to the bloc over four years, EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic said on Oct 9, though volume limits and terms for shipments above those quotas remain unclear. Shrinking domestic sales reflect broader economic weakness, with subdued consumer spending and a prolonged property downturn weighing on demand. Regulators have shifted focus from growth to safety and value, proposing rules that would curb rushed vehicle launches lacking sufficient validation. REUTERS

events.title: Nearly 70 million kids now have a Trump Account—but parents have to claim it first. Here’s who gets the $1,000
events.summary: The Trump administration says nearly every child in America now has a Trump Account. Whether the money in those accounts ever adds up to much is a different question. The Treasury Department announced Oct. 1 that it had finished automatically enrolling eligible children in the tax-advantaged investment accounts, creating accounts for more than 60 million kids who didn’t already have one. Combined with the families who signed up on their own, that brings the total to nearly 70 million accounts, according to the White House . “Today, I’m pleased to announce that every single eligible minor child in America has now been automatically enrolled in a Trump Account,” President Donald Trump said at an Oval Office event on Oct. 7. But having an account doesn’t mean it’s ready to use. A parent or guardian still has to claim it through the official Trump Accounts app before they can manage it, accept contributions from family and friends, or collect the government’s $1,000 seed deposit for eligible children. The switch to automatic enrollment followed slow uptake. Before the change, Treasury had processed about 5.6 million sign-up forms, less than a tenth of the roughly 73.4 million children eligible, InvestmentNews reported . Fortune previously reported that some families who signed up early were still waiting on their promised $1,000 . Where the money is coming from Since the program launched on July 4, more than $4.5 billion has been deposited into Trump Accounts, including $1.3 billion in government seed contributions, more than $600 million from family and friends, and $2.6 billion in philanthropic gifts, according to the White House. Spread across nearly 70 million accounts, that averages out to about $64 per child. Much of the philanthropic money comes from Michael and Susan Dell’s $6.25 billion pledge, which provides $250 to up to 25 million children age 10 and under who live in ZIP codes with median household incomes below $150,000. More than 70 companies have also signed on to contribute to employees’ children’s accounts, the White House said, following early commitments from firms like JPMorgan Chase and Bank of America . The administration has pitched the accounts as a path to serious wealth. The calculator on TrumpAccounts.gov projects that a lone $1,000 seed could grow to $243,000 by age 55, and that an account receiving the $5,000 annual maximum could reach $13 million. Those numbers assume the S&P 500 returns more than 10% a year without interruption for 55 years. Financial planners who spoke with Fortune put more conservative estimates at roughly $1.5 million to $2 million by 55 for a maxed-out account, assuming a 7% return. Stock gifts, with strings attached Most money in Trump Accounts goes into low-cost index funds . But Treasury said in July it would also accept large philanthropic donations of publicly traded stock, and the IRS released a rule on Sept. 30 setting the procedures. Qualifying stock is transferred to Treasury and allocated to eligible children according to donor instructions and Treasury guidance. “By accepting contributions of publicly traded stock, Treasury is creating a practical pathway for large-scale private giving to support the next generation,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a July statement . The rules are narrow. Stock donations can come from companies or charities set up by stockholders, not from relatives, and must be spread across at least 5,000 accounts in a qualified geographic area, according to Yahoo Finance . The shares must be held for at least five years before they can be sold. SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell is among the first to use the option, pledging one share each to more than 2 million children’s accounts. Single-stock gifts can give children a stake in corporate growth, but they also concentrate risk. “A child could, hypothetically, receive $10,000 of Company X stock and suddenly at least 67% of the minor’s portfolio is concentrated in Company X,” U.S. Bank wealth management advisor Jonathan Lee told Yahoo Finance. Who benefits most Critics argue the program’s biggest winners will be families who can afford to contribute. “The program may be open to every child, but its benefits will flow overwhelmingly to families with the means to contribute thousands of dollars a year,” Stanford economists Neale Mahoney and Adam Shaw wrote in Time last December. Researchers at the New School reached a similar conclusion in an analysis for Fortune , based on 15 years of 529 college savings data. The White House counters that about 80% of Trump Accounts are linked to families earning less than $200,000 a year. Who is eligible and how to claim an account Every child under 18 with a valid Social Security number now has an account. The government’s one-time $1,000 seed contribution, however, is limited to U.S. citizen children born between Jan. 1, 2025, and Dec. 31, 2028, and the account must be claimed for the child to receive it. Parents and guardians can claim accounts through the Trump Accounts app for iOS and Android; more information is available at TrumpAccounts.gov. Once an account is claimed, family and friends can contribute up to $5,000 a year combined, while employers can add up to $2,500 annually. The government’s $1,000 seed and certain contributions from state and local governments and nonprofits don’t count toward the $5,000 cap. When a child turns 18, the account essentially becomes a traditional IRA. Withdrawals are taxed as ordinary income, and early withdrawals may face penalties unless they’re used for qualifying expenses such as education or a first home, so families should review the tax rules before deciding how to use the money. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Model blitz at Paris motor show as Europe-China rivalry heats up
events.summary: The DS F3VER concept car, by DS Automobiles, at a Stellantis NV presentation ahead of the Paris Motor Show in Meudon, France, on Oct 11. Europe’s car makers used the Paris motor show to fight Chinese competition with new launches and support from Brussels, after an EU deal capped Chinese hybrid imports at 350,000 a year. Chinese brands, including BYD, Chery and Changan, are expanding fast in Europe, with around 20 brands at the show and more plans for local production to meet possible “Made in Europe” rules. European firms face pressure from weak demand and higher costs, with Volkswagen’s deliveries down 14.3% and Stellantis and Renault pushing new EV plans to regain market share. PARIS – Europe’s car industry fought back against rising Chinese competition at the Paris car show on Oct 12 with a wave of new model launches and fresh support from Brussels, even as Chinese auto makers expanded their push into the region. The show opened days after the European Union announced a deal with China to curb imports of Chinese hybrid vehicles into the bloc, with a cap of 350,000 a year, according to a European Commission official. While details of the arrangement have yet to be finalised, it was welcomed by European manufacturers. Stellantis chief executive officer Antonio Filosa said the deal was a “good milestone”, but that the Fiat maker was also seeking help with high energy costs from the Italian government and wanted Brussels to move more quickly on carbon emissions rules. The flood of hybrid imports into the EU is “not sustainable” for Europe, said Renault chief executive officer Francois Provost, with the current deal “better than a trade war”. Zhao Fei, president of Chinese auto maker Changan, said he was “not that concerned” by the deal, which he viewed as a precursor to “Made in Europe” local content rules that could be dealt with by setting up production in the region. Around 20 Chinese brands, including BYD and Chery, are attending the show, double their presence in 2024 as they seek growth overseas amid intense competition and weaker demand at home. Chinese brands have gained share rapidly in Europe in the last three years, while total Chinese exports of hybrids to the EU’s 27-member states tripled to US$7.5 billion (S$9.6 billion) in the first half of 2026, according to Chinese Customs. The EU-China deal could hit BYD, Chery and state-owned SAIC’s MG brand hardest as between them, they accounted for 90% of Chinese brand hybrid sales in the EU in the first eight months of 2026, said analysts at Jefferies on Oct 11. BYD said the deal amounted to short-term pressure but that it remained committed to Europe. Underscoring the challenges facing European manufacturers, Volkswagen said on Oct 12 its deliveries fell 14.3% in the third quarter, the steepest quarterly drop in four years, dragged down by a further decline in demand in its top market, China. Deliveries also fell in North America and Western Europe. As part of its efforts to regain market share in Europe, Stellantis is launching six new models across its European brands at the show and unveiling nine concept cars. On Oct 11, Stellantis chief executive officer Antonio Filosa hailed “the reinvention of a European icon” as he unveiled an affordable retro electric version of Citroen’s 2CV. The company is adopting faster Chinese-style development cycles, chief technology officer Ned Curic said, outlining plans to build small EVs in Italy using a platform being developed with Leapmotor. Renault’s head of growth, Fabrice Cambolive, said the car maker could increase EV production in France by at least 50% over the next 12 months. Like other Western car shows, Paris had been in decline until Chinese auto makers started showing up in Europe in force four years ago. Alongside BYD and Chery, this year’s show will feature new Chinese brands like Aito, while state-owned auto maker Changan is launching its Nevo and Avatr brands in Europe. Chinese auto makers also used the event to outline further European expansion plans. Changan president Zhao Fei said the company was in talks with manufacturers about producing vehicles in Europe and hoped to build its first European-made car in early 2027. BYD is studying the possibility of building a factory in France, executive vice-president Stella Li told broadcaster BFM TV on Oct 12. The EU imposed tariffs on Chinese-made fully electric vehicles in October 2024. Brussels is also working on “Made in Europe” rules requiring minimum local content levels for EVs to access large parts of the bloc’s market. Agreement between France and Germany on the provisions is “imminent”, French President Emmanuel Macron said at the show. Chinese auto makers have sought European production bases ahead of the proposed rules, often in partnership with established manufacturers. In July, China’s Geely Auto said it would produce electric SUVs at a Ford Motor factory in Spain.

events.title: McKinsey strips partner of leadership role over LinkedIn posts
events.summary: The decision came after an internal review sparked by Chris Bradley’s LinkedIn comments on a book that discusses the “glass cliff” for women. McKinsey & Co removed a senior partner from his leadership role at the firm’s research arm after he posted online comments questioning the uphill battle female executives face in the workplace. Chris Bradley, one of a handful of directors at the McKinsey Global Institute, its high-profile business and economic research unit, was removed from that role, the consulting firm said in a statement on Oct 11. He remains a senior partner at the firm and is based in Australia. The unusual decision came after an internal review sparked by Bradley’s LinkedIn back-and-forth in September with one of the authors of a new book discussing the workplace “glass cliff” for women. The comments were deleted, and McKinsey previously distanced itself from Bradley’s remarks. “Following our conduct review process, we have removed the partner from his leadership roles, including at the McKinsey Global Institute. His public comments fell well short of the standards we expect at our firm,” McKinsey spokesman Taylor Burns said in an e-mailed statement. Bradley also served as a leader on some internal committees, Burns said. Bradley could not be reached immediately for comment outside of normal business hours. The term “glass cliff” was coined by academics to describe the phenomenon in which female leaders are more likely to be offered CEO jobs at struggling companies. Proponents of the theory say research shows that women are more likely to get an opportunity to be CEO when a company is in crisis or turnaround mode. Bradley called the glass cliff “a very convenient way to always be a victim in the rain” in the deleted posts and generally questioned whether the concept even exists. McKinsey has long sought to advance the conversation about challenges women face in the workplace. The company has published a Women in the Workplace study, compiled with Sheryl Sandberg’s LeanIn advocacy group, for more than a decade. It surveys about 9,500 employees from 124 organisations; participants consistently report that women leaders face stronger resistance than men and are more likely to have their judgment questioned. A 2020 report from McKinsey about women working in healthcare even references the term “glass cliff” when outlining hurdles cited by women of colour. Over the past decade, women CEOs of Russell 3000 companies left after an average tenure of 6.2 years versus 8.9 years for men, according to Exechange, a researcher that tracks corporate leadership changes and scores them on the likelihood that the exit was forced or voluntary. In examining the reasons for CEO departures over the same period, the research firm found that women were more likely than men to be forced out. Just one in 10 S&P 500 companies is led by a female CEO. BLOOMBERG

events.title: UK van drivers face extra £2.5bn in diesel costs this year, figures show
events.summary: Calls for planned fuel duty rise to be scrapped as analysis finds average fuel bill could hit £1,965, up from £1,294 Millions of British van drivers face a combined £2.5bn cost to cover the rising price of diesel this year, according to figures, fuelling calls for the government to scrap its planned fuel duty rise. The owners of diesel vans and pickups can expect to collectively spend almost £8.5bn at the pump this year, according to analysis for the Guardian, after diesel prices climbed to record highs due to a global fuel shortage caused by disruption to refineries in the Middle East and Russia. The estimated fuel costs, calculated by analysts at Moneysupermarket, is significantly above the £5.95bn spent last year, raising concerns that the price of food and goods transported by road could rise sharply as retailers pass on increased logistics costs. The comparison site warned last week that the average fuel bill for a van driver could reach £1,965 this year, up from £1,294 for the average van in 2025 based on typical mileage and fuel consumption. The number of vans on British roads has grown significantly in recent years fuelled by the boom in online shopping, home deliveries and the rising number of self-employed people working in trades . Although the adoption of electric vans has begun to increase, about 95% of light commercial vehicles are still powered by diesel. The average pump price climbed to a above £2 a litre for the first time this month, up over 40% since late February, when the US-Israel war on Iran began disrupting supplies of crude and refined oil products from the Gulf, leading to cost increases across the economy. The rising cost burden has led to calls for government help in the upcoming budget, including abandoning plans to raise fuel duty from next year. The planned increase – postponed from September – will add 3p a litre in duty from 1 January, and another 2p from 1 March, in “a hammer blow” for costs, according to the Road Haulage Association (RHA). Richard Smith, the RHA’s managing director, said: “Many of our members run on margins of around 2%. Surging diesel prices are impacting firms across the country, with some spending many thousands extra every week on fuel. “Adding [fuel duty rises] on top of today’s fuel prices would be a hammer blow for many firms that move goods and the households that buy them. A fuel duty hike is a food price hike.” Data from the motoring group RAC showed that, despite a recent dip in the cost of diesel, the price remains about 57p a litre higher than before the US-Iran conflict while petrol remains 42p higher. This means households are paying £31 and £23 more respectively every time they fill up a family sized car, according to the group. The fuel duty rise “will only make prices at the pump even more expensive,” according to Simon Williams, the head of policy at the RAC. “As things stand, this year is still set to be the second most expensive year on record for drivers,” Williams said. “The government has the power to take some of the sting out of higher fuel costs, either by extending and increasing the fuel duty cut or reducing VAT as they’ve done with domestic electricity.” Smith added that the RHA was calling on the chancellor to bring in a 15p a litre rebate for British van, coach and haulage operators after Spain, France and Italy offered similar help for commercial vehicle businesses. “It’s time we caught up,” he said. On Friday, the US president, Donald Trump, attempted to ease pressure at the pump for US drivers by announcing a deal for Russian deal, in a move which infuriated the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy . The government was contact for comment.

events.title: The Gulf has entered a new era of instability. If its leaders think they can rely on old alliances, they are wrong | Nesrine Malik
events.summary: The Gulf has entered a new era of instability. If its leaders think they can rely on old alliances, they are wrong The latest attack by Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia may prove to be more calamitous for the region than the world imagines O n Saturday, Houthi rebels launched a shocking and deadly attack on Saudi Arabia’s capital city, Riyadh. At the time of writing, the missile strike on King Khalid international airport has killed at least 13 people and left 300 injured, marking a significant turn in a regional conflagration that is only getting more intense. It was the single most deadly attack on any Gulf country since the US and Israel launched their war on Iran in February. In Saudi Arabia, a country that is unaccustomed to such fatalities, the death toll is bewilderingly high and likely to prompt a bloody response. Over the past year, the Gulf has entered a new era of instability that is not temporary and cannot be reversed. This may feel like an overstatement – casualties have been relatively low, after all, compared with Gaza and Iran – but the gradual erosion of peace and security in places such as Saudi Arabia , Qatar and the UAE has changed the region more dramatically than its leaders would like to acknowledge. The first audacious and unthinkable thing happened just over a year ago, when Iran fired missiles at an airbase in Qatar that hosts American troops, in retaliation for US strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities. Lighting up Doha’s skies and scattering shrapnel, it was a dismaying moment for the Qataris, who have tried to maintain good relations with Iran. But even then there was a degree of warning and coordination that signalled this was a face-saving measure on the part of the Iranians. Yet later in 2025, with no similar warning or choreography, Israel struck Doha , targeting Hamas members and killing five Palestinians and one Qatari. That was the beginning of the end of a longstanding norm and expectation – that there was a sanctity to Gulf lives and sovereignty, one secured by the management of the relationship with Iran and alliances with the US. Then came Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu’s war on Iran , which drew the Gulf once and for all into the fray. In retaliation for what Iran perceives to be political, military and logistical support for the offensive against it, Tehran struck Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman. Iran targeted military sites, energy facilities, desalination plants – an entire infrastructure that underpins the economies of these countries. Much damage was inflicted by the suspension of normal life, the shuttering of schools for months, the closure of airports and airspace. The most disastrous consequence of all, from the perspective of Gulf rulers, has been the way the attacks have disrupted the integration of these countries into the cosmopolitan international community as places for tourism, entrepreneurs, sports and entertainment. They spent billions in securing Formula One , golf and boxing franchises and tournaments, only for a flurry of cheap drones to put it all at risk. The result is a fractious unravelling that has reactivated hostilities that had laid dormant. Yemen’s civil war began in 2014 when Iran-backed Houthi rebels, in aspiration to greater autonomy in the minority Shia homelands, took over the capital city, Sana’a . In 2015, a coalition of countries led by Saudi Arabia led a brutal campaign to dislodge the Houthis from territories they had gained, intensifying a grinding civil war that killed hundreds of thousands and triggered a humanitarian catastrophe . The war deescalated in 2022 with a de facto but unformalised division of the country between the Houthis and an internationally recognised, Saudi-backed government; the ceasefire was followed by rapprochement between Saudi Arabia and Iran. But the 2026 war against Iran opened up strategic opportunities and stirred political loyalties, triggering a surge of Houthi advancement in Yemen. The closure of the strait of Hormuz, for example, shifted more commercial traffic along Yemen’s coastline, prompting the Houthis to make advances and seize territory in order to gain control of the now crucial Bab al-Mandab strait in the Red Sea. Tensions came to a head five months after the start of the war, with Saudi Arabia escalating strikes against the Houthis, and the Saudi-backed government bombing its own airport in Sana’a to prevent an Iranian plane from landing. These developments are not just the result of a mischievous group seizing the moment, acting as spoiler in a bigger contest between Iran and the west. The Houthis are backed by Iran, but they are not empty proxies for Iran; they have domestic ambitions and sharp regional animosities, particularly against the House of Saud, which they see an imperious and arrogant master to whom they shall never submit.

events.title: Drivers forced to use parking apps can pay up to 40% more
events.summary: Council car parks have switched away from ticket machines to cut costs, leading to extra fees for users Drivers are unwittingly paying up to 40% more to park as more councils switch to app-only payments and force customers to pick up the tab. Many councils across England have removed pay and display machines and replaced them with app payments, including a number in London. Most local authorities encourage drivers to pay by app to beat queues, while apps are often the only way to pay when ticket machines are out of order. However, many car park signs fail to mention that app payments may incur an additional service fee. Parking apps save councils money by removing the cost of installing and maintaining ticket machines, but while a few pay the app providers directly for their services, many leave drivers to foot some or all of the bill through “convenience fees” or “service fees”. These typically range from 10p to 30p, but they are not included in the advertised parking tariffs in car parks, even when an app is the only payment option, and they are often not strongly flagged within the apps. Of the parking apps tested by the Guardian, none clearly displayed the service fee until the payment stage, and even then, some required customers to click on an information symbol to find out why the price had increased. These surcharges can push up the cost of an hour’s parking slot dramatically. In Harrogate, North Yorkshire, drivers who park in the town centre and pay by app are hit with a mandatory 30p service charge – a 38% rise on an 80p tariff. Meanwhile, the price of two hours at the council’s Christleton Road car park in Chester soars by 40% when the 20p convenience fee is added to the 50p tariff. Extra fees are added if drivers agree to receive booking confirmation and expiry alerts. They are typically between 10 and 30p per text. According to the Advertising Standards Authority, quoted prices must include all mandatory fees for a contract to be valid. Drivers enter a contract with a council as soon as they accept the car park’s terms and conditions and park their vehicle. However, few realise that they enter a separate contract with the app provider if they choose to pay online. App fees, therefore, may not legally have to be displayed on parking council signs. Because service fees are agreed between local authorities and individual app providers, and since they can vary depending on location, drivers have no way of predicting what they will be charged. The Guardian tested the apps by booking an hour’s parking at car parks around the country. RingGo’s convenience fee added an extra 20p to the £2 tariff at Kings Yard in Lancaster. Drivers have to click on a small “see prices” link above the prominent “Next” button when they have chosen their location to see the charge. It is mentioned again on the payment page, but only when the “i” symbol beside the final price is clicked. PayByPhone charged a 15p service fee on top of the £5.10 parking tariff at Dudley Street car park in Birmingham. The existence of the charge was not explained until the payment page and was hidden behind the Apple Pay button. Customers have to scroll down to the end of the page to see it. Customers using JustPark have to click on a tiny pale grey “i” symbol beside the final price at the end of the booking process to discover its transaction fee. This added 12p to a £3.50 parking charge at Charmouth Road car park in Lyme Regis, Dorset. MiPermit listed its 10p convenience fee above the final price at the end of the booking. This was levied on top of the £1.90 parking charge in Littlehampton, West Sussex. RingGo said the fee funded the service it provided and that it was up to the councils it worked with whether or not to display it on car park signs. “In line with existing regulations, wherever pricing information is shown in the RingGo app, we also display any additional fees,” said Adam Dolphin at its parent company Arrive. JustPark said mandatory fees were included in the price quoted during payment. “Nothing is added at the payment stage,” said a spokesperson. “The ‘i’ icon simply shows how that all-in price is made up, for drivers who want the detail.” PayByPhone said its pricing was transparent. “The pricing elements related to parking, SMS options and service fees are presented before payment confirmation,” said a spokesperson. “Applicable pricing information – whether fees, parking rates or options – is available on the website and in the app.” MiPermit was contacted for a comment. The Local Government Association, which represents councils, said it was up to app providers to ensure their fees were clear and upfront. The Department for Transport said parking tariffs and surcharges were a matter for councils. “Drivers should be able to see clearly what they will be charged before they pay for parking,” a spokesperson said.

events.title: Father was asked for DNA test to get a passport for his daughter
events.summary: New post-Brexit rules mean that dual nationals cannot enter the UK unless they have a British passport My teenage daughter is unable to see her grandparents because of the UK’s new requirement for dual nationals to hold a UK passport. I’m a UK citizen, married to a French national, and we live in France. Our two older children have both French and UK passports. Our third child was born while we were living in Zimbabwe and only has a French passport. I began her application for a British passport in February. I had to submit photos of my wife when pregnant, family photos from the birth to the present day, hospital records and official translations of French marriage and birth certificates. During an official interview I was asked about my job, commute and the layout of my house, but very little about my relationship with my daughter. I was then told that there was insufficient evidence to prove my paternity and was invited to consider a DNA test, which will cost £600 and take yet more time. We need to visit my elderly father who is unwell in the UK but cannot risk it in case our daughter is denied boarding. Your daughter is a victim of new rules that came into force in February and effectively deny entry to the UK to dual national Britons who do not have a British passport. Foreign nationals can enter freely on passports issued by their country of residence, but expats cannot unless they stump up £589 for a certificate of entitlement. The law has caused chaos, with children being stranded abroad or arbitrarily denied a passport granted to their siblings. Since the UK government is not accepting that your daughter is a UK national, you asked if she could travel on her French passport. No one could answer the question. As a result, you face Christmas apart from your parents. Home Office rules state that officials must consider a passport application on the “balance of probability” if an applicant refuses a DNA test. They must also explain why an application is refused. You have never been told why your copious proofs of paternity have been deemed inadequate. The Home Office will not comment on individual cases, but it did tell me that additional evidence, such as the layout of a home, may be requested to add “credible authenticity”. Soon afterwards, you were informed that the application had been accepted after all, despite no new paperwork having been sought since April. I can only assume that press scrutiny prompted the realisation that your domestic floorplan is credibly authentic. We welcome letters but cannot answer individually. Email us at consumer.champions@theguardian.com or write to Consumer Champions, Money, the Guardian, 90 York Way, London N1 9GU. Please include a daytime phone number. events.title: IFS: budget will be ‘work of fiction’ without clear plan to cover UK’s £35bn spending pressures
events.summary: Thinktank’s influential pre-budget report urges key decisions to be made now and not put off until next year John Healey has been warned by Britain’s leading tax and spending experts that his budget risks being a “work of fiction” unless he sets out plans to cover £35bn in spending pressures. As the war in the Middle East rattles the public finances, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the damage from higher inflation meant the chancellor would need to either top up funds for his current government spending plans or impose deep real-terms cuts by the end of the decade. Against a febrile backdrop in the bond market, the thinktank warned Healey that failure to address the issue at his 28 October budget risked leaving the impression that Labour was setting unrealistic spending plans. Helen Miller, the director of the IFS, said: “Simply pencilling in implicit cuts that he has no intention of delivering would make the budget a work of fiction.” Her comment echoes a criticism levelled at Jeremy Hunt , the former Conservative chancellor, who before the 2024 general election was accused by the then head of the Office for Budget Responsibility of setting unrealistic spending plans. Publishing its influential “green budget” report, which analyses the public finances before Healey’s speech to the Commons, it called on the chancellor to avoid announcing a “steady as she goes” budget that delayed decisions until next year’s spending review. “If John Healey sets out spending envelopes for public services that he would not be willing to live within, his plan for meeting the fiscal rules will not be credible,” it said. Last week, the governor of the Bank of England, Andrew Bailey, said fiscal policy “must be credible and be seen as such by financial markets”. The following day, the Times quoted a government source as saying: “Andrew Bailey needs to focus on doing his job.” Miller said the Treasury adopting an assumption that “everything can be kicked forward” to next year’s spending review risked undermining the chancellor’s credibility. “We would be better served by a chancellor who hopes for the best, but plans for the worst, rather than sets out plans that either say, ‘I hope it’ll be fine and some money will come in’, or ‘I’ll get a plan in a year’s time’.” Attention before the budget has largely focused on the hit to the chancellor’s headroom against Labour’s main fiscal rule to balance day-to-day public spending with revenues in 2029-30. With the war in the Middle East fuelling a dramatic sell-off in the market for government debt, higher borrowing costs are expected to erase a significant chunk of the £24bn buffer left by the former chancellor Rachel Reeves at the spring statement. Leading economists have predicted the market moves since the start of the war in February could wipe out about half of the headroom, adding to nerves in the Treasury over the risk of a market backlash. The IFS said that although the surge in debt interest costs could add £10bn to borrowing in 2029-30, the exchequer would benefit from higher inflation boosting tax revenue – meaning Healey could see headroom cut by only £4bn. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning However, it warned against focusing on this buffer because the inflation shock rippling from the Middle East would also dramatically hit the government’s plan for funding public services. Higher inflation squeezes public spending power, forcing the government to choose between accepting real-term cuts and finding efficiency savings or topping up departmental budgets either by raising taxes or allowing an increase in borrowing. The IFS said a choice to leave spending totals unchanged at the budget would implicitly mean allowing the quality or quantity of public services to fall. However, it said compensating for the inflation shock, and funding Healey’s pledge to raise defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030, would require tax rises or benefit cuts of about £35bn. “Choosing to stay the course with the inherited tax and spending plans would mean allowing inflation to blow departments’ spending plans off course,” Miller said. “It would be a choice to tolerate chunky cuts to the quantity or quality of some public services – cuts that would be larger if defence spending was increased within existing totals.” She said Healey would not need to make detailed plans for the next spending review period at the budget but merely set out overall spending envelopes that he would be prepared to live within. A spokesperson for the Treasury said: “The chancellor is fully focused on his priorities to boost business, help with the cost of living and support people in every postcode, underpinned by fiscal discipline and a commitment to meet the fiscal rules with a buffer against uncertainty.

events.title: Why some have no choice but to pay costly oil prices
events.summary: Published 12 October 2026, 06:27 BST As the temperature drops, some of us will start putting the heating on but for the one-and-a-half million people across the UK that are not on the mains gas network - and who are relying instead on heating oil - that decision may give them pause. The vast majority of those people live in rural locations. The heating oil market is unregulated, unlike gas and electricity, so any changes in the global price quickly gets passed on to customers . Tensions in the Middle East and the ongoing war in Ukraine are two issues currently both affecting supply which is causing prices to rise. Many heating oil customers are having to buy early in preparation for the colder months Author shares how books have 'magical way' of reaching you when struggling Published 1 day ago Accessible playground to 'allow all children to play' Published 1 day ago 'What terminal cancer has taught me about life' Published 2 days ago Until March this year, the price was quite stable at about 60p per litre (ppl) but when the war in Iran started in March, it jumped to a high of 134ppl . After a dip in the past few months, it is rising once again and it currently stands at 111ppl, according to price comparison site Boiler Juice. The BBC has spoken to a number of business and homeowners across the West about how that rise is affecting them. Peter Mason lives in Minety, in north Wiltshire, where most homes rely on heating oil. "I'm getting toward the end of the tank and need to top up for winter... it will be over £550," he said. Mason said that last year "it was about £300 to fill up - it is horrendous". He said: "The price goes up and down. It can vary plus or minus £50 but it has never been as high as it is today. "It means I'll have to eek out what I spent my money on. I'm retired, its not like I can change jobs. "I have to be really careful and pull money out of savings." Most tanks hold 500 litres of oil and would cost about £550 to fill currently Dylan Williams owns van-driving business Van & I of Monmouth, Wales and regularly operates in the Forest of Dean, Stroud and South Gloucestershire. The 51-year-old said he was currently paying more for fuel than he ever had in the three years of running his business. He said he had had to put the prices of his services up to offset the rise. At the start of the year he would pay between £120 and £130 for a full tank, he said, but that had now gone up to £160. "It's ever increasing, ever worrying - keeping an eye on the news, keeping an eye on the diesel prices," he said. "I mean I've got fuel cards... you don't pay the pump prices, you pay the fuel card prices but it doesn't make much a difference these days. Tristan Holland (pictured with Mel Holland) runs a small team of community care workers Yvette Farrell, volunteer director for Dean Forest Kitchen, which cook fresh meals every day and delivers them to clients within the Forest of Dean, said they might have to increase prices as there's "not going to be much choice in the future". She said: "It's impacted us a lot because we work on a not-for-profit scenario so there is not a lot of wiggle room when it comes to increase in any expenses. "So the cost of fuel is really, really hitting the business hard and we're having to do our best to still keep going to our clients who are spread across a very rural area with no public transport. "But we have to take these meals to them because... they will not have somebody coming to see them during the day because they're so isolated." Tristan Holland, company director at TLC Support Service, manages a small team of community care workers who travel around Wotton-under-Edge and Dursley. Staff use their own vehicles and the company pays mileage at 55p per business mile. He said: "We had an increase in our fees back at the start of the year, just kind of taking into account all the extras that were coming in this year but even that does make it tight. "Everything has risen - the cost of the fuel, the training, even the uniforms that we purchased. "Everything has gone up and so we try to keep our services as affordable as we possibly can but there has to be a profit or else we just can't carry on going." The Iran war has disrupted the production and transportation of wholesale oil and prices can rise or fall based on the words and actions of key political figures. It is thought prices could come down if there is a peace deal between the US and Iran. For people who rely on heating oil, it means feeling helpless. Richard Willan, who runs the Nadder Oil Buying Club in Wiltshire where more than 1,000 residents buy in bulk together to get a better price, said rural residents were increasingly vulnerable as the colder months set in. "We are watching to see what happens with (Donald) Trump in the mid-term elections in America, that might change things again," he said.

The vast majority of those people live in rural locations. The heating oil market is unregulated, unlike gas and electricity, so any changes in the global price quickly gets passed on to customers . Many heating oil customers are having to buy early in preparation for the colder months Author shares how books have 'magical way' of reaching you when struggling Published 1 day ago Accessible playground to 'allow all children to play' Published 1 day ago 'What terminal cancer has taught me about life' Published 2 days ago Until March this year, the price was quite stable at about 60p per litre (ppl) but when the war in Iran started in March, it jumped to a high of 134ppl . After a dip in the past few months, it is rising once again and it currently stands at 111ppl, according to price comparison site Boiler Juice. The BBC has spoken to a number of business and homeowners across the West about how that rise is affecting them. Peter Mason lives in Minety, in north Wiltshire, where most homes rely on heating oil. "I'm getting toward the end of the tank and need to top up for winter... it will be over £550," he said. Mason said that last year "it was about £300 to fill up - it is horrendous". He said: "The price goes up and down. It can vary plus or minus £50 but it has never been as high as it is today. "It means I'll have to eek out what I spent my money on. I'm retired, its not like I can change jobs. "I have to be really careful and pull money out of savings." Most tanks hold 500 litres of oil and would cost about £550 to fill currently Dylan Williams owns van-driving business Van & I of Monmouth, Wales and regularly operates in the Forest of Dean, Stroud and South Gloucestershire. The 51-year-old said he was currently paying more for fuel than he ever had in the three years of running his business. He said he had had to put the prices of his services up to offset the rise. At the start of the year he would pay between £120 and £130 for a full tank, he said, but that had now gone up to £160. "It's ever increasing, ever worrying - keeping an eye on the news, keeping an eye on the diesel prices," he said. "I mean I've got fuel cards... you don't pay the pump prices, you pay the fuel card prices but it doesn't make much a difference these days. Tristan Holland (pictured with Mel Holland) runs a small team of community care workers Yvette Farrell, volunteer director for Dean Forest Kitchen, which cook fresh meals every day and delivers them to clients within the Forest of Dean, said they might have to increase prices as there's "not going to be much choice in the future". She said: "It's impacted us a lot because we work on a not-for-profit scenario so there is not a lot of wiggle room when it comes to increase in any expenses. "So the cost of fuel is really, really hitting the business hard and we're having to do our best to still keep going to our clients who are spread across a very rural area with no public transport. "But we have to take these meals to them because... they will not have somebody coming to see them during the day because they're so isolated." Tristan Holland, company director at TLC Support Service, manages a small team of community care workers who travel around Wotton-under-Edge and Dursley. Staff use their own vehicles and the company pays mileage at 55p per business mile. He said: "We had an increase in our fees back at the start of the year, just kind of taking into account all the extras that were coming in this year but even that does make it tight. "Everything has risen - the cost of the fuel, the training, even the uniforms that we purchased. "Everything has gone up and so we try to keep our services as affordable as we possibly can but there has to be a profit or else we just can't carry on going." The Iran war has disrupted the production and transportation of wholesale oil and prices can rise or fall based on the words and actions of key political figures. It is thought prices could come down if there is a peace deal between the US and Iran. For people who rely on heating oil, it means feeling helpless. Richard Willan, who runs the Nadder Oil Buying Club in Wiltshire where more than 1,000 residents buy in bulk together to get a better price, said rural residents were increasingly vulnerable as the colder months set in. "We are watching to see what happens with (Donald) Trump in the mid-term elections in America, that might change things again," he said.

events.title: Documents falsified to evade tax on Abramovich's wealth, BBC finds
events.summary: Watch: The documents that were falsified to allow Roman Abramovich to evade tax Published 12 October 2026, 06:00 BST The world's biggest accountancy firm helped in falsifying documents to hide Roman Abramovich's wealth and evade tax, BBC Panorama has found. Accounts signed off by Deloitte in Cyprus meant assets such as superyachts, mansions and private jets worth $672m (£508m) vanished from Abramovich's company accounts. Deloitte also appears to have advised on a scheme to evade a huge tax bill on the oligarch's wealth through the falsification of documents. Barrister Andrew Mitchell KC, an expert in financial services law, said Panorama's evidence showed the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion and "it couldn't be more blatant". Roman Abramovich's lawyers said he denies that he evaded tax or concealed his fortune. They said Panorama provided no evidence he knew about, authorised or directed the falsification of any document and said it was legitimate to rely on advice from professionals. Deloitte Cyprus said it "acts in compliance with applicable laws". The findings are being revealed following a joint investigation between BBC Panorama and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism. For nearly two decades, Roman Abramovich was the most famous Russian oligarch in the UK, welcomed in London where he bought Chelsea Football Club in 2003 and bankrolled the club's most successful period. But after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, he was sanctioned by the UK government as an associate of President Vladimir Putin and forced to sell the club. Abramovich has been reported to be living in Turkey, a safe haven for him because it did not apply sanctions. In the Channel Island of Jersey, £5.4bn of his assets remain frozen and a criminal investigation has been going on for four years. The oligarch's lawyers told the BBC he denies the allegations in the Jersey investigation and says it was "undertaken for political purposes". Our investigation has uncovered new evidence about the way Abramovich's business empire has been run. It also raises serious questions about the integrity of some of his professional advisers. Chateau de la Croe (top left) in the south of France, Fyning Hill in Sussex and two superyachts vanished from company accounts The evidence is contained in a leak that includes thousands of documents about the oligarch's finances and the operations of a network of offshore companies administered from Cyprus - which used to be a tax haven popular with Russians - between 1995 and 2022. The BBC and media partners including the Guardian, Paper Trail Media, the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project, and the Cyprus Investigative Reporting Network - as well as the Bureau of Investigative Journalism , external - have been reporting on the leaked files since 2023 as part of the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists' Cyprus Confidential , external investigation. In 2022, Panorama also reported on how Abramovich had made his fortune from a corrupt deal to buy a Russian state-owned oil company in the 1990s, selling it back to the government a decade later for billions in profit. He has previously said allegations of corruption in the deal are false. The profits from Abramovich's oil deals in Russia were funnelled into a web of offshore companies. They were administered from Cyprus by a corporate services firm called MeritServus, in Limassol, the island's second-largest city. Until 2005, Deloitte - now the biggest of the "big four" firms which dominate the accounting industry - owned MeritServus. After they split, the two companies worked closely together with Abramovich's associates to manage his global fortune. The leaked documents from MeritServus reveal some of their practices. Panorama - Roman Abramovich: How He Hid His Fortune He was the Russian oligarch who brought his wealth to the UK. But what’s the truth about Roman Abramovich’s fortune? Panorama investigates the documents that were falsified to hide his wealth and evade tax. Watch now on BBC iPlayer or on BBC One at 20:00 BST on Monday 12 October. Our first example of backdated paperwork comes in 2006, after a new law in Cyprus meant that company accounts had to be made public. The new transparency law threatened to expose the secrets of Abramovich's vast wealth. Deloitte Cyprus had prepared draft accounts for 2003 - but had not yet finalised them - for his Cypriot company Amiscan Investments. The accounts detailed $672m of luxury property. A mansion in West Sussex, a luxury flat in London and an estate in the south of France were all included - plus helicopters, private jets and a small fleet of boats the oligarch owned at the time, including the $147.5m Pelorus. Deloitte in Cyprus appears to have advised Abramovich's company on a scheme to evade tax To keep them secret, Abramovich's associates and Meritservus decided to rewrite history.

events.title: Roman Abramovich aides falsified paperwork to disguise assets and dodge tax, records suggest
events.summary: Accountancy firm Deloitte Cyprus among those that appear to have backdated records outlining the Russian billionaire’s assets A ides of Roman Abramovich – including staff at the global accountancy firm Deloitte – falsified paperwork mapping the oligarch’s sprawling offshore business empire, records suggest, helping his businesses dodge tax and disguise assets. New analysis of leaked corporate records uncovers what appears to have been a long-running and carefully orchestrated strategy of backdating documents. The Russian billionaire’s closest aide, London-based Eugene Tenenbaum, appears to have been involved in the backdating and may also have given false evidence to the UK high court during a potentially costly lawsuit, the papers indicate. Abramovich’s personal and financial affairs are now restricted, owing to sanctions imposed by the UK and EU in response to Russia’s war on Ukraine. But the documents raise questions about how Abramovich was able to shield his financial affairs from the authorities for more than a decade, with the apparent assistance of apparatchiks and blue-chip advisers. The findings are based on the Cyprus Confidential leak , more than 500,000 documents, first released to the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ) and analysed by organisations including the Guardian, the Bureau of Investigative Journalism and the BBC. The digital paper trail charts the reorganisation of billions of pounds that the former Chelsea FC owner obtained via the controversial acquisition of oilfields in the frozen wastes of Siberia, amid the break-up of the Soviet Union. From 1999 until at least 2013, a cadre of aides and accountants tasked with shifting the funds between offshore jurisdictions deployed tactics that experts say may have constituted fraud and tax evasion. This, it seems, involved backdating documents to create a convenient paper trail showing that agreements and transactions had taken place years earlier. Lawyers for Abramovich denied any wrongdoing and said he relied on the advice of his advisers and Deloitte Cyprus. Tenenbaum denied any wrongdoing and said he also relied on the specialist advice given by Deloitte Cyprus. Deloitte Cyprus said that it “acts in compliance with all applicable laws” and that it could no longer access the relevant material because of the time that has elapsed. A crown jewel in Russia’s rich seam of natural resources, Sibneft’s oilfields fell into Abramovich’s hands during the chaotic post-Soviet privatisation era. The famously shrewd entrepreneur obtained the business for roughly $250m, reportedly spending as little as $19m of his own money. By the time he sold the last of his shares to Gazprom in 2005, Abramovich had raised $16bn, money he ploughed into investments, mansions, superyachts and Chelsea FC. One Cyprus-based company, Kravin Investments, was among several early vehicles through which that cash flowed. Kravin received a $3bn windfall in May 2003, of which it retained about $2bn. The money sat in Kravin’s bank account or was loaned to other companies, accruing interest that was, in theory, taxable in Cyprus. But Abramovich’s aides soon began devising plans to “eliminate” a tax liability that one financial adviser warned could be “very large”, records suggest. The gatekeeper to Abramovich’s fortune was Demetris Ioannides, who was the chair of Deloitte Cyprus before spinning out his own business Meritservus. That firm became Abramovich’s go-to financial advisory, serving him for nearly 20 years, before it was sanctioned by the UK in 2023 , along with Ioannides, for its role helping Russian oligarch hide their wealth. “It will be necessary to change the [Kravin’s] financial statements and the accounting records accordingly for 2003 and 2004,” Ioannides wrote in an August 2005 email, citing discussions with Deloitte Cyprus partners and erstwhile colleagues Antonis Taliotis and Nicos Charalambous. The following month, in an email copying in staff at Meritservus and Abramovich’s investment vehicle, Millhouse, Taliotis appeared to agree. “Certain changes will have to be made to the accounts […]” he wrote. Millhouse and Meritservus duly began producing paperwork showing that Kravin was simply holding and investing the Sibneft billions as a trustee for another business, the British Virgin Islands-based Kelvedon Worldwide. Documents detailing this supposed fact, including correspondence and trust agreements, were given dates between March and December 2003, despite being created at least two years later. The result was simple: although the billions had sat in Kravin’s accounts for years, it now appeared that the money had never really been Kravin’s at all. Deloitte Cyprus, apparently aware of the deception, duly signed off the accounts. History had effectively been rewritten, analysis of the documents suggests, disappearing $2bn from Kravin’s balance sheet – and with it any tax liability.
