events.title: Environmental watchdog to review new Kimberley gas project
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Buru Energy sends gas project for EPA approval, saying it could power northern WA by 2029 Buru Energy's proposed Rafael conventional gas project in the Canning Basin. ( Suplied: Buru Energy ) Buru Energy has referred its Rafael conventional gas project to WA's Environmental Protection Authority for assessment. Environmentalists claim it could be a "Trojan horse for fracking" — something the company rejects. Buru expects a decision from the EPA by the end of the year. The company behind a proposed gas project in Western Australia's Kimberley says it could meet the region's power demands with locally produced energy for the first time. Buru Energy referred its Rafael conventional gas project to WA's Environmental Protection Authority (EPA) for review in early October. The proposal involves developing a facility at the project site, located in the Kimberley's Canning Basin about 85 kilometres south of Derby, to process conventional gas from two co-located production wells. Conventional gas is natural gas extracted using simple drilling and pumping methods, as opposed to unconventional extraction methods like hydraulic fracturing, or fracking. Well testing underway at Buru Energy's Rafael conventional gas project. ( Supplied: Buru Energy ) Buru executive chairman David Maxwell said the Rafael project was the only proven conventional gas and liquids resource in the greater Kimberley region. "At the moment, the Kimberley relies on imported energy … from Karratha, Perth, Darwin, and Asia," he said. He said the Rafael project would improve energy security and be cost-effective, with reduced road traffic another potential benefit. Up to 300 tonnes of Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) would be produced at the Rafael plant per day — the equivalent of about 16 or 17 terajoules of energy — alongside LPG and condensate. Mr Maxwell said the Kimberley used between six and 13 terajoules per day for power generation, with the amount varying based on the time of year. "We'll also supply beyond the Kimberley into, for example, the northern Pilbara. "In the case of LPG, we would be supplying in the order of a quarter to a third of the Kimberley's LPG demand." The West Australian government has banned fracking in over 98 per cent of the state, but this does not include parts of the Kimberley including the Canning Basin. Earlier this year, WA's EPA recommended a fracking proposal by Black Mountain Energy subsidiary Bennett Resources go ahead subject to conditions. The Valhalla Gas Exploration and Appraisal Program would see up to 20 exploration and appraisal wells drilled in the basin. A record 8,000 appeals were lodged against the project. Community members gather in Broome to protest the Valhalla fracking proposal. ( ABC Kimberley: Dunja Karagic ) When asked about the fracking proposal in Broome this month, WA Mines Minister Daniel Pastorelli said the method had drawn varied perspectives. "I understand everyone has differing views on these types of things and I respect that completely," he said. "Obviously our policy and our approach is based on science, and that is what we're doing when it comes to hydraulic fracturing." Daniel Pastorelli acknowledges fracking is a controversial topic. ( ABC News: Keane Bourke ) Environmentalists have expressed concern Buru's Rafael project, although a conventional gas project, could pave the way for fracking to occur in the future. Environs Kimberley executive director Martin Pritchard said Rafael "could be a Trojan horse for fracking". "They (Buru) might be saying right now that they're not intending on fracking, but their statements to the ASX clearly say that they want to undertake fracking in the future," he said. Buru's David Maxwell rejected the accusation. "It's got nothing to do with fracking at all," he said. "And if there was any fracking involved — and I stress there is not — that would be a separate [EPA] referral, a separate application and a separate approval process and we're not in that process at all." Buru Energy's Yulleroo 2 wellhead 60 kilometres east of Broome was fracked in 2010. ( ABC Kimberley: Ben Collins ) The company previously used the hydraulic fracturing technique at its Yulleroo gas field also in the Canning Basin, but Mr Maxwell said it no longer did so. "We do not currently practice hydraulic fracturing," he said. "In the past Buru has, but Buru has put that on the shelf, and at the moment we have no plans for fracture stimulation." Mr Pritchard said solar and batteries, rather than gas fields, were the way forward for cheaper and cleaner electricity in the Kimberley.

events.title: Six senators call for Trump administration to 'immediately reverse course' on Russian diesel plan
events.summary: A bipartisan group of six senators are calling on President Donald Trump’s administration to “immediately reverse course” on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia as part of an effort to lower high fuel prices WASHINGTON -- A bipartisan group of six senators on Sunday called for President Donald Trump's administration to “immediately reverse course” on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia as part of an effort to lower high fuel prices. Trump shocked lawmakers when he announced on social media Friday that he struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call. He said Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the American and global market, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote. Four Republican senators and two Democratic senators signed onto the statement released Sunday in protesting the deal. They said the administration failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation to justify its decision as required by statute. “The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course,” they wrote. The Republican senators who signed onto the statement are Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Curtis of Utah. The Democratic senators are Sens. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut. Tillis, in an interview that aired Sunday on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” said there's a legitimate case for saying the president is not following the law if the administration goes through with its diesel purchase plan. “We were very clear that Russia is the aggressor. Russia is the one who can end this war by backing out of territory that they occupied,” Tillis said. Trump's announcement came just a few weeks after Congress passed legislation that directed Trump to impose substantial tariffs on the top importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports. The congressional effort was aimed at cutting the flow of money Russia receives from oil and gas sales to finance its war against Ukraine. The lawmakers also noted that Congress explicitly banned Russia energy imports in 2022 to prevent the United States from financing the war. “Congress was clear: the U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO Allies,” the six lawmakers wrote in their statement. “President Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law.” Sen. John Barrasso, R-Wyo., said Trump is focused on reducing the cost of energy when asked whether the president's action would be in violation of U.S. law. 8 people, including 2 kids, pregnant woman, killed at home: Police Man attacked by tiger after entering enclosure at England wildlife park Hasan execution will be live-streamed, Pentagon official says “The president is balancing and has to make tough decisions,” Barrasso said on CBS's “Face the Nation.” He also encouraged Trump to enforce the sanctions law that Congress passed last month. “This is just another point of leverage for the president to use against Putin in an effort to get a long-term solution in that part of the world,” Barrasso said. Energy experts say the Russia deal is unlikely to make a dent in high prices at the pump. Richard Nephew, a senior research scholar at Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy, noted that the total amount of diesel appears to be less than what the U.S. uses in a day. Nephew argued that Iran and Russia might benefit more than the U.S. “The Iranians are probably very excited because it shows that there’s a lot of pressure still on the U.S. And the Russians are excited because it puts a big hole in the sanctions regime,” he said. Trump has recently sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran , which has elevated world energy prices. Associated Press writer Mae Anderson in New York contributed to this report. events.title: Buttigieg gambles on a different path for 2028
events.summary: Pete Buttigieg has been able to campaign for Democrats across the country more than many of his potential 2028 rivals this past year. One reason: He doesn't have a job. That's by choice. Buttigieg said no when top Democrats urged him to run for governor or the U.S. Senate in Michigan this year. Why it matters: That decision is a gamble for Buttigieg's presidential ambitions. He's been able to build a national network over the last two years but hasn't added to his relatively thin resume as a former mayor of South Bend, Ind., and Joe Biden's transportation secretary. Buttigieg, 44, became a national political figure without following the typical path. He ran for president in 2020 as a small-town mayor and won the Iowa caucus by offering an optimistic vision and impressing voters with his communication skills — including in hostile environments. Driving the news: In early 2025, Democratic lawmakers and strategists including New York Sen. Chuck Schumer and former Michigan Sen. Debbie Stabenow urged Buttigieg — who had moved to Michigan — to run for office in his new state. Winning such an office, they argued, would help Buttigieg build his resume for a future White House run and give him a chance to distance himself from the unpopular Biden administration. Buttigieg passed, citing both a desire to stay home more with his husband and young twins, and figuring that he could still get his message out without being in the Senate. Instead, he set about building a larger national network among Democrats — particularly with Black voters in the South, where he had struggled in the 2020 Democratic primary. Buttigieg has traveled to 37 states since he left the Biden administration, Politico reported last week. Democratic candidates in vital swing districts and states have welcomed him to campaign for them this year while resisting offers from other potential presidential candidates such as former Vice President Kamala Harris , New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and California Gov. Gavin Newsom. In Buttigieg, many Democrats see a surrogate who can draw attention and crowds without the degree of negative attention that other prominent Democrats attract. Buttigieg also will campaign in key races in the final weeks before the Nov. 3 election. He's scheduled to be in Michigan and Virginia — which happen to hold early contests in the 2028 presidential primary. Between the lines: Buttigieg has tried to position himself as a candidate of the next generation who also has enough experience in the executive branch to be able to deliver. He's betting that the traditional ladder of running for president — becoming a senator, governor, or vice president first — no longer applies, especially after the Trump era. What they're saying: Buttigieg "knows what no one else on the Democratic side does, which is what it's actually like to run for this office — the pacing, the pressures and imperatives," David Axelrod, a former senior aide to President Obama and an outside adviser to Buttigieg in the past, told Axios. "At a time when the party and country will be searching for youth and forward-looking vision, he has the capacity to articulate one in a powerful way," Axelrod added. Axelrod said that if Buttigieg runs, "it will be because he feels the timing is right for someone like him, and the big mission is more compelling than the statewide races on which he took a pass." A Buttigieg spokesperson said that "when Pete decided not to run for office in Michigan, he promised he would still get to work to help candidates everywhere. He's been doing just that."

events.title: Turning AI Ambition into Real-World Advantage
events.summary: As enterprises race to adopt AI, Amitabh Sarkar, argues that AI’s real test is on infrastructure, and durable transformation will depend on converging networks, cloud, security, governance and trust. When executives talk about artificial intelligence today, they often talk in absolutes: an existential threat, a historic opportunity, the next great productivity leap. For Amitabh Sarkar, Tata Communications’ Vice-President, Asia Pacific and Japan, the more important story lies beneath the rhetoric and inside the data centres, networks and operating models trying to empower corporate ambition to meet their targets. “In the last 20 to 30 years, technology has moved from supporting the business, to enabling the business, to increasingly becoming the business,” he says. That shift has transformed corporate technology leadership. Once, CIOs were judged largely on uptime, efficiency and cost control. Today, the question is whether an enterprise has the infrastructure to launch new digital services across markets in weeks rather than months. For Tata Communications, the evolution has also been internal. Long associated with global connectivity, the company is positioning itself as a digital infrastructure and intelligence partner. The story is no longer only about pipes and bandwidth, but about platforms, AI readiness, cybersecurity and measurable business outcomes. A decade ago, customers came to Tata Communications with a simple request: connect one location to another. “Ten or fifteen years back, the prime reason clients talked to us was: can you connect country A to country B, data centre A to data centre B?” Sarkar recalls. “Transactional connectivity and interconnected data centres are all still important, but it’s now just one part of the story.” Enterprises today operate across multiple clouds, legacy and modern applications, overlapping cybersecurity tools and fragmented data. What they need is not another layer of complexity, but a partner who can simplify and orchestrate it. Tata Communications has built its business around that shift. Today, it positions itself as a digital infrastructure and intelligence partner. Its network fabric still underpins global connectivity, but it now sits alongside cloud and edge capabilities, security services, digital platforms and customer experience tools. The aim is to help enterprises connect, secure and control complex environments end to end. The story is no longer only about pipes and bandwidth, but about platforms, AI readiness, cybersecurity and measurable business outcomes. That evolution has changed not just what the company offers, but whom it serves. “Yesterday it was just the chief network officer,” Sarkar says. “Today the buying centre has expanded to several functions - the CMO, CDO, CTO, CIO and line-of-business leaders. Decisions on customer experience don’t always sit with IT any more.” As a result, Tata Communications’ teams have moved from selling technology to selling outcomes: revenue growth, cost efficiency, customer experience, resilience and security. The question is no longer whether a network is fast, but whether the architecture can support the business model the organisation wants to build. Sarkar’s view of the future begins with a contradiction at the heart of the AI boom. Boardrooms are moving quickly, but enterprise infrastructure is often the least regarded vector in the equation. “There is a widening gap between AI ambition and AI readiness,” he says. “Boardroom ambitions have perhaps moved faster than the infrastructure required to support these ambitions.” The mistake, he argues, is treating transformation as a purchase, and buying the latest model, tool or cloud service to automatically deliver transformation. “Technology is the easy part to buy,” he says. “The harder questions are those that technology alone cannot answer. What business outcome are you actually trying to change? Can your operating model support it? Can your data move across the organisation? Will your people adopt it? And can your infrastructure scale it securely?” Many companies can build impressive AI demonstrations quickly. The challenge is turning pilots into production systems connected to real workflows, governed data and secure infrastructure. Without that foundation, AI risks becoming a boardroom showcase rather than an operating advantage. The rise of AI agents will make those questions more urgent. Sarkar believes organisations may soon manage more digital agents than human employees. “You and I walk into an office with an ID card. Agents don’t,” he says. “How do you identify, govern and securely manage them? What are they allowed to access? What actions can they take? Can we trace why they made a decision and pivot quickly if it’s not the right move?” His conclusion is clear: the real AI story is increasingly an infrastructure story, not simply one about models and GPUs. Hybrid cloud is where many of the stress fractures are already visible.

events.title: askST Jobs: I keep having to pick up a colleague’s work. How should I raise it with my boss?
events.summary: An employee’s role is to highlight the issue and its impact, while managing the colleague’s performance is ultimately the manager’s responsibility. - Workers should raise workload concerns calmly, with clear examples of extra tasks, missed deadlines and work they covered for a colleague. - Experts say to avoid blame, scorekeeping and phrases like ‘pulling their weight’; focus on the impact on the team and ask for solutions. - Managers should be asked to clarify duties, rebalance work or reset priorities, while performance issues remain the boss’s responsibility. In this series, business correspondent Timothy Goh offers practical answers to candid questions on navigating workplace challenges and getting ahead in your career. Get more tips by signing up to The Straits Times’ Headstart newsletter . How can employees raise concerns about an uneven workload without blaming a colleague? Raising a genuine workload concern is not the same as complaining, but the difference lies in how employees present it, said Michelle Koh, managing director at executive search firm The Edge Partnership. “Raise the issue when you are calm rather than in a moment of frustration... If you approach your manager when emotions are running high, it can easily come across as a complaint about a person rather than a genuine concern about the work,” she said. Before speaking to their manager, employees should have specific examples ready, including the tasks they have taken over, deadlines they have stepped in to meet and instances where responsibilities have fallen back on them. “Avoid sweeping statements such as ‘I’m always doing their work’ unless you can back them up,” said Koh. “Keep the conversation focused on the impact on the work and the team – once it sounds like an attack on your colleague, it becomes personal and your point gets lost.” Koh noted that it also helps to remember that employees may not know the full circumstances behind a colleague’s performance. Their role is to highlight the issue and its impact, while managing the colleague’s performance is ultimately the manager’s responsibility. “Above all, go into the conversation looking for a solution... Ask whether responsibilities can be clarified, workloads redistributed or priorities reset,” she said. Tan Weixi, managing partner at Workplace Asia, said the biggest mistake employees can make when raising concerns about a colleague is framing the issue around whether the person is “pulling their weight”. “That is a judgment, and it puts the boss in the uncomfortable position of having to referee between two employees,” he said. Employees should also avoid keeping a running scorecard of every mistake and instead focus on patterns that genuinely affect the delivery of work, Tan said. Where appropriate, they could speak to the colleague first, as there may be circumstances that they are unaware of. “Don’t make your boss the judge of your colleague. Make your boss aware of the work problem – and be clear about what you need them to help resolve,” he said. Timothy Goh is a business correspondent at The Straits Times. He covers commodities and currencies, with occasional forays into listed companies.

events.title: Aaron Sorkin’s ‘The Social Reckoning’ is off to a weak start
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. “The Social Reckoning,” Aaron Sorkin’s follow-up to “The Social Network,” is on track to make only $5.5 million at the domestic box office this weekend, according to Sunday estimates. That’s below the already underwhelming $7 million to $8 million the studio had projected, and it means Sorkin’s new movie is unlikely to become a “Social Network”-sized hit. The earlier film had a $22 million opening weekend and made a total of $97 million domestically (and that’s at 2010 ticket prices). It also won Sorkin an Oscar and became one of most influential on-screen depictions of Silicon Valley and startup culture. Beyond the fate of a single film, the weekend box office could also offer hints about audience excitement, or lack thereof, as we kick off a fall full of movies starring villainous, real-world tech CEOs . There’s Alex Gibney’s four-hour documentary “Musk” (which also opened this weekend), Nathan Fielder’s apparently uncategorizable Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything” (coming next weekend!), and the OpenAI boardroom drama “Artificial” (which has a new distributor after being dropped by Amazon). Outside of theaters, Netflix also has a series called “The Altruists” coming in November , telling the story of Sam Bankman-Fried and the collapse of FTX. As for “The Social Reckoning,” while “The Social Network” was a notable success, the theatrical landscape has changed significantly in the last 16 years. And where the first film focused on the excitement and drama of Facebook’s early days, the sequel is darker and heavier — it’s all about whistleblower Frances Haugen’s decision to leak what became known as the Facebook files. So maybe a movie about Senate hearings and algorithm changes was never going to be a big hit. Or maybe the real audience is among older moviegoers who have only returned sporadically to theaters . And I wonder if critiquing Facebook feels a bit less urgent to audiences who are more likely to be losing sleep over AI. Maybe just as importantly, the new movie’s reviews just aren’t very good . (For what it’s worth, I enjoyed “The Social Reckoning” but will fully admit that it’s overloaded with Sorkin’s trademark speechifying. And I couldn’t help dreaming about a version directed — like the original — by David Fincher, with a score by Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross.) “Musk,” meanwhile, made $69,000 during its opening weekend in four theaters. It will roll out more broadly in the coming weeks, but given its length and subject matter, the documentary will probably reach many more viewers once it starts streaming on HBO Max. events.title: Mildura and South Australia connected by bus service after six-year hiatus
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts New bus service re-establishes link between Mildura and South Australia The Monty Express can drop Mildura residents off in South Australia, and SA residents off in Mildura. ( ABC News: Wade Stephens ) The Monty Express coach will re-establish a direct road transport link between Mildura, Renmark and Adelaide. The route has not been serviced in almost six years. The service will make its first interstate journey on October 12. A new bus service has launched connecting Mildura in Victoria's north-west to South Australia. From this week, a bus named The Monty Express will be travelling the Sturt Highway between Sunraysia and Adelaide via Renmark. It has been nearly six years since the route was serviced, with Greyhound Australia canning its Mildura to Adelaide coaches in 2016 , and another bus company ceasing its operations in 2020, in the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic. The lone direct flight between Mildura and Adelaide also no longer exists, with Rex Airlines terminating the service in May 2023. Ever since, getting into the festival state from Mildura involved detours via Ouyen, Horsham or Broken Hill, or at greater cost, flying to Adelaide via Melbourne or Sydney. The Monty Express will start taking passengers from October 12. ( ABC News: Wade Stephens ) Former Sunraysia resident Stuart Saunders ran a survey six months ago to gauge interest in restoring a Mildura to Adelaide bus service. He said support was overwhelming, and he soon prepared to pivot from his information technology career to become a bus driver. He purchased a 36-seat bus, which he named The Monty Express after the family's pet Cavoodle, Monty. "There's very much a sense of community in the coach industry," he said. Stuart Saunders and his family in front of their new business venture. ( ABC News: Wade Stephens ) The Mildura–Renmark–Adelaide service begins today. It will initially run twice a week, departing Adelaide on Mondays and Thursdays and returning on Tuesdays and Fridays. It will run as an express service with pick-ups at Mildura, Renmark, Adelaide Airport and the Adelaide Central Bus Station. Under a service agreement with the SA government, The Monty Express cannot pick up South Australian residents unless they go to Mildura. Stuart Saunders with his children, Matilda and Gabriel, wife, Melody and dog, Monty. ( ABC News: Wade Stephens ) The agreement exists to avoid impacting passenger numbers on the existing Stateliner coach service route between the Riverland and Adelaide. Mildura man Steven Haby describes himself as a transport enthusiast. The former Melburnian is a member of the Bus and Coach Society of Victoria and the Australian Timetable Association. He will be travelling from Mildura to Adelaide to experience the first service of The Monty Express on Monday. Steven Haby has booked his ticket on The Monty Express. ( Supplied: Steven Haby ) "I'm very much an advocate and supporter of public transport," Mr Haby says. "I thought this was a really good opportunity to support the service going forward and be one of the first passengers on the run. "You can have a sustainable public transport network in a city like Mildura … making it frequent, reliable, cheap, and to places where people want to go." Mr Saunders hopes The Monty Express will not only benefit Mildura residents, but will connect people in the Riverland with Sunraysia's V/Line bus services and flights. "Not only are we trying to give an express service into Adelaide from Mildura, but the challenges for the Riverland people trying to get into Mildura, I'm hoping we can solve some of their problems as well," he said. Tamille Hunter is a resident of Cobdogla, a South Australian town less than two hours from Mildura by car. Ms Hunter is unable to drive and has occasionally used existing transport options to get to Mildura. The journey she took involved catching a bus to Adelaide, a flight to Melbourne, a train to Swan Hill and a bus to Mildura. The Monty Express can seat as many as 36 passengers. ( ABC News: Wade Stephens ) "At the moment, for us to go to Mildura it takes us 24 hours and over $600," Ms Hunter said. She said getting The Monty Express to Mildura would open up lots of opportunities for her. "From there, I could visit my family and friends in Melbourne on the V/Line," she said. events.title: Ongoing Birdsville Track closure hits outback businesses
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Birdsville Track's long-term closure hurting outback businesses Cooper Creek over the Birdsville Track, in June 2025. ( Supplied: Marree Roadhouse ) The Birdsville Track has been closed for 400 days of the past two years. The road is a major freight and tourism route cutting through outback South Australia and Queensland. Part of the track is expected to reopen next week, while northern sections could remain closed for many months. One of Australia's most iconic outback roads has been closed for 400 days out of the past two years due to rain damage, with remote businesses feeling the pinch. Stretching more than 500 kilometres, the Birdsville Track connects Birdsville in south-west Queensland, to Marree in far-north South Australia. It provides access to local pastoral properties to move cattle, allows stock to flow to the South Australian market and has become increasingly popular with outback tourists. The track is largely unsealed, meaning flooding and heavy rain have periodically closed the track over the years — but never for this long. Despite the challenges, Lyall Oldfield is "very happy" living in the outback. ( Supplied: Marree Roadhouse ) Marree Roadhouse owner Lyall Oldfield said his business was "probably one third of what it normally is". "It's just dreadful what's happening with the roads. It's not even a joke." Business at the Marree Roadhouse is one third of what it normally is. ( Supplied: Marree Roadhouse ) About 230km north of Marree is the Mungerannie Hotel, which was taken over by new owners in 2023. Three years later, the business has not opened all year, with road closures stopping the daily water deliveries it relies on. Cattle coming off Clifton Hills Station on the Birdsville Track in South Australia after flooding. ( Supplied: Pete Nunn ) Co-owner Andrew Norman said it was a similar tale in 2025, when there was "no sort of season whatsoever". Mr Norman said the closure north of Mungeranie is having the biggest impact, deterring tourists from making the trip. The Birdsville Track has sustained significant damage from rain events. ( Supplied: Department for Infrastructure and Transport ) Mungerannie Hotel secures water source The owners of the Mungerannie Hotel on the Birdsville Track will now truck 13,000 litres of water to the pub each day, after being told they can no longer use a nearby bore. "Nobody's really coming up to Mungeranie to turn around and go back," Mr Norman said. "If they can get that road open just north of us and get the Birdsville Track open, next year should be fine. "If the track is open, we'll be open. But without a track, we're not open." The SA Department for Infrastructure and Transport hoped to reopen the 200km section between Marree and Mungeranie "next week", but the route north of Mungeranie is expected to remain closed for some time. Large parts of the Birdsville Track remain underwater. ( Supplied: Department of Infrastructure and Transport ) Regional north and outback road maintenance manager Juanita Chester said with some northern parts of the Birdsville Track still underwater, it would be "several more months before [the department] can even consider reopening". While the construction of a single-lane access route has been considered, Ms Chester said the local pits where materials are sourced have flooded too. The track has sustained damage from several significant rain events in the past 24 months. ( Supplied: Department for Infrastructure and Transport ) "They're like a dam when it rains, they fill with water," she said. "If we can't get in there to get material, there's very little we can do short of carting material from a long, long way away, which then impacts the roads." The department is assessing the scope and price of the remaining work, which will then require approval before it can begin, and Ms Chester said this would be unlikely in the next two months. events.title: From crane rental to marine transport: How this third-gen leader is steering his family business up the value chain
events.summary: Led by Michael Ang, Tiong Woon Corporation, multiple award winners at the Singapore Corporate Awards 2026, is investing in talent and engineering expertise to take on haulage and large-scale projects Tiong Woon Corporation chief executive officer Michael Ang is steering the third-generation family business beyond its crane-rental roots. It is past midnight in Pasir Ris. With sections of the road closed to traffic, massive precast girders are lifted, manoeuvred into position and lowered onto their supports for a new flyover. Beam-launching work like this is usually done overnight, when there is enough space to move heavy equipment safely with minimal disruption to other road users. Behind the operation is Tiong Woon Corporation, whose role in projects like this reflects how far the business has moved beyond its beginnings in crane rental and transport. In recent years, the 48-year-old family business has expanded into engineering and marine services, allowing it to take on bigger and more complex projects. Its fleet has grown with that ambition: The company now operates several hundred cranes, with the single largest rated at 2,200 tonnes. “A lot of people still perceive Tiong Woon as purely a crane rental company,” says chief executive officer Michael Ang. “Crane rental is still our core business, but we also offer marine, transport and engineering services. We want to show our clients and stakeholders that we can provide a more integrated solution.” For Ang, who joined the company 23 years ago, the transformation is also part of his role as the third-generation leader of his family business. Tiong Woon’s first 300-tonne crane, acquired from Soon Douglas in 1987. His grandfather, the late Ang Choo Kim, founded Tiong Woon in 1978 with a single 20-tonne crane. Two years later, the business was incorporated as Tiong Woon Crane & Transport by the next generation of the family. Today, Ang represents the third generation of leadership, while his father, Ang Kah Hong, serves as executive chairman and his uncle, Ang Kha King, remains on the board as an executive director. His family’s involvement across several generations has deepened his understanding of how far the company has evolved from its beginnings as a crane and transport operator. Over the past five years, Tiong Woon has worked towards an integrated model that combines its heavy lift equipment with its haulage and marine fleet and engineering expertise. Instead of supplying a crane or vehicle, it aims to take on more parts of a project and provide customers with a more complete heavy lift solution. For contractors and project owners, that can mean dealing with one company rather than coordinating several across different stages of a job. The Tiong Woon team dismantling a 200-tonne gantry crane at PSA Singapore, an example of the more integrated heavy-lift work the company now undertakes. The company is also expanding into new sectors. Oil and gas, petrochemical and construction firms have traditionally made up the bulk of its customer base. Data centres, semiconductors and biopharmaceuticals are newer targets. In February 2026, the company announced more than $40 million worth of projects across the semiconductor, public infrastructure and biopharmaceutical sectors, ranging from crane deployment to lifting engineering and project support. But taking on more complex work requires more than a larger fleet and workforce. Today, the company has about 1,300 employees across Singapore and markets including Malaysia, Thailand, India and Saudi Arabia, and is looking to hire more crane operators, engineers and technicians as the business expands. As the company tries to move up the value chain, its next stage of growth will depend not only on adding physical assets, but on building the human expertise needed to take on bigger projects and new revenue streams. A 4,500-tonne module being loaded out at Laem Chabang, Thailand, where Tiong Woon is expanding its heavy-lift capabilities. In the last financial year ended June 2026 (FY2026), the wage bill reached $65 million, about a third of revenue. “Our single largest investment is actually our human capital,” says group chief financial officer William Tan. The challenge is particularly apparent in Singapore, where Tiong Woon has more cranes than operators, Tan says, reflecting the shortage of skilled trades workers in the built environment sector. Knowing when to move, and when to wait In December 2023, Tiong Woon formed a strategic alliance in Thailand with Netherlands-headquartered heavy lift specialist Mammoet and acquired heavy lift, haulage and transportation equipment to strengthen its capabilities and position in the market. The move reflects the broader direction of the business: using the heavy lift expertise it has built in Singapore over decades as a base to take on a larger and more complex role in overseas projects.

events.title: China’s debt interest costs are soaring above U.S. levels and growing faster than any other budget category as Beijing struggles to prop up growth
events.summary: The world is flooded with debt, but while the U.S. and Europe have caused angst on global markets lately, China’s fiscal situation isn’t looking so great either. In fact, China’s debt has shot up so much in recent years that interest payments on all its borrowing are commanding a bigger share of public spending. Debt-servicing payments will account for 19.2% of the central government’s general public budget this year, up from 12% in 2014, according to new Conference Board estimates cited by the Financial Times . That tracks with a separate report earlier this year from the Center for Strategic and International Studies , which found that 19% of Beijing’s spending is earmarked for interest on debt. That’s more than the 14% of the U.S. federal budget that goes to interest costs, though less than Japan’s 25.6%. CSIS added that China’s spending on interest payments skyrocketed 341% between 2013 and 2025, faster than any other major budget category. By comparison, total spending jumped 102% in that span, with outlays on social security and employment up 207%, science and technology up 137%, and defense up 141%. To be sure, U.S. debt-interest spending looks grim, too, and has surged about 390% since 2013 to $1 trillion, which also tops the Pentagon’s budget. But the world’s two biggest economies have been diverging in key ways with implications for future growth and indebtedness. The U.S. economy is accelerating, helped by the AI boom, and despite high inflation, resilient consumers have continued to spend. Unemployment is low and signals full employment, while stock markets are at or near record highs. Of course, hyperscalers are racing to issue bonds to fund their data centers and chip purchases, but they are also raising money with fresh stock offerings and IPOs. Meanwhile, China’s GDP has been decelerating and is on pace to undercut its annual target of 4.5% to 5%. And while export-facing sectors are growing at a fast clip, trade partners are putting up barriers; Chinese consumers remain reluctant to spend; investment is weak; the property sector is still digging out from an epic crash; and Chinese stocks have been anemic. Beijing has also steered state banks to provide financing to priority industries like electric vehicles, robotics, artificial intelligence, and renewable energy. But under pressure to lend, many loans went to questionable borrowers. Business debt has doubled since 2019, while revenues are only 30% higher. Creditors continue to roll over loans to keep struggling firms afloat, even as nearly a third of them are losing money. China’s state-led growth model now looks like it’s running out of steam, and the rapidly expanding mountain of debt is a warning sign as local governments often seek to boost favored industries with low-cost loans. According to the International Monetary Fund , China’s general government gross debt hit 107% of GDP this year, up from 41% in 2015 and on a path to reach 124% in 2030. A broader measure of indebtedness across the public and private sectors reveals an even worse picture. China’s total debt-to-GDP ratio, excluding the financial sector, doubled since 2010 and has now topped 300%, Capital Economics estimated earlier this year. But in the U.S., total public and private debt  last year was about 265% of GDP, down sharply from pandemic-era highs. Not only has China’s debt boom hit diminishing returns, but it’s also becoming a drag on the economy. “The irony is that one driver of both government borrowing and the lax lending standards of [state-owned] banks is the desire to prop up economic growth and prevent job losses,” Mark Williams, chief Asia economist at Capital Economics, wrote in May. “But the product of a credit boom that has been underway for 18 years is a banking system propping up unproductive firms, widespread losses across industry, and entrenched overcapacity.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: This intelligence building is top secret. Here's what we know about it
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts This National Security Office Precinct will cost more than $1 billion. What do we know about it? Some details about the National Security Office Precinct were revealed to Senate estimates in May. ( ABC News: Callum Flinn ) A stone's throw from Parliament House, six giant cranes have been working on the biggest Commonwealth construction project in Canberra in almost 40 years. The development of a National Security Office Precinct has been heralded by the federal government as a solution to "critical accommodation and capability requirements" of several agencies. Despite the huge scale of the project, many of the details have been kept secret. We know the precinct in Barton will be utilised by a range of Commonwealth entities. That includes the Office of National Intelligence and the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT). In Senate estimates in May, we heard some details and there may be more to come. Construction of the National Security Office Precinct in Canberra continues. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) "We are engaging with other agencies as part of the development for the precinct going forward," said Nick McClintock of the Department of Finance, which is leading the development. Next to the main buildings, there will also be hospitality and retail venues, servicing both the wider public and workers in the precinct. Up to 5,000 workers are expected to be based at the precinct. At the sod turning for the project, Finance Minister and ACT senator Katy Gallagher said a "purpose built" and "specifically designed" building was needed to allow the national intelligence community "to do the work they need to do in a changing world". "[It's] clearly needed in terms of our national security agencies being able to work in a facility that actually allows them to do their job properly." Katy Gallagher says the new building will be more secure. ( ABC News: Pete Garnish ) She said the precinct would be "more appropriate" and "more secure" than existing buildings, with several government agencies reaching, or at, capacity. The project's price tag has not been revealed because of "commercial-in-confidence and national security sensitivities". But, we know it will cost at least $1 billion. "It is the most significant investment we've seen in the territory in a long time," Senator Gallagher said in 2023. The total cost of the precinct is expected to be revealed publicly once it's completed. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) She also told Senate estimates "it is a very significant infrastructure spend" and she has also described it as a "multi-year billion-dollar investment". The final cost is expected to be revealed publicly, but only after construction is completed. The precinct is the biggest Commonwealth construction project in Canberra since the development of the new Parliament House, which opened in 1988. Senator Gallagher has previously rejected claims Canberra had missed out on its fair share in recent federal budgets, pointing to the precinct as an example of spending in the territory. Construction is expected to be completed by the end of 2028, with the precinct starting to be occupied from 2029. The federal government has said the project will support more than 10,000 jobs over the construction period, which commenced in late 2024. The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade is consolidating its presence in the ACT into two new buildings. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) Due to the "security requirements" of the project, it was exempt from needing the green light of the public works committee, which scrutinises major public capital expenditure projects. We also haven't seen any artist impressions or plans for the precinct, which means we won't know exactly what it will look like for a while yet. The precinct is being built on the site of a former car park. What happens to the buildings after agencies move out? A Department of Finance spokesperson said as existing buildings were "privately owned commercial properties", their future use was a commercial decision for the landlords. We know DFAT is consolidating its presence in the ACT into two new buildings — the precinct and another new building also being built in Barton. The head office of the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade will be vacated. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) It means its current head office, the RG Casey building, will be vacated. The lease is due to run out in 2031, and as noted by the department, its future after that will be up to the private landlord. It was revealed in Senate estimates in June that staff will be moved into the new precinct as soon as they are "reasonably able to".

events.title: Trump bears down on Zelensky as Russia keeps up attacks on Ukraine
events.summary: President Trump's announcement Sunday about an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine referred to a potential deal that includes each side stopping attacks on oil refineries — and he expects Volodymyr Zelensky to abide by it, a White House official said. The official said if attacks on oil refineries cease, a deal to stop hitting power plants and energy grids could come next. Why it matters: Trump appears to be singlehandedly trying to will a partial ceasefire into existence. But for now Russia hasn't accepted any kind of ceasefire — and Ukraine wants one that forbids attacks on power plants. Reality check: The "refinery for refinery" proposal, as the official dubbed it, is lopsided. A Ukrainian official told Axios that the country has a single oil refinery which the Russians have attacked multiple times and isn't fully functional. Russia, by contrast, has a vast network of refineries. "We import diesel and gas. What we need is for the Russians to stop attacking our electricity grid," the Ukrainian official said. "The Russians are thinking about" it, the White House official said. "We will know soon if they are ready." Case in point: Hours after Trump's announcement, Russia conducted strikes on power plants in Ukraine, according to Ukrainian media. What he said: Trump's Truth Social post sounded at first like a major breakthrough. "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" he wrote. It appears much more tenuous than that. Zelensky said the announced ceasefire "was news for me." State of play: After reaching a deal with Russia Friday to lift diesel sanctions, Trump remains focused on stopping Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. He believes the strikes are driving up U.S. gas prices. White House officials warn that Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries are hurting Zelensky's relationship with Trump more than they're damaging Russia. "Trump is really mad. He feels Zelensky is taking the U.S. for granted," the White House official said. Zoom in: Amid the crisis with Ukraine, presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have put their planned trip to Moscow on hold, at least until they get clarity on whether Ukraine and the Europeans are ready to agree to a new unified proposal for Putin. A Ukrainian official told Axios on Friday that during a meeting with U.S. negotiators in Miami on Friday, Witkoff and Kushner threatened that Trump could stop sharing U.S. intelligence if it continued to ignore his requests. A U.S. official denied that, saying Witkoff and Kushner told the Ukrainians that the U.S. was a strong partner, providing munitions and intelligence. Ukraine therefore shouldn't take actions that hurt American consumers, the two said. On Sunday, the Financial Times reported that the U.S. told European countries it might stop selling weapons to Ukraine through NATO if Ukraine continues to strike Russian refineries.

events.title: Insurer underpaid hundreds of NSW accident victims in 'mind-blowing' error
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts NRMA Insurance underpaid hundreds of injured motorists in NSW since 2019 NRMA Insurance initially estimated that about 700 people had been underpaid, a number later revised down to 400. ( Facebook: NRMA Insurance ) Hundreds of people injured in car accidents have been repaid by NRMA Insurance after the company miscalculated some compulsory third party benefits since 2019. The company said 700 people were affected but the number was later revised down to 400. Neither the insurer nor the State Insurance Regulatory Authority noticed the error. NRMA Insurance has been forced to repay hundreds of people who were injured in motor vehicle accidents, after failing to correctly calculate some compulsory third party (CTP) benefits since 2019. The original error was not detected by the insurer, nor was it noticed by NSW's State Insurance Regulatory Authority (SIRA), despite it having previously launched an audit of the company's practices. Instead, the mistake was spotted by a lawyer who realised their client's weekly payments did not add up. Neither the insurer nor the State Insurance Regulatory Authority picked up on the original error. ( Supplied ) Initially, NRMA Insurance estimated about 700 people who had been injured in motor vehicle accidents had been underpaid, before revising the number down to 400. However, the company told the ABC it had also identified a "further cohort" of people it believed were owed interest, after previously receiving lump sum payments. Greens MP Abigail Boyd said NRMA Insurance, a trading name of Insurance Australia Limited, should have been capable of indexing payments correctly. "It actually blows my mind," she said. Abigail Boyd says it was "extraordinary" that NRMA had not discovered the issue itself. ( Four Corners: Rob Hill ) She said it was "particularly extraordinary" that NRMA had not discovered the issue itself. "You have this massive power differential between these insurers and these injured people who are going through some of the worst times of their lives. "[Yet] it's somehow expected that [the victims] are the ones, or their lawyers … that will pick up these errors." Under the state's CTP scheme, people injured in motor vehicle accidents are entitled to income support payments if they are unable to work as a result. It starts at 95 per cent of their pre-accident weekly earnings, before dropping to a maximum of 85 per cent from 14 weeks onwards, depending on their capacity to work. The payments, made by CTP insurers like NRMA Insurance, are supposed to be adjusted twice a year, in line with average weekly earnings. The insurer markets itself as a "help company". ( Supplied: NRMA ) However, NRMA Insurance, which markets itself as "a help company", acknowledged it had incorrectly applied this principle, costing the average affected claimant $940. "We became aware in late April this year, through a customer's legal representative, that the statutory indexation may not have been correctly applied to weekly benefit payments for customers who continued receiving payments more than 78 weeks after their accident," a spokesperson said. "Our investigation confirmed an error in the application of indexation in our system, which has been corrected. We apologised to the customer, paid the amount outstanding (and interest) and notified the regulator." NRMA Insurance, which is a separate entity to the NRMA, said it had recently completed the process of repaying customers, along with the interest they were owed. "We sincerely apologised to all affected customers," the spokesperson said. This is not the first time NRMA Insurance has failed to properly pay the required weekly benefits to people who have been injured in motor vehicle accidents. In February 2023, SIRA issued a letter of censure to the company, after finding it had contravened NSW legislation and its licence conditions by underpaying more than 2,000 customers. NRMA Insurance repaid more than $735,000 to those affected, but it was not fined. In March the same year, another censure letter was issued over the late processing of weekly benefits. No fine was issued. And in June 2023, SIRA sent another censure letter to NRMA Insurance over delays in commencing weekly payments. No financial penalty was imposed. In 2023, NRMA Insurance had to repay more than $735,000 to people injured in car accidents. ( ABC News: Adriane Reardon ) Ms Boyd said SIRA's enforcement actions to date had given NRMA Insurance little incentive to raise its standards.

events.title: Gas shortage culprit to slip through reservation 'loopholes', say critics
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Critics say 'Santos-sized loopholes' will make gas reservation a joke Liquefied natural gas ships from Curtis Island in Queensland. ( Supplied: Photopia Studio ) Gas market players say the federal government's draft gas reservation scheme has been weakened by loopholes. They argue that changes to the policy favour the Santos-led GLNG venture, which has been blamed for rising prices on the east coast. The government is expected to release legislation for the scheme in the coming weeks. A giant LNG plant blamed by critics for driving up east coast gas prices could largely or totally escape a federal scheme designed to protect local buyers, observers have warned. The Albanese government last month released a draft plan to force gas exporters to set aside up to 20 per cent of their production for the domestic market in a bid to force prices lower. But analysts and industry players say the draft is full of loopholes that will allow some exporters to reduce or even eliminate their exposure. They point to the Gladstone LNG project, a plant on Curtis Island in Queensland that is operated by Adelaide-based Santos, as the exporter most likely to benefit. An ABC investigation revealed GLNG had sucked up and exported the equivalent of 20 per cent of eastern Australia's domestic gas demand over the past 10 years. This was because the venture built an LNG plant with a capacity of 7.8 million tonnes a year despite not having nearly enough gas of its own to fill it. By contrast, the other two LNG projects in Queensland — run by global super-major Shell and Australian company Origin along with US firm ConocoPhillips — had overwhelmingly been supplying the local market in net terms. Paul Farrow is unsympathetic to Santos. ( ABC News: Kit Mochan ) Australian Workers' Union (AWU) national secretary Paul Farrow said "Santos-sized loopholes" threatened to turn the government's reservation plans into a joke. Mr Farrow said that, compared with earlier iterations of the plan, the draft had been watered down in significant ways that appeared to favour GLNG above all others. "Australian industry and Australian consumers deserve to derive an advantage from Australia's gas because it's our sovereign wealth," Mr Farrow said. "The government is so close to getting it right. "But the exposure draft, as it stands, contains a bunch of Santos-sized loopholes. Curtis Island in Gladstone is home to three gas plants that export Australian gas. ( Supplied: Nearmap ) Under the draft policy, the Australian Energy Regulator would be able to reduce an exporter's supply obligation below 20 per cent, while the minister could cut it to zero. But critics say a raft of other provisions in the bill could enable Santos and its GLNG partners to slip the net themselves. They say the draft, unlike earlier iterations, effectively allows GLNG to count contract extensions as "existing contracts" that are exempt from consideration. Crucially, this would allow GLNG to extend a supply agreement with South Korea's KOGAS for five years from 2030. The current deal is for 3.5 million tonnes of LNG a year, an amount equivalent to about 40 per cent of annual east coast gas demand. Observers also say the draft will give rise to "take-or-pay" deals that allow Santos to generate paper sales to the domestic market without actually supplying any gas. And they argue the government has given too much ground to Santos over questions about whether the company can "reasonably" find enough gas without breaking export contracts. Mr Farrow said the provision should require Santos to explore all practical options, such as buying gas from other providers in the local market, substituting LNG cargoes from its international operations or using flexibility in its contracts to reduce overseas sales. Instead, he said the draft appeared to allow Santos itself to set those terms, which he argued the company would do so however it liked. "If a massive project like GLNG wants to claim that it simply doesn't have enough gas to share with the Australian market, it should have to prove it's actually explored all practical options to get hold of that gas," Mr Farrow said. "These options might incur a small cost for Santos' shareholders. The government hopes its reservation plans can encourage more gas wells. ( ABC News: Hamish Harty ) As well as these provisions, Mr Farrow said the draft contained other clauses that would allow GLNG off the hook. Among them was a so-called "additional gas" test. While Mr Farrow said the test was theoretically supposed to encourage new production and increase supplies, in reality he said it was likely to be gamed.

events.title: Citroen revives the 2CV for an electric age
events.summary: French carmaker Citroen has brought back its 2CV brand in a bid to boost sales of electric cars in a difficult market. The new model, unveiled at the Paris Motor Show, is a small city runabout with retro styling which harks back to one of the company's most famous designs. As a "concept car" intended to show Citroen's direction of travel, it is not yet ready to go on sale but the plan is to have a version in showrooms by 2028. As they face mounting competition from Chinese manufacturers, Citroen and other European brands are exploiting their heritage as a means of selling modern motors. Citroen chief executive Xavier Chardon described the new car as "a modern, ingenious and refreshing response to the mobility challenges of tomorrow". The original Citroen 2CV was launched in 1948, as Europe was recovering from the ravages of World War Two. It was designed as a cheap, robust way for French farmers and country folk to get around. The car had high wheel arches and soft suspension, letting it travel across a ploughed field or rough roads - as legend would have it, without breaking a tray of duck eggs. Its high roof let drivers wear a hat at the wheel. It was easy to drive and simple to repair. The car was so popular, it remained in production for more than 40 years. Over time, it went from being a utilitarian tool for the countryside to a cult classic, and a favourite of hippies and counter-culturalists. Fans of Citroën's 2CV hold annual meet-ups such as this muddy gathering in Switzerland Now, Citroen wants to draw on that heritage to sell an electric, small city car that is expected to sell for about £13,000. The look of the new 2CV may well evolve as Citroen develops its design. But as it stands, it shares plenty of styling features with its famous predecessor. The high, flared wheel arches, the tall, curved roof and the eye-like headlights are all reminders of the original "deux chevaux" or "two horses". By using memories of an old car to sell a new one, Citroen is following a well-travelled road. VW notoriously brought back the Beetle in the late 1990s, with limited success. BMW's Minis have always carried styling designed to hark back to the very British original. Fiat has been selling a retro-styled Fiat 500 for the past two decades. But the retro-nostalgia trend has accelerated recently, as carmakers have looked for ways to sell electric cars to sceptical consumers. Citroen's French rival, Renault, has led the charge. It started with the Renault 5 E-Tech, which visually echoed the distinctive boxy styling of the original Renault 5, once an ever-present sight on French streets. It has since revived the Renault 4 and Twingo brands as well. VW has the distinctive ID-Buzz minivan, a throwback to the classic T2 Transporter, while Ford is working on a new EV which is widely expected to be called the Fiesta. Rachel Burgess, senior editor of Autocar magazine, thinks it is a strategy that makes perfect sense. "It's a brilliant differentiator from all-new car brands", she says. "An older audience might remember the originals and feel warmly towards them, and a younger audience might find an appeal in the retro aspect." Finding new ways to make cars appealing has become more important than ever, at a time when European manufacturers are facing growing competition from Chinese brands. "Many in the industry believe the big automotive players in Europe…face a very serious existential threat from aggressive Chinese manufacturers," says David Leggett, automotive editor at Global Data. Back to the future: VW looked to the past when designing its ID-Buzz minivan In this hostile business environment, heritage and nostalgia could prove to be powerful weapons for more established brands, thinks automotive researcher and author Dr Paul Nieuwenhuis. "In a world where a wave of credible decent quality Chinese EVs are hitting Europe, linking European designs back to their history while using the latest powertrain technology is something the Chinese cannot do," he says. "The Chinese can establish new design trends, but there is limited history there." But Leggett thinks Citroen will need more than a heady whiff of nostalgia to turn its new car into a best-seller. "A reimagined Citroën 2CV should give a big nod to its ancestor - especially on price and design simplicity as well as visual cues," he says. "But it also needs to be a credible modern electric car in terms of functionality and features, with widespread appeal." events.title: Can the AI industry persuade data center opponents by getting rid of NDAs?
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Amazon recently followed Microsoft’s lead and said it will no longer use nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) while negotiating with local governments over data centers. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Sean O’Kane, Rebecca Bellan, and I discussed Amazon’s announcement, which came in the middle of a longer blog post making the case that data centers are actually good for communities. Rebecca was a bit skeptical that the recent spate of data center moratoriums will have a lasting effect, especially since the moratoriums only last for a year or two and “these data centers aren’t coming online for the next two, three, four, five years,” though I countered that data center backers definitely seem worried. Sean, meanwhile, suggested that a big reason for the backlash is the industry’s poor communication. “We’ve seen, through a lot of the controversy and backlash to AI and data centers, that the industry just does a really poor job explaining itself, and that they are obviously and constantly frustrated with the fact that most people can’t envision a world in which this stuff is useful for them,” he said. Keep reading for a preview of our conversation , edited for length and clarity. Sean: It’s an interesting thing that it was sort of buried in the blog post and part of a larger story that Amazon’s clearly trying to tell. I guess I understand why they weren’t putting it in the foreground, but to me, this is at the root of so many of the problems that the tech industry currently faces when it comes to AI broadly, but data centers in particular. There are so many things that could be said about whether or not people should be worried about the effect that data centers have on their property values, on their electricity bills, on their water usage in the area, and whether or not those things are real problems, inflated problems, etc. I think so much of that just really goes back to the fact that a lot of these projects are being negotiated essentially in secret. Sometimes they’re being negotiated [with the public knowing] that it’s a data center, but just not knowing who’s actually going to use it or occupy it at any point. This is a long-standing issue with the tech industry. I always go back to the mid-2010s when Uber was expanding really fast. Uber was one of the companies that really used this tactic a ton when it came to working with local governments. In particular, I remember I was working at The Verge at the time and we had a freelancer write a story about a city outside of Orlando where Uber was trying to negotiate tax subsidies to subsidize rides for people to use public transit after the Uber trip. The whole thing was negotiated in secret. And not only that, which was frustrating on its face, but also, because of the secrecy, you could just see Uber getting really comfortable with asking for a lot of other stuff, too. So there needs to be more of this. I’m glad Amazon’s doing this. We’ll see if it actually does have any positive effect, but people are pretty entrenched right now. Rebecca: Yeah, I’m curious about what effect this will have and whether it will lead to communities successfully delaying or or killing any infrastructure that the companies need to build. What I’ve heard from some people I’ve spoken to, who deal with data centers every day, a lot of these moratoriums that are getting passed — and there are a significant number of them, including one recently in San Francisco , which is pretty ironic — but they’re only for like a year or two years. But these data centers aren’t coming online for the next two, three, four, five years. All of the buildouts are going to be massively delayed for a number of reasons from zoning to funding. Of course, if the pushback keeps going, then it might have an effect, but I often wonder just how much of an effect this political pushback is having on this. Anthony: The moratorium I’m most familiar with is the one in New York . I believe it’s a one-year moratorium, and that’s on permits for large projects. [Technically, it’s until the state finalizes an environmental review process, which is expected to take a year.] So already, there’s some wiggle room within that. And often, they’re framed as: “It’s not like we think [data centers are] bad, let’s not do this. It’s [that] we need to take the time to study this.” Which gives them a lot of room to say later on, “Actually, we’ve decided this is great. We love it.” But you can tell that the people trying to build these data centers are worried, which is why you have these unhinged tweets from people like Trump or David Sacks. Only time will tell in terms of how long and how deep that [community] resistance is, but I do think they are worried.

events.title: Trump sticks with tariffs even as US voters turn against them before the midterms
events.summary: President Donald Trump shows no signs of budging from a trade policy that many Americans don't like as the midterm elections loom NEW YORK -- Maybe President Donald Trump really does believe that “tariff” is the most beautiful word in the dictionary . Despite higher prices, criticism from trade experts and displeasure among voters, Trump holds fast to his belief that imposing the highest import duties on U.S. trading partners since the Great Depression is a winner . A recent poll suggests that is a big gamble with less than a month before the Nov. 3 midterms. Most U.S. adults disapprove of his trade policies, with more than 64% saying he has gone too far with his latest tariffs, compared with 58% in January. A look at the political, legal and economic challenges to the Republican president's approach to trade. The United States has set taxes on imports from most countries in the low double digits, although the rates have gone up and down because of legal setbacks as well as Trump's habit of changing them seemingly on a whim . In the biggest round last year, Trump levied what he called “reciprocal” tariffs and other duties on dozens of countries. He cited a 1977 law that he said allowed him to act without congressional approval in an economic emergency. After the Supreme Court struck that down in February, Trump turned to an array of other trade laws to accomplish his goals. The primary one he is using now, Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 , allows him to impose tariffs on countries that he believes are engaging in unfair trade practices, such as not adequately enforcing a ban on forced labor. The new duties range from 10% to 12.5% on imports from 60 economies, including big U.S. trading partners such as the European Union, India, Japan, Canada and Mexico. Trump is taking a sledgehammer to a relatively open global trading system that many mainstream economists think has benefited the U.S. enormously. It has helped boost growth, keep prices low and make U.S. businesses more competitive and often dominant in global industries. The U.S. is the second-largest exporter in the world, after China. It exported $3.4 trillion in goods and services last year, far ahead of third place Germany’s $2.3 trillion. Although Trump claims foreign exporters are paying tariffs, it is mostly Americans who are footing the bill. Studies, including ones from New York Fed and Harvard , have shown that overseas companies have largely not lowered their prices to offset the tariffs that U.S. businesses pay at the border. Those businesses are absorbing the added costs or passing them along to consumers through higher prices. Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded 8 people, including 2 kids, pregnant woman, killed at home: Police Christa Pike asked 'Where am I?' after waking up following botched execution: Lawyer The White House responds that the factory boom is already underway and points to statistics showing that manufacturing jobs, after falling last year, are on the upswing and work in certain nonresidential construction trades is rising, too. “Factory construction jobs of today mean more manufacturing jobs down the road once those factories come online,” said White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers. In the four years after China joined the World Trade Organization in 2001, nearly 3 million U.S. manufacturing jobs were lost, accelerating a shift away from factory work. Even global trade enthusiasts recognize the damage. Many U.S. companies struggled to compete with an influx of discounted products from China, which has suppressed consumption to encourage exports It also is true that some countries have higher tariffs than the U.S., manipulate their currencies lower to ensure to make their exports to the U.S. cheaper and help industries with subsidies. But tariffs among U.S. major trading partners are low, often comparable to U.S. rates and sometimes lower. Before the trade war, the U.S. rate averaged 1.47% for goods from the European Union, slightly above the average 1.35% imposed by the EU on American products , according to the Brussels think tank Bruegel. Europeans are big buyers of what America wants to sell. About 30% of European imports are from U.S.-owned companies, according to the European Central Bank. The relationship with Canada, America's big trading partner to the north, was also similar before trade talks broke down this summer. Canada's effective tariff rate on U.S. imports was about 2.4%, less than half the 5% that the U.S. had on Canadian imports, according to calculations by Oxford Economics. Now the countries are mired in a tit-for-tat dispute, with both countries escalating tariffs on each other. Self-driving truck companies Aurora Innovation and Kodiak AI received a federal exemption this week that removes a massive barrier to commercialization. Under federal regulations, if a traditional big rig runs into trouble, the human driver must pull over, activate the hazard lights, and then physically place reflective warning triangles on the road within 10 minutes to alert other road users. But if a mechanical problem forces a self-driving truck to pull over, there’s no human driver to deploy those warning devices. It was a big enough hurdle that Aurora took federal safety regulators to court over the requirement. After the court denied its request for an exemption, the company escalated the fight to the District of Columbia Court of Appeals. (Companies did have a temporary waiver as it awaited a decision.) Now Aurora and other self-driving truck developers have been given the green light from the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration . The agency has granted a five-year exemption allowing companies to replace roadside warning devices, such as reflective warning triangles, with cab-mounted warning beacons. Check out Aurora’s first responders page to see how it works. Daniel Goff , vice president of external affairs at Kodiak AI, said the exemption will help the industry “usher in an autonomous era of freight movement on U.S. roads, one that can save lives and improve the efficiency of goods delivery.” Gerardo Interiano , Aurora’s head of government relations and public affairs, echoed that sentiment, saying the decision underscores the government’s recognition of the economic and community benefits of autonomous trucking. He described the high-visibility, cab-mounted warning beacons as a “critical, 21st-century solution that enhances roadside safety by immediately alerting other road users without ever needing to put a person in harm’s way.” One question I’m left with: Could these cab-mounted warning beacons eventually become standard equipment across the entire trucking industry?
